News.title: Manchester mayoral election results LIVE: Labour and Reform go to second round of votes after major delays
News.content:
Andy Burnham ally dismisses 'cash for tax cuts' call from Reform and Tory mayors

Andy Burnham will today be touting his policy to give local mayors a slice of income tax receipts from their areas for the first time - to invest back into their area.

But some mayors have suggested they could use the funding to give their residents a tax rebate.

Conservative Tees Valley mayor Lord Ben Houchen said he would “let families keep more of the money they earn”.

But Louise Haigh - a top Burnham ally and First Secretary of State - told Times Radio this morning: “I’m not convinced that it would be possible for him to set up a rebate scheme. We’d have to see the details of that, but it certainly isn’t possible at the moment…

“Those kind of schemes necessitate HMRC to set up full schemes, that’s just not possible at the moment.

“The way that the mayors are set up and work is to reinvest the money into their public services, into their local economies. It’s not possible at the moment.

“We’d have to see, obviously, plans and a scheme put forward by Ben Houchen, but that’s not how these powers and resources are intended to be used.”

News.title: Woman saw start of Suffolk wildfires and tried to stamp it out - but 'it went up like a torch'
News.content:
Woman saw start of Suffolk wildfires and tried to stamp it out - but 'it went up like a torch'

The Mirror captured the images on Dunwich Heath, near Sizewell nuclear power station, after firefighters took us inside the cordoned-off site in Suffolk

View 7 Images Emergency services near the scene of the wildfire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

Burnt out, blackened and still smouldering, this is part of the heartbreaking aftermath of the Suffolk wildfire.

‌



The Mirror captured the startling images on Dunwich Heath, near Sizewell nuclear power station, after firefighters took us inside the cordoned-off site, estimated to span 150 hectares - the size of 220 football pitches. Other poignant images showed firefighters covered in soot, rescue workers surrounded by the barren landscape and a camp site abandoned by residents and holidaymakers since the blaze began two days ago.

‌



Local resident Charlotte Du Cann today told how she witnessed the fire begin and tried to stamp it out with a friend before calling 999 at around 5pm on Wednesday. Speaking about the aftermath, Ms Du Cann told us: "It's just devastating and absolutely heartbreaking. It's like a bomb site".

‌



View 7 Images Two fire service workers being driven away from the site covered in soot (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily mirror)

The writer and editor, 70, said she and a friend were alerted to the fire after hearing the crackle of the blaze before smelling smoke near a kissing gate in woodland. She said: "I heard it first... this crackle. I thought 'that sounds like fire'. I looked down and my friend said 'I can smell smoke'.

"We went down and saw this circle on fire, maybe 20ft across. We tried to stamp it out, but it didn't work. We didn't have enough force. We were trying to stamp it out for a few minutes, but then it just caught the heather... umph... up it went, it hit the Scots pine and just got out of hand." Ms Du Cann added: "It went up like a torch - the noise of it was horrible. It escalated fast - within minutes. It was furious."

‌



Asked if she was scared, she said: "You can't be scared if you've got to act, you've got to get in and do it. But I was pretty stunned afterwards."

Ms Du Cann, who lives in the nearby village of Eastbridge, did not see any evidence of what caused the ignition. She said: "People are saying it's human induced, but we don't know. There was nobody else there, we didn't see anyone, didn't see a cigarette butt, camping equipment or a BBQ - nothing. It wasn't by the path, it was away, not somewhere somebody would casually smoke a cigarette."

View 7 Images Smoke rises at the scene of the wildfire (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

‌



More than 100 firefighters, including some from as far afield as London, Sussex and West Yorkshire, are tonight still fighting the blaze in other parts of the sprawling rural area, which is a flagship UK nature reserve. They are also using water backpacks, 4x4 vehicles and quad bikes in order to get water to hard to reach areas while also being helped by a helicopter dropping up to 1,000 litre buckets of water over the area, which includes RSPB Minsmere.

Officials today said the winds are currently pushing the fire away from Sizewell nuclear plant and added the bird sanctuary, which includes marshes and other waterways, is acting as a natural fire break between the fire and the plant.

Around 200 families, including residents and holiday makers staying in caravans and lodges near the heath, were evacuated around two miles to a pop-up rescue centre at Westleton Village Hall late on Wednesday night after police banged on their doors telling them they were in danger.

‌



Those who had remained in the area were finally allowed to collect essential belongings from their properties this afternoon after being escorted in and out by police officers in what officials described as "a very small window of opportunity" lasting just 15 minutes.

View 7 Images A general view of tents that were evacuated near the scene (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

Among them were holidaymakers Dave Johnson, 67, a retired IT technician, and his wife Jen, 55, an artist, own two lodges at Cliff House holiday park. The couple drove in convoy, escorted by the police, to pick up their essentials from their lodge.

‌



Dave said: “It looked better than I expected, although there’s still fires breaking out. We didn’t go as far as where most of the destruction is so you get the false impression it’s probably better than it is. From what we could see, [Cliff House] it’s alright at the moment, but there’s talk of the fires still.”

David Knapp, 59, and his wife Alison, 59, from Herne Bay, were also allowed to retrieve their motorhome. David said: “When you’re driving down, there’s no sign of fire. There’s no smoke, nothing. Its totally clear. You pull in the campsite and its absolutely deserted, all you see is empty tents. There’s no people."

He added: “The motorhome stinks of fire. The window was slightly open and the vent was open so it stinks of smoke. I was going to change my clothes, put a new top on, but what's the point.”

‌



View 7 Images A burnt and discarded parking sign at an evacuated and deserted camp site (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

The National Trust, who have been caring for Dunwich Heath since 1968, today launched a public appeal in a bid to gain donations to help restore the iconic site to its former glory. Hilary McGrady, the Trust’s Director-General, said: “We are looking at total devastation of a beloved and important landscape.

"We’ve lost precious habitats, wildlife, trees, and a place where people have made memories over generations. It’s heartbreaking. But together we can and will restore Dunwich, and crucially, make it more resilient and better adapted for the climate we’re facing now, and the climate we’ll be facing in future. We’re working hard to tackle climate change and prepare for more of it, but there’s more hard work to be done. We can’t do it alone."

‌



Countryside manager for Suffolk Matt Wilson added: "The impact on this site in particular is looking to be fairly catastrophic. We're looking at total devastation across the National Trust site."

Adam Rowlands, Suffolk area manager for the RSPB, said it is too early to know the full scale of the impact on wildlife. But he admitted: "Shockingly, one of our site team at first light spoke about the acrid smell and said it's not just smoke, you have a sense that animals have perished in the flames so it's not a pleasant sight.

View 7 Images A bench remains amid the barren landscape (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

‌



"We'll wait to see in time really. With a lot of this you can only really assess the impact once you see a full season, but I think we can be pretty assured we're going to see some shocking results." Mr Rowlands added the recovery will "take years, decades, in come cases."

Suffolk fire service deputy chief fire officer Henry Griffin said: "It remains a significant and dynamic incident. We've been working with the Met Office, looking at the wind directions to monitor and mitigate in the hotspots to prevent flare-ups and re-ignition."

He added: "There has been some heat damage to some buildings - scorched cladding, melted gutters, things like that. But based on the information I have at this point in time, there has been no total loss to any buildings, which is a remarkable feat."

‌



Shortly before 5pm on Friday, a spokesperson said: "While the incident remains significant and resource intensive - and is still classified as a Major Incident for Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service and Suffolk Resilience Forum partners - conditions are currently improving and planning for the recovery phase has begun.

View 7 Images Cottages were saved despite all around them being burnt to the ground (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily mirror)

"Firefighters and partner agencies will continue to monitor the weather and situation closely over the coming days. Thank you to everyone affected for your patience and co-operation."

Article continues below

Meanwhile, England is on track for its driest July on record, the Environment Agency announced on Friday. It said reservoir storage stands at 72%, down from 75% a week ago and nearly 10 percentage points below the long-term average for the time of year.

It added three reservoirs were now classed as having "exceptionally low" levels, including Blagdon in Somerset (56% full), Hanningfield in Essex (65%) and Wimbleball in Somerset (54%).

A further seven reservoirs are "notably low": Ardingly in West Sussex (66% full); Blithfield in Staffordshire (63%); Clatworthy in Somerset (56%); Clywedog in Powys, which provides water for central and north-west England (69%); the Dove group of reservoirs in Derbyshire (77%); Grafham in Cambridgeshire (78%); and the Lower Thames group of reservoirs in Berkshire and west London (74%).

News.title: Suffolk wildfire live: Drone images show devastation as helicopter scrambled
News.content:
A wildfire ravaging Dunwich Heath in Suffolk is still 'unstable' according to the local council with the number of firefighters at the scene increasing

A wildfire that has already destroyed a massive area of land in Suffolk and forced scores of people to evacuate remains "unstable" days after it first ignited, the county council has warned.

The blaze at Dunwich Heath has devastated wildlife habitats which could now reportedly take up to 25 years to recover after it went up in flames at about 5pm on Wednesday before engulfing an area equivalent to about 140 football pitches near Sizewell B nuclear power plant.

People evacuated from a local caravan site have now been given a short window to collect their belongings but Peter Langford, emergency planning officer for Suffolk County Council, warned them: "It is still a fast moving situation. From the fire perspective, is still an unstable situation.

"In fact, they've increased a number of pumps back there and they're just about to bring in the helicopter as well." On Thursday afternoon, an EDF spokesperson said the fire was "not affecting operations at Sizewell B power station".

Another wildfire that ignited near Colchester today has now been extinguished after dozens of firefighters rushed to tackle the flames.

News.title: Washington fire live: 'Explosions' at factory as 'close windows' warning issued
News.content:
Thick black smoke coming from the scene of the fire

Emergency services rushed to the incident at a factory in the Crowther Industrial Estate, Washington, in Tyne and Wear, with witnesses telling of 'several explosions'

Massive plumes of smoke can be seen coming from a raging fire at a factory after reports of "several explosions" in the North East.

Emergency services rushed to the incident in the Crowther Industrial Estate, Washington, in Tyne and Wear, with witnesses saying that there's no signs of the fire easing.

Northumbria Police says officers are on the scene to support the Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service in responding to the fire in Washington, with a 'cordon currently in place'.

Pictures from the scene show five fire brigade appliances and an aerial ladder platform dispatched. Thick black smoke is billowing into the sky which can be seen for miles.

News.title: Andy Burnham says extra cash for mayors should be used to 'empower' regions - not for short term tax cuts
News.content:
Andy Burnham says extra cash for mayors should be used to 'empower' regions - not for short term tax cuts

Prime Minister Andy Burnham says plans for mayors to keep a share of taxes will give them the opportunity to empower their regions, and warns against quick-fire tax cuts

View 4 Images Andy Burnham announced more cash for regional mayors (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Andy Burnham says he’s “not comfortable” with regional mayors using extra cash from devolution to fund tax cuts.

‌



The government has announced England’s mayors will soon be able to keep a share of income tax generated in their areas, as well as business rates totalling tens of millions. This would allow them to invest in projects to grow local economies under “transformational” plans to shift power out of Whitehall.

‌



Mr Burnham said his plans for mayors to keep a share of taxes will give them “more in their hands” to empower their regions. But, Ben Houchen, the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley, has suggested he would use the income tax to hand out rebates to local people.

‌



View 4 Images Andy Burnham visits community centre in Sheffield (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The PM shot down his plans, saying: “No, I'm not comfortable. Because this is not about making them mini Chancellors of the Exchequer, sort of undermining, or rewriting, policy on tax and personal finance.

“This is a policy for growth and investment. It’s a very clear policy of the kind that Greater Manchester has benefitted from over the last decade. Where if you get more growth in your economy, you’re given an incentive to do that, because you can keep more of the proceeds of that, to then keep investing and keep the growth going.

‌



“So, you can't just get a little bit of growth and then abandon the investment, because then you won't grow. So this is, it's a growth policy, and I think, you know, people need to kind of understand what this is and what this isn’t.”

View 4 Images Andy Burnham spoke on a number of issues in Sheffield (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/POOL PA via AP)

He added: “Britain has got low growth and low investment, and we've had that for a long time. This is about breaking that, breaking that cycle. And if they went down that path that they’re proposing, they wouldn't have any money to give away the next year because the growth would have stopped because they're not building that growth, they would just have taken short term, and then there wouldn't be anything to redistribute.”

‌



Speaking at a community centre in Sheffield, Burnham tackled a number of issues, including indicating he will scrap plans to curtail jury trials in England and Wales. He said he had concerns about the proposals - which were proposed under Keir Starmer - and that his instinct was to keep juries at the heart of the justice system.

Citing his experience campaigning for justice over the Hillsborough disaster, he said: “So I want to really look in detail at that proposal, and my instincts are that we need to find ways of not reducing access to jury trial.”

The original plans were met with a fierce backlash from legal bodies and some Labour MPs including Karl Turner, who was suspended over his criticisms of Lammy and Starmer Burnham said he had asked the chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, to speak to Turner about being readmitted to the parliamentary party. The PM also said he would visit Dover soon to see first hand the issues around small boat arrivals.

‌



He said he was open to a discussion about devolving powers on asylum hotel contracts and HMOs, saying: “I’m open to a discussion with regional mayors - and I’m sure the Home Secretary is - where local solutions would be better than the situation that we have at the moment.

“It is a top-down process. It does result sometimes in local partners not being adequately consulted about accommodation, not even notified sometimes, so I can understand why people want to see change and we’re open to that discussion.”

View 4 Images Andy Burnham said first two weeks as PM had been "intense" (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/POOL PA via AP)

‌



Speaking about his first two weeks as PM he said it had been “intense … but in a good way”.

He said: “I suppose you think you’ll understand what the job will be like until you actually experience it, and it is intense – but in a good way as well.

“I’ve just decided to embrace every part of it, the whole thing, and keep the way I’ve always worked and the way I’ve always done my politics. It would be easy to be changed by it but I’m not going to let that happen.

Article continues below

“It’s an incredible privilege. I feel that I do have to try and make this a circuit-breaker, I feel really strongly about that, changing the way we think about politics, changing the way we think about running the country but not doing it in a confrontational or adversarial way.”

News.title: UK weather maps show fifth heatwave coming as 11 counties hit 35C or more – list
News.content:
UK weather maps show fifth heatwave coming as 11 counties hit 35C or more – list

Weather forecasting models show temperatures in the UK may soon reach 35C again, as the Met Office says ‘hot’ conditions could make a return

View 4 Images Anomaly maps show temperatures will rise well above the seasonal average in August (Image: WXCHARTS)

The UK has seen four heatwaves so far this year - and a fifth now looks to be on the cards within days.

‌



Temperatures reached 35C this week as southern and eastern parts of England reached the heatwave threshold. Although the mercury should drop slightly this weekend, it shouldn’t be too long before we see 35C again.

‌



The GFS weather model shows temperatures rising on August 11, with highs of 31C possible across much of eastern, central and southern England, as well as parts of Wales close to the border.

‌



Maximum possible temperatures could reach 35C on August 12, GFS model data shows. The Midlands and south-east are expected to be the warmest regions, although 33C is possible as far north as Yorkshire.

View 4 Images Maximum possible temperatures (C) on August 11 (Image: WXCHARTS)

UK weather maps show new 34C heatwave within days as 15 counties hit 32C or more READ MORE :

Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Friday – downpours in 22 counties READ MORE :

Highs of 34C are possible in East Anglia on August 13. The data shows much of central, southern and eastern England, as well as South Wales, could reach 31-33C. These temperatures would constitute the fifth official heatwave of 2026.

‌



An official heatwave is declared when temperatures hit the ‘heatwave threshold’ three days in a row. The threshold stands at 28C in the south-east, where conditions tend to be warmer, and drops to 25C the further away from the south-east you go.

Temperature anomaly maps for August 11 to August 13 show the UK shaded in areas of dark red. This indicates that temperatures will rise well above the seasonal average.

View 4 Images Maximum possible temperatures (C) on August 12 (Image: WXCHARTS)

‌



The GFS model maps suggest 11 counties could reach 35C or more later this month. They are all in England.

UK counties facing 35C or more

Warwickshire

Lincolnshire

Northamptonshire

Hertfordshire

Buckinghamshire

Oxfordshire

Gloucestershire

Worcestershire

Herefordshire

Surrey

Cambridgeshire

View 4 Images Maximum possible temperatures (C) on August 13 (Image: WXCHARTS)

‌



Met Office weather forecast

The Met Office says temperatures could turn “very warm or hot” as we head into August. However, there is also a risk of “thundery plumes” in places.

The Met Office forecast for August 5 to August 14 states: “A generally rather changeable period looks likely, with many places likely to see some much needed rain or showers at times but also some more sunshine. Initially, some rain or showers will affect many parts, this heavy and possibly thundery in places.

“After a drier, brighter few days, further changeable or unsettled conditions may develop as we head towards mid-August. This may be due to frontal systems moving in from the Atlantic or thundery plumes moving north from the continent or a combination of both.

Article continues below

“Temperatures will likely be a little above average overall, and there is the potential for some very warm or hot and humid spells, especially in the south, although perhaps not the heat we have seen in recent weeks.”

News.title: 'Families had tears streaming down faces - and wicked funeral director Robert Bush refused to look at them'
News.content:
When ‘wicked’ undertaker Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years, I watched him stand solemnly. He bowed his head, hands clasped in front him, as if he was at the head of a funeral procession.

There was total silence as he was taken down, escorted from the glass-lined dock to the cells below.

There was silence because the families who had been sat watching from the packed public gallery had seized back the dignity Bush had so mercilessly stolen from their loved ones. It was as if everyone was sat remembering their grief and those they’d lost.

View 5 Images Robert Bush has been sentenced to 20 years in prison (Image: Humberside Police)

‌



'Monster' funeral director Robert Bush jailed for 20 years as heartbroken families demand public inquiry READ MORE :

Britain's sickest funeral director Richard Bush devastated grieving relatives to fund his fantasy lifestyle READ MORE :

It was so quiet throughout Bush’s sentencing at Hull crown court on Friday that when the two knocks were heard on the wooden door, to announce the arrival of the Judge, a few even jumped. Justice Hilliard KC, sat down and took his heavy black-rimmed glasses off, to look at the families. He told them how they’d ‘honoured the memories of those who died’ with their behaviour in court.

While in contrast, Bush frowned and kept his dead down as the Judge spoke of the ‘anguish and pain beyond comprehension’ he’d caused them. And these extraordinary families kept silent despite tears pouring down their faces and even when the Judge spoke of Bush's remorse.

View 5 Images Court artist drawing of funeral director Robert Bush (Image: Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire)

He told how an expert had reported Bush felt ‘remorse’, and it seemed genuine. Even then, the families didn’t utter a word, just shook their heads in disagreement. Others put their hands over their mouths as if to keep the emotion in.

‌



One lady had a gentle hand placed on her back by someone behind her, as her shoulders heaved up and down as she sobbed, again silently. I was one of only a few journalists allowed in court to watch Bush learn his fate after an emotional five-day sentencing hearing.

View 5 Images Police outside Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull (Image: Danny Lawson/PA Wire)

Witness after witness had broken their hearts as they told of the damage bush had caused, the trauma, their PTSD, suicide attempts and their heartbreak. Their evidence appeared to touch everybody in court, including the Judge and the Det Superintendent who led the investigation.

But not Bush.

‌



View 5 Images Robert Bush listened to victim impact statements for days with his head down (Image: legacyfuneraldirectors)

The only time the money-obsessed funeral director showed any interest throughout the five-day hearing, was when the court heard about the £3million he raked in. Then he was paying attention, referring to his notes next to him and looking straight at the Judge, no longer staring at his feet.

At least 50 family members had queued up to hear his fate, but only half managed to get into the public gallery at Hull crown court. One of those who couldn’t get it in, watched on a video link in a nearby court. She told how they too were silent as they watched proceedings.

View 5 Images Funeral director Robert Bush breached the trust of grieving families “on an almost industrial scale” while spending their money on himself (Image: Danny Lawson/PA Wire)

‌



Tracey Crowther, 62, had chatted to me earlier as we queued to get into the main court, and revealed Bush had carried out ten of her loved ones' funerals, including her son’s.

She said later: “I watched him closely and there was no remorse. He is so evil and looked more sorry for himself. He got up and walked away as if nothing had happened. He’s vile. It’s not long enough, he should have got life.”

As everyone filed out, some spoke out saying ‘It’s a joke’ and ‘we’ve been failed again’. But others were silent, just hugging each other.

You could see the ‘heartbreaking’ bond they had formed from being the victims of Bush’s ‘unimaginable’ crimes.

News.title: New BBC row over Naga Munchetty getting 'special treatment' on 5Live breakfast show
News.content:
New BBC row over Naga Munchetty getting 'special treatment' on 5Live breakfast show

EXCLUSIVE: Insiders on BBC Radio 5Live say there is "disquiet" over the terms of her appointment on the flagship show

View 2 Images Naga Munchetty has landed the breakfast gig on 5Live (Image: BBC)

A row has broken out over Naga Munchetty’s “plum” breakfast job on BBC Radio 5 Live amid claims she has received "special treatment." The 51-year-old star was handed the gig presenting the station’s flagship show after quitting the BBC TV sofa after 17 years.

‌



But insiders at the station claim there is "consternation" behind the scenes at 5 Live over the Corporation’s handling of the situation. There is uproar over the fact that Munchetty has negotiated a deal to present three days in the Salford studio, and two days a week from London near her Hertfordshire home.

‌



It comes as her prospective co-presenter will be expected to do five days a week in Salford. A source said: “Many don't feel that is particularly fair, and that bosses have afforded her special treatment." There is also upset that the role wasn’t advertised, unlike that of her co-presenter. The source added: “There is disquiet that the role has been handed to her on a plate, whereas prospective co-presenters will have to battle it out for the job.”

‌



View 2 Images Naga Munchetty has landed a new job (Image: BBC)

The advert for the two-year fixed term contract role confirms that shortlisted candidates will be expected to record pilots, as well as being “five days a week from our Salford studios.” The source adds: “Naga was a shoo-in whereas her co-presenter is expected to jump through various hoops…it doesn’t strike some as particularly fair.”

BBC sources told the Mirror that it was not unusual for 5 Live presenters to broadcast from different locations across the UK, and that it was normal for both established presenters to move between programmes and different presenting combinations to be tested.

‌



The advert for the “chief presenter” lists a number of attributes needed for the role including a “warm personality with the ability to see the funny side of life. ” It comes after Munchetty, one of the corporation's highest-paid stars with a salary of £365,000, had faced allegations that she had bullied junior staffers. Insiders claim she was accused of "humiliating" one female colleague and reprimanding an intern for incorrectly spreading Marmite on her toast.

One source said: “The wording of the ad has raised a few eyebrows given all the hoo-ha on BBC Breakfast.”

Munchetty, who currently hosts a mid-morning talk show on 5Live, also reportedly received a telling-off from station bosses in 2022 after a "crass, inappropriate and wildly unprofessional" off-air reference to a sex act. She has never commented on any of the allegations. However the Corporation launched a review into the BBC Breakfast claims against her last year, which is now no longer active.

‌



The Mirror told this week how insiders at BBC Breakfast were hoping for a “reset” on the troubled show in the wake of Munchetty’s exit. A BBC source said: "The new job for Naga seems the best result for everyone. It was not a happy ship on Breakfast." They added: "However you look at it, hosting BBC Breakfast is a much bigger job than working on Five Live." A second source added: "After all the turmoil, it's clear a reset is needed."

It also comes after a disagreement with BBC Breakfast's editor Richard Frediani, with Munchetty having reportedly raised concerns about his conduct. He was later cleared of bullying allegations. Munchetty and her new co-host will take over from Rachel Burden and Rick Edwards, who announced that they would step down in December. She first joined Breakfast in 2009 and has co-hosted with Charlie Stayt since 2014. She has presented Radio 5's midmorning programme since 2021.

Announcing the news, Naga said: "I'm thrilled to be joining 5 Live Breakfast in January. Live news, great conversations and connecting with audiences are what I love most about broadcasting, and 5 Live does all of that brilliantly. It has been a privilege to be part of the BBC Breakfast TV team for the past 17 years, working alongside an incredibly talented and hard-working group of journalists who are not only outstanding colleagues but also great friends. Presenting a flagship programme on 5 Live is an opportunity that was simply too good to pass up. It will take a huge amount of work and require 100% of my focus and energy, and I'm really looking forward to throwing myself into the role.

Article continues below

"Over the last five years, I've been privileged to build a relationship with 5 Live listeners on the mid-morning programme and help shine a light on the issues that matter most to them. I'm excited to build on that and to start each day with our listeners every morning. Between now and January, "I'll continue presenting the two programmes I love. I'm sure there will be plenty of news to cover, and it will very much be business as usual."

News.title: 'If that means I lose my job, so be it': Top Fifa official questions Infantino's World Cup plan
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's position came under further scrutiny on Friday as the governing body's chief operating officer strongly criticised his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

In a statement released to the Associated Press, Kevin Lamour described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and said "the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions".

He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project. BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

The lengthy statement did not mention Infantino by name.

It came on the same day a third confederation spoke out against the plans, a senior adviser to Infantino resigned, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Swiss was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

US President Donald Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Lamour said in his statement: "Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football.

"A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite."

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

News.title: No sentence long enough for jailed funeral director Robert Bush, say families
News.content:
Karen Dry, who organised monthly vigils for the victims' families when the investigation began, said: "No sentence was ever going to be enough."

She said families were hoping Bush would be sentenced to more than 30 years, but what was "really messing with people's heads" was the prospect of him only serving half of his sentence.

When asked does it feel fair? She replied: "No, it really doesn't.

"For some people, I totally get that today is the end of it for them.

"But I'm my mam and dad's daughter, and we are a bit more determined than just letting these things lie."

She said without regulation of the industry, "in five or 10 years' time there will be another funeral director with another 300 families in a courtroom somewhere".

"We've got to put a stop to it and it's got to stop now."

News.title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
News.content:
This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean.

"[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".

He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".

When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".

It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.

Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".

A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.

Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.

It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".

The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".

News.title: Passenger on British Airways mayday flight describes fear and shout of 'I don't want to die'
News.content:
A passenger on a British Airways flight that issued a distress call on approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month has described the rising fear in the cabin and a lack of information from the crew.

Edward Killiwick had been travelling back from a friend's birthday party with his partner Julie, on the flight from Dusseldorf in Germany on 6 July.

He said passengers were told that the landing had been aborted, and then he felt a "very violent manoeuvre" and "did think we could crash". He and his partner had to comfort a woman who "completely lost it and started screaming, 'I don't want to die'".

The flight landed safely, but the incident is being investigated with assistance from BA.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident", and France's accident investigation authority, the BEA, said on Wednesday that the plane, an Airbus A320, had issued a distress call.

Edward said: "The violent manoeuvre almost felt like it was avoiding another aircraft. You could feel the engines going at full power.

"It was a bit odd going around in a holding pattern with no information. I thought if they're not talking, then they're not in a good place."

He said they were in a holding pattern for about 15 minutes.

The BEA said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet â which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

Edward said: "I was definitely scared. After the violent manoeuvre I thought, there is definitely something very badly wrong here. I did think we could crash.

"I did think it was a possibility, and I think everyone else did."

News.title: Two more small boat pilots jailed for Channel crossings
News.content:
Two men who piloted overcrowded small boats have been jailed for endangering others while crossing the Channel.

Omar Heidari, a 34-year-old Afghan national who steered a dinghy carrying 95 people to the UK in June, has been jailed for two years.

Manas Yuk, an 18-year-old Sudanese national, was sentenced to 18 months in youth detention after piloting a boat carrying 81 people - including a number of children - just days prior.

The men were sentenced at Canterbury Crown Court on Friday having earlier pleaded guilty to endangerment.

It means 10 people have now been sentenced under a law targeting those who risk the safety of others by piloting small boats since it came into force in January.

The Home Office said Heidari had endangered the largest number of lives of anyone so far sentenced for the offence.

The boat was overcrowded during the crossing on 23 June, with some passengers hanging their legs over the sides of the vessel, it said. A number of the passengers were not wearing life jackets.

He was jailed for endangering others as well as arriving in the UK without valid entry clearance.

News.title: Parents sue school over 'inhumane' calming rooms after BBC report
News.content:
Parents are suing a special school after a BBC investigation uncovered CCTV footage showing autistic children being locked inside calming rooms and abused.

Ten families are claiming that their children â all of whom had learning disabilities or several mental disorders - were amongst those harmed by their treatment in the rooms.

A police investigation into the abuse, recorded inside the rooms at Whitefield special school in north London, ended two years ago without any charges.

The school is now run by a new trust which says the failings have led to "important learning".

Many special schools use seclusion spaces such as calming rooms outside of classrooms to address sensory needs or challenging behaviour.

But the leaked footage obtained by the BBC showed children being shoved into padded rooms, thrown to the floor, restrained by the neck - or left alone, sitting in vomit.

One 12-year-old boy appeared in over 55 hours of CCTV footage filmed inside the rooms.

At the time, the Children's Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, said the use of the rooms was "horrifying".

Leigh Day is now bringing a civil legal claim on behalf of 10 families against the trust which ran the school and the London borough of Waltham Forest.

The law firm says the use of the rooms was "barbaric", according to its clients. The claim alleges that children were falsely imprisoned and their human rights were breached.

"What was done to these children was profoundly harmful, and its impact continues to be felt by families every day", says Alison Millar, who is leading the case.

The CCTV obtained by the BBC had been recorded between 2014 and 2017 but only emerged in 2021.

Last month, a long-delayed review commissioned by Waltham Forest found that restraint and seclusion became "normalised" and a culture developed that allowed "pejorative views of non-compliant children".

It added that parents were clear that the practices were "unimaginable" and "inhumane".

The BBC has also found evidence of mistreatment in seclusion rooms at other schools across the UK.

CCTV from a different school showed a boy being "brutally" and "unlawfully" restrained, while elsewhere an autistic child was kept inside a cage.

News.title: Burnham faces criticism over plans for mayors to get share of income tax
News.content:
The government is facing criticism over its plan to allow regional mayors to keep a share of income tax and business rates in England.

Andy Burnham says that the proposals, expected to be phased in from next April, will give metro mayors powers to invest the money in their communities for public services.

The prime minister said on Friday that this amounted to "the biggest shift of power out of Whitehall and Westminster" to regions across the UK.

But Lord Houchen, the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley, argues he should be able to offer taxpayers a rebate instead, while opposition parties say the plans could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out.

"The prime minister has said he wants to alleviate the cost of living [crisis] and give people room to breathe - what better way to do that than allow them to keep more of their own money?" the Tory mayor told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told the BBC that there was not currently a mechanism in place for mayors to offer a rebate.

But Lord Houchen said it was "not beyond the wit of man" to create a system, adding it would not be "overly complicated" and would not be particularly controversial.

"I think the prime minister and what this government is doing on fiscal devolution is a move in the right direction, but for it to be real devolution we've got to have local decision-making and choose what's best for the people we represent."

Burnham later directly rejected the idea of mayors giving their taxpayers rebates, telling reporters the plans were not about making local leaders into "mini-chancellors of the exchequer, undermining or rewriting policy on tax and personal finance".

As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding by central government grants.

Mayors are expected to start retaining some revenue from business rates from April 2027 and receive a portion of income tax from April 2028.

The rates of income tax will not change as a result of the reform.

Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, has made devolution a centrepiece of his agenda in the early weeks of his premiership.

He said this policy would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

Chancellor John Healey will set out more of the detail when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.

News.title: Disgraced funeral boss who failed to bury bodies jailed for 20 years
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

The court heard Bush defrauded nearly 200 families out of Â£562,117 and had acted out of "financial greed".

Hilliard warned that unless a body was one of those recovered by police in 2024 and properly identified, no-one who had used Legacy's cremations services "at any time can be absolutely certain they received the ashes of their loved one".

"He must have a heartless side to him - which allowed him to treat the living and the dead in the way he did, and he was very confident he would get away with what he was doing."

The judge added: "I don't think I have ever known offences affecting so many people and so deeply."

The court was told relatives of 46 people who were cremated between 2017 and 2024 were given the wrong ashes and the loved ones of another 11 never received any.

"How betrayed they now feel," said the judge.

"Husbands and wives, partners, parents, children, grandchildren, now discovering that they are left with nothing, or in some cases we heard, an empty plastic bag or a teaspoonful of ash which the police managed to recover for them."

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three attacks while in prison and possessing a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

The 19-year-old murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

In May 2025, it was reported boiling water had been thrown on a prison officer at Belmarsh. They were taken to hospital and discharged on the same day.

When Rudakubana was jailed, the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to him being under-18 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

On 23 July, the MoJ confirmed Rudakubana was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The decision to transfer him was criticised by a lawyer representing the families of victims.

News.title: Puberty blockers trial can start recruiting children after judge rejects legal challenge
News.content:
A high-profile clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty in children questioning their gender can go ahead after the High Court rejected a legal challenge by campaigners.

The Pathways trial, run by researchers at King's College London (KCL), will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.

The study was commissioned to assess the benefits or risks of puberty blockers, after a landmark review into gender services found the evidence for treating young people with the drugs was "remarkably weak".

Campaigners who brought the legal action had argued the safeguards in place were inadequate and raised concerns about the long-term physical and psychological effects on young people.

The judge, Mr Justice Chamberlain, refused the application for a judicial review saying that none of the claims made by the campaigners had a realistic chance of success.

He said that each patient involved in the trial will have been assessed over "many months" by specialist doctors who will have "formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment".

A spokeswoman for KCL welcomed the court's decision, saying the "safety and welfare of young people will remain our highest priority in carrying out this research".

Campaigners, including parents of gender-questioning children, said they were disappointed by the decision saying the "world is watching" a case which has "global implications and high stakes".

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told BBC Radio 4's Today programme areas without mayors would also benefit from investment because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.

Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.

But Labour backbencher Perran Moon said the government's plans were "discriminatory" and could create a "two-tier system".

The MP for Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall said the area would never have a mayor or become a combined authority and so risked not having access to devolved powers that other areas would have.

"What we're asking government to do is to provide us with the same powers, the same funding that mayoral combined authorities have without the requirement of becoming a combined authority or having a mayor."

The government has also announced that mayors will be given a fast-track route to building new tramways, roads and light rail in their areas.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the threshold at which local leaders need to seek approval for projects will rise to Â£500m, up from Â£200m.

News.title: England and Wales on course for driest July on record
News.content:
England and Wales are on course for their driest July since records began 190 years ago.

The Met Office reports that England has seen just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it is 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

The UK as a whole is currently on track for its third driest July, and driest nationally since 1868.

News.title: Budget to be held in October, Healey announces
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has announced the date of his first Budget will be Wednesday, 28 October.

In aâ¯video message,â¯ he said: "This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.

"It will be built on fiscal discipline. It will meet our fiscal rules. It'll give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future. Now, let's get on with the job."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

Burnham also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain shouldl lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

But questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.

Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.

The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.

Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.

Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.

Sainsbury's bought Argos â together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â in 2016 for Â£1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around Â£720m in 2024.

In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Roberts said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.

He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat products

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.

Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops â and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.

News.title: Thames Water boss says leakage targets 'not realistic'
News.content:
Water companies have performance commitments on issues such as leakage.

It is illegal to release raw sewage into rivers and seas during "normal" weather conditions, but firms are allowed to do so when it rains heavily, to prevent homes being flooded.

Thames is the UK's largest water company, supplying water and wastewater services to 16 million customers across London and parts of southern England.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Weston said the company treats 4.3 billion litres of waste a day, and "99.5% of the time" it gets treated successfully, although "sometimes something goes wrong".

"We want to do better when it comes to pollutions," he said, but added, "the targets that the company is expected to make are not realistic.

"[For example], we have to hit a certain level of leakage, but it is so far in excess of what we are capable of doing, I think anyone would be capable of doing, however much money you invested, that it is not going to be achievable."

The chance of getting to zero pollution was "very, very slim", he added.

Ofwat told the BBC: "With around a fifth of water put into supply still lost through leakage, companies must deliver on the commitments they have been funded to achieve.

"Water company targets are intended to be ambitious and drive better outcomes for customers and the environment."

A spokesperson for the Environment Agency said: "[We] and the public expect Thames Water to comply with the law," adding that the agency would continue to hold companies to account where performance falls short.

James Wallace, chief executive of campaign group River Action, said: "Thames Water's tactics of opacity and deflection fool no-one. Telling the public to save water while this wasteful profit-obsessed corporation leaks 570 million litres of treated drinking water every day is offensive.

"There is nothing 'realistic' about accepting sewage pollution as inevitable. The choice is simple: keep propping up a failed privatised financial model, or put Thames Water into special administration and rebuild it as a public utility serving customers, rivers and the public."

Ilia Topuria has shown the extent of his recovery from brutal facial injuries caused by Justin Gaethje, revealing his face without sunglasses for the first time in six weeks.

Topuria suffered the first defeat of his career in June, when he retired on his stool after four rounds of action at the White House. The Spanish-Georgian was headlining an unprecedented UFC event on the South Lawn, defending the lightweight title against Gaethje.

And the American outstruck Topuria so severely that the latter was left with cuts and bruises all over his face prior to the stoppage. Topuria even tried to hide his face as he was escorted away from the cage by Aleksandre – his coach and brother.

Ilia Topuria (centre) after his defeat by Justin Gaethje at the White House ( AFP/Getty )

Topuria continued to hide his face in the ensuing weeks, sporting sunglasses whenever he ventured out in public, including while celebrating Spain’s victory in the men’s World Cup final earlier in July.

Now, however, Topuria has appeared on camera in a series of photos and videos, with his facial injuries appearing almost fully healed.

In the images and clips, the 29-year-old’s face did seem somewhat swollen still, with a series of small lumps on his eyelid possibly stemming from stitches, but it was otherwise visibly healthier than in June.

Topuria’s next move is unclear, with Gaethje saying the former lightweight and featherweight champion does not deserve an instant rematch.

Topuria has been linked to a long-awaited grudge match with Paddy Pimblett, whom he famously confronted in a hotel in 2022 after accusing the Liverpudlian of posting anti-Georgian tweets.

Pimblett, 31, suffered his first UFC loss in January as he was comprehensively put outstruck and outpointed by Gaethje in an interim-title fight. However, “Paddy The Baddy” bounced back earlier in July by submitting Benoit Saint-Denis inside one minute.

News.title: 18-year-old found dead in home owned by congresswoman’s husband had been shot, cops say
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

The death of an 18-year-old woman found shot inside a Boston rental property owned by the husband of U.S. Representative Ayanna Pressley has been officially ruled a homicide, authorities announced Thursday.

The Boston Police Department formally identified the victim as Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio, of Boston. Officers responding to a call at 1:52 p.m. on Saturday, July 18, found Ocasio dead in a rear bedroom at 25 Malta Road in the city’s Mattapan neighborhood, according to a police report shared with The Independent.

The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner determined Thursday that Ocasio died from a single gunshot wound and officially classified the case as a homicide.

Ocasio’s mother, Elenie Ocasio, told Boston 25 News on July 20 that she believed her daughter was killed, emphasizing that the teenager was not suicidal.

“This coward killed my baby. He put a gun to her head, took my baby in that house and left her to die,” Elenie Ocasio told the station. “My daughter didn’t deserve this. My daughter did not deserve this, and it’s all going to come to light. Everything’s gonna come out.”

open image in gallery Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio, 18, was fatally shot on July 18 inside a Mattapan, Massachusetts, home. The rental property is owned by Conan Harris, the husband of US Representative Ayanna Pressley ( GoFundMe )

No arrests have been made, and police released no suspect information. However, law enforcement officials stated there was “absolutely nothing that indicates any connection to the owners of the property,” according to The Boston Globe.

The two-story, seven-bedroom multi-family home is owned as a rental property by Conan Harris, the husband of Pressley. The house had been listed for sale for $1.15 million, but real estate listings show it is currently off the market.

A spokesperson for the listing realtor told ABC affiliate WCVB that the tenants living in the rental had been there for a while, though they did not specify the exact duration.

Pressley and Harris do not live at the Malta Street address and never have, a person familiar with the matter told The Independent. The couple resides in the Hyde Park section of Boston, according to Pressley’s website.

open image in gallery Neither Pressley nor her family were involved in the incident, a spokesperson for the lawmaker confirmed ( AFP/Getty )

A spokesperson for Pressley previously confirmed that neither the lawmaker nor her family were involved in the incident.

In a recent statement, Pressley expressed her grief over the teenager’s death, noting that as a parent of a teenager herself, “the thought of a young person violently losing their life in this way is beyond crushing.”

“I am devastated about the death of Yoseliani Marte, an 18-year-old with so many dreams ahead of her, her life cut short by domestic violence,” Pressley said. “I stand with our community and everyone who loved Yoseliani as we grieve this deep loss. May we all honor her life and humanity and extend compassion to her loved ones as they navigate this heartbreaking tragedy.”

Pressley’s office added in an earlier statement, “The Congresswoman extends her deepest condolences to the impacted family.”

First elected to Congress in 2019, Pressley represents Massachusetts’ 7th congressional district, which encompasses several Boston neighborhoods. She is a prominent member of “The Squad,” a group of progressive Democratic House members that includes Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.

open image in gallery Officers responded to a call on Malta Street in Boston’s Mattapan neighborhood on the afternoon of July 18. Upon arriving, police found Ocasio deceased in a rear bedroom ( Google Maps, 2019 )

Local community members have also paid tribute to the 18-year-old. Shea Butter Smoothies, a Dorchester juice bar where Ocasio worked, posted a remembrance to Facebook on July 20 honoring her contributions to their team.

“Liani was a brilliant and motivated young lady whose passion and dedication had a profound impact on our team and the work we do,” the business wrote. “Her innovative ideas, particularly in enhancing Shea Butter Smoothies, brought a unique touch that our customers adored. She approached every project with enthusiasm, creativity, and an unwavering commitment to excellence.”

The post added, “Liani brought joy and positivity to our workplace. Her infectious laughter, kindness, and willingness to help others made her not just a colleague, but a cherished friend to many. She will be missed immensely, and her legacy will live on in the hearts of those who had the privilege of knowing her.”

The business announced it would donate 50 percent of the proceeds from sales of its “Big Papi” smoothie to assist the family with funeral costs.

“We encourage our community to join us in this effort, as we remember the beautiful person she was," the business stated. "Rest in peace, Yoseliani. You will always be remembered.”

Her family has also organized a GoFundMe campaign to assist with funeral and unexpected expenses, raising more than $18,500 toward a $20,000 goal.

“No words can truly express the pain of losing someone so young, with so many dreams, hopes, and milestones still ahead of her,” Elenie Ocasio wrote on the fundraising page. “Yoseliani was deeply loved by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched. Her kindness, beautiful spirit, and bright future will never be forgotten.”

A Boston Police Department spokesperson told The Independent that additional updates would be released as the investigation progresses.

The Boston Police Department Homicide Unit is actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the shooting. Anyone with information is urged to contact Boston homicide detectives at 617-343-4470.

Europe faces a fresh border crisis after around 60,000 migrants from Morocco crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in just 24 hours.

At least 43 people died as border security struggled to deal with the sudden influx, with extraordinary footage capturing the huge crowds making their way into Spain’s North African territory.

Some drowned in the crossing while others were killed in a stampede at the Tarajal beach fence near a border checkpoint with Morocco.

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sanchez called the incident an “attack on Spain’s territorial integrity” and vowed to “use all the resources of the state to guarantee security and coexistence”.

open image in gallery Migrants attempting to cross into Ceuta gather on a hilltop during clashes with Moroccan security forces ( AFP/Getty )

Ceuta and the larger Spanish territory of Melilla that is some 250 miles east of it, are located on the Mediterranean coast at the tip of Africa. They hold the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, called the scenes a “cause for concern” as the shadow home secretary Chris Philp warned Spain’s border crisis could “rapidly become our border crisis”.

The incident has also sparked a diplomatic row across Europe with Italy’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni calling for Spain’s suspension from the Schengen zone.

Thousands of people were seen attempting to breach the border by land and sea by swimming around coastal barriers and forcing their way through land-border infrastructure. It is one of the most significant breaches of the territory’s border in years.

Rachid Sbihi, head of the association representing Guardia Civil officers in Ceuta, described the scenes as “absolute chaos” and said the border had “totally collapsed”. He said the event was a “humanitarian crisis”.

open image in gallery Many of the migrants have been sent back after the border breach ( AFP/Getty )

Spain has deployed police and military personnel to deal with the crisis and promised that those involved will be sent back to Morocco.

On Friday, authorities confirmed that half of the migrants had already returned, many of them voluntarily.

Moroccan forces used water cannons, batons and tear gas at the Ceuta gates to prevent more crowds storming the autonomous Spanish territory.

Mr Sanchez went on to blame gangs for the crisis, saying that they “deceive so many young people, and ultimately lead many of them to their deaths, whether in the ocean or, as in this case, at Spain’s border in the autonomous city of Ceuta”.

Right-wing leaders in Europe were quick to condemn the incident, urging tighter controls of EU borders.

open image in gallery Migrants sit on rocks after swimming through the waters close to the border with Morocco ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery Children were among the crowds trying to make it across the border ( AFP/Getty )

Ms Meloni said that the “striking” images confirmed that “uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe’s borders”.

“Italy will not stand by and watch,” she wrote. “We are convening the relevant bodies, and following these meetings, we are prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain.

“On illegal immigration, we will not yield an inch: defending the borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriations will continue to be the line of this government.”

open image in gallery Spain’s leader Pedro Sanchez has called the breach an attack on the country’s territorial integrity ( Reuters )

France’s far-right politician Marine Le Pen accused the Spanish government of “encouraging” the crisis.

“Faced with the massive and coordinated influx of migrants into Spain, encouraged by the Spanish government, France must without delay strengthen controls at its borders,” she wrote in a post on X.

“And in 2027, we will put an end to this madness by reserving Schengen free movement for EU nationals.”

President of the EU Commission Ursula von der Leyen called for the swift return of migrants to Morocco, while German chancellor Friedrich Merz said: “The protection of the EU’s external borders is crucial for combating illegal migration.

“I support Spain’s intention not to allow illegal migrants onto the European continent. The EU’s Return Directive must now be implemented without delay.”

The surge is reportedly linked to a recent ruling by Spain’s supreme court, which concluded that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be deported or returned back under new rules. The decision does not apply to crossings by land.

Mr Sanchez said that the ruling had been misinterpreted.

“It appears that this interpretation of the Supreme Court’s ruling spread like wildfire over the past few hours through the networks of human trafficking organisations, triggering the kind of mass surge we witnessed yesterday,” he said.

Juan Jesus Vivas, mayor-president of Ceuta, called on the government to declare a national emergency. The interior ministry rejected the calls on the grounds that migration did not constitute a national emergency, but vowed to provide additional resources.

Opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo described the situation as a “national security crisis” and urged the government to take stronger action.

The chaotic scenes of tens of thousands of irregular migrants pouring into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, on the tip of the north coast of Africa, are simultaneously distressing and misleading.

The distress derives not only from the sight of people risking harm by trampling border fences or swimming around using inflatables, but also from the grievous fact that at least 57 have died in the process.

Some of those who’ve made the journey, by land or sea, are unaccompanied children from bordering Morocco, including a number who did not even tell their parents what they were doing.

The sheer scale of the numbers involved reminds us how the migration crisis continues, even with the most strenuous international efforts to restrain it. As many as 60,000 people are thought to have made it into Ceuta – whose population is just 85,000 – in a couple of days, with roughly half already back in Morocco. That is around the same order of magnitude as the number of small-boat arrivals in Britain in an entire year.

As a result, the Spanish government is in crisis, the army has been sent in, and the European Union has asserted its authority. On behalf of the European Commission, its president Ursula von der Leyen has called the situation “unacceptable”: “We cannot allow anyone to come to our union without abiding by our rules.”

There have been calls for the EU, and for certain member states, to suspend the Schengen Agreement, which facilitates passport-free travel within most of the continent. This is despite Ceuta and Melilla, the other tiny Spanish exclave in the area, actually lying outside the Schengen zone. Clearly, the proximity of the European mainland – just 10 miles off the coast of Ceuta – is too close for comfort for many. In any case, an emergency returns agreement has been reached between Madrid and Rabat. That will help.

Plainly, the security around Ceuta and, presumably, Melilla, is inadequate, though geography makes things unusually difficult. There have been similar surges before. Spain’s claim of sovereignty over the two exclaves is problematic and complicates matters: it is one of several continuing post-colonial-era grievances between the two countries that disrupt cooperation.

Yet highlighting the undeniably dramatic events in Ceuta can be misleading. In fact, more migrants enter Spanish territory in the Canary Islands and the Balearic Islands, and most of the new entrants will shortly be back in Morocco, if not sent further afield.

Moreover, the EU and its member states have had more success in reducing Mediterranean crossings recently. The numbers are certainly down by around a quarter compared to 2025, according to the EU’s border operation, Frontex. A combination of factors is at work here. The EU is able to use its collective diplomatic and financial muscle to persuade and fund its neighbours to take a more proactive approach to migrants arriving from Asia and Africa – Afghanistan and Eritrea, for example, being two of the major sources of would-be refugees. Nations such as Italy have also taken a tougher stance, in this case, paying the Libyan and Tunisian coastguards to intercept people on their way to Europe.

It is also important to recall that irregular migration into the UK is also now falling. Overall, in the first half of 2026, 190 boatloads of people have arrived in the UK, compared to 372 boats in the same period last year. Home Office data suggests 12,469 people had arrived in the UK on small boats by 10 July – down some 43 per cent from the same period in 2025.

Much always depends on weather conditions and geopolitics – wars normally cause a surge – but the trends in irregular and (far more significant numerically) legal migration are both firmly downwards.

So despite the immediate scaremongering by Reform politicians in Britain, the people being filmed breaking down fences and careening through the streets of Ceuta are not about to turn up in Dover or anywhere else in the UK.

The current crisis in North Africa merely underlines how difficult and intractable the migration issue continues to be – and how it cannot be easily resolved in a matter of weeks as the more irresponsible populists of the British right lazily claim.

It is clearly an international, cross-continental challenge that demands a multi-layered response; migration has to be balanced against an economic need for labour (skilled or otherwise) and universal human rights.

It is worth repeating at such a moment that migration can be welcome, is greatly beneficial, even if sometimes disorderly. This is an argument and a reality too frequently ignored. The Ceuta crisis doesn’t change that either.
