World.title: The Dislocated Dream: South Africa’s xenophobic problem and future of African unity, By Aitanu Elegbenosa Emmanuel
World.content:
Pan-Africanist dreams of enforced Pan-African unity and brotherhood as promised by Kwame Nkrumah are questioned by many commentators, citing instances of repeated xenophobic violence in South Africa as proof that Pan-African unity is not what Africans desire. The late Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and the late Nelson Mandela of South Africa both believed that Africa should be a continent of no boundaries where people from all African nations could live and work freely. But rather than a borderless Africa free of prejudices, South Africa has seen the emergence of waves of threatening xenophobic violence lately.

For instance, last month’s protests have resulted in the deaths of at least 7 people and have led thousands of businesses to shut down, forcing thousands of migrants from other African countries to flee to neighbouring countries. The ongoing diplomatic standoff between South Africa and its African neighbours may potentially derail attempts to create the world’s largest free trade zone in the near future, ruining the idea of Pan-African unity altogether.

The vision of a united Africa has long governed the interactions between Africa and the rest of the world. This vision is rooted in the principles of Pan-Africanism and is backed by contemporary agreements such as the African Continental Free Trade Area. But now, this dream has been put at risk by a very serious diplomatic and humanitarian crisis. Lately, there has been a noticeable rise in xenophobic attacks in South Africa against migrants from Nigeria, Ghana, and other African countries.

This has led many people to leave their homes, and there was an unprecedented response from two of the most powerful West African countries. The issues are so serious that even Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the current president of Nigeria, refused to meet with a delegation from South Africa. At the same time, Ghana stopped a visit by the president of South Africa. Thus, the issue that was originally about immigration within South Africa has quickly transformed into diplomatic problems in the region. Now, considering the consequences of these brutal attacks and the diplomatic crisis, there is a question about African unity and cooperation. Both Nigeria and Ghana are outraged over the situation – Nigeria states it does not approve of the killing and the attacking of its nationals.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

At the same time, Ghana laments the death of one of its citizens in the protests. To enhance the safety of people involved, emergency programs are launched aimed at delivering migrants to their home countries. Nigeria has already returned about 1,500 of its people on commercial flights, and Ghana has brought back more than 900 of its nationals.

However, there are still thousands of migrants waiting to depart in temporary camps at the borders of South Africa, which is the major economy of Africa – people are living in terrible conditions and want to get out. When the meeting began, Ambassador Enikanolaiye made his dissatisfaction known, opening up about the issues his administration was having. Ambassador Enikanolaiye welcomed the South African officials warmly, stating, “We are pleased to have brothers from South Africa.” But although his tone was nice, it was evident that there was concern and urgency in the air.

Echoing his earlier statement, he told one of the participants that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu requested this meeting to discuss the recent spate of incidents of Afrophobia in South Africa. These events had left Nigerians and Africans reeling. The fact that this meeting was taking place meant that Nigeria was sending a message loud and clear from Abuja – the time for mere condolences was over. In fact, Nigerian lawmakers had already begun taking a tougher approach and had called for the cancellation of the licenses of the South African companies operating in Nigeria.

The same chill has descended upon the capital of Ghana, Accra. The country has decided to cancel President Ramaphosa’s planned visit, originally scheduled for August 2026. The decision came amid fears that the visit could lead to public unrest in Accra. Felix Kwakye Ofosu, the spokesperson for the government of Ghana, notified the press about the decision to postpone the meeting. He stated, “We have suggested to them that they should postpone the visit in light of the current climate of xenophobia with respect to the fact that they are not favourable to foreigners.”

Pretoria made efforts to clarify the situation about the diplomatic crisis between Ghana and the Republic of South Africa. They have emphasised that the meeting was always planned to be a routine session of the South Africa–Ghana Bi-National Commission and not the official visit as President Ramaphosa initially intended. South Africa’s presidential spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya, is trying to downplay the significance of the crisis between the two countries and assures that South Africa remains open to further cooperation with Ghana through diplomatic channels and will try to find a date that fits both parties. “We will find a date which will work for both parties,” says Magwenya.

South Africa is facing some serious troubles. There are big discrepancies in wealth in the state, unemployment is very high, and crime is a serious problem. Occasionally, foreigners face accusations in connection with these problems, but the government disagrees with this stance, claiming that the real culprit is illegal migration. They are convinced that if they manage to sort out law enforcement and immigration issues, everything will be back to normal; however, the reality is more complicated. The issues facing South Africa are rooted in the country’s history and its socio-economic structures.

The government must consider how to solve the problems and make long-term plans that address the root causes, including job creation, reducing inequality, and providing equal access to socio-economic opportunities. The process of solving these problems is arduous but the only possible way to establish an equitable and peaceful society.

Minister Ronald Lamola’s statements regarding the visit of the Nigerian delegation in the city of Abuja indicate South Africa’s firmness in fighting against intolerance, in any form it may appear. When it comes to immigration issues, Lamola insisted that South Africa will protect its sovereignty as well as its citizens from becoming victims of crimes committed by illegal immigrants and their actions. He is sure that the law will be enforced as a sign of South Africa’s stand.

It seems that a new change is appearing in African politics and that Nigeria is joining Ghana to fight against the phenomenon called “Afrophobia”. In popularising their ideas, they got the help of their fellow politicians from West Africa. They are likely to make this issue one of the points on the agenda for the next meeting of the African Union. They argue that Africans are being persecuted too much – which is contrary to the principles of free movement and economic integration in Africa. It is a significant issue as it affects the ability of African nations to cooperate and develop their economies.

The African Union has laid down specific provisions for the free movement of people among nations, but the practice of targeting African nationals undermines the stated objectives. Nigeria and Ghana are demanding that this issue be put on the agenda of the meeting and have the backing of several West African countries supporting their position. It could be a significant step toward a more united and prosperous Africa.

Finally, the xenophobic crisis in South Africa is no longer merely the internal problem of the country, but has transformed into a serious test for Pan-African solidarity. The diplomatic steps that the governments of Nigeria and Ghana made exemplify a zero-tolerance policy pursued by the countries, which are no longer prepared to pay either the human or economic costs of anti-migrant violence.

Now, when the African Union was about to respond to the crisis, it could not be more serious. If the leading countries of the continent cannot find common ground between the sovereign right to rule the country the way they deem it right and the obligation to protect the lives of Africans, then the concept of borderless Africa will never be transformed into reality.

Why did the crisis emerge?

The economy of South Africa is undergoing severe difficulty. Inequality in South Africa is amongst the highest in the world. Statistics South Africa reported that the rate of unemployment in the first quarter of 2026 was 32.7%. Unemployment amongst youth alone was slightly below 45%. In informal settlements where there are no services available, and infrastructure is poor, migrants have become scapegoats of the failure of the state to provide basics.

While some advocates of tightening migration regulations allege that those undocumented migrants flooding the country are vanquishing hospitals, schools and the informal labour market, President Cyril Ramaphosa observes this pressure and pretends to seek stability in the country. “We should never allow the legitimate concerns of our communities regarding illegal migration to breed prejudice against our fellow Africans,” he stated during his Freedom Day speech in April 2026. He also warned against “trampling to dust the African fellowship that made our freedom possible.”

The anti-immigrant campaigns are a betrayal of Pan-Africanism for numerous people across the continent. Recently, Nigeria, Ghana, and Malawi have started programs for their citizens returning voluntarily to their respective countries based on concern for them in South Africa, where violence against foreigners is on the rise. The African Union has been urging governments to find solutions to this issue.

“We condemn the killings in the strongest terms possible,” the Chair of the African Union Commission, Moussa Faki Mahamat, said, demanding that South African authorities punish the offenders and act against any outbreak of violence in the country.

The Uncertain Future of Integration

The South African crisis is not just about racism and race relations, but is also related to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which will be the world’s largest free trade area based on the number of signatories. The success of AfCFTA depends on how well Africans manage to behave in a business-like manner. There would be no integration and free trade in Africa as a solution for poverty unless there is a guarantee for safe entry of Africans from other countries into South Africa.

“Economic integration also necessarily implies trust and communication between people,” says one of the documents from the Nkafu Policy Institute. “In case of being threatened with violence and discrimination in other African countries, there can be no regional economic integration.”

The South African government is in a difficult position. It has pledged to uphold the Constitution by ensuring the rule of law and safeguarding all individuals within its territory. Nevertheless, a huge political challenge remains for it—the obligation to demonstrate that in the current sluggish economic realities it puts its citizens first.

Last month, South Africa’s Minister of International Relations and Cooperation, Ronald Lamola, said: “Leading with a Pan-African heart means that we will continue to respect the right of people to move.” “At the same time, migration has to be based on principles of cooperation, compassion, and continental responsibility,” he further stated. According to Lamola, the African Union has to deal with the “push and pull factors” that force people to leave their homelands where there is neither law nor economic activity.

In conclusion: The Crossroads of Unity

The menace of xenophobic violence looms over South Africa, frightening other African nations. South African xenophobia indicates a huge underlying problem concerning the disparity between Pan-African statements and economic reality. Therefore, South Africa’s experience is a warning for the continent. If the agreements signed in Addis Ababa are to mean anything, something must be done to improve social cohesion in such areas as Soweto or Alexandra. The time ahead requires South Africa to resolve its imploding economic model without losing its moral authority earned during the anti-apartheid struggle.

As for the rest of Africa, Project Africa should realize that unity is not something we received with independence; this is something we must work hard to achieve and preserve.

*Emmanuel Elegbenosa Aitanu serves as the CEO of EEA & GOA Investment Ltd, where he plays a pivotal role in steering the company’s strategic direction across diverse investment sectors, including cryptocurrency, real estate, and agricultural ventures.

World.title: NITDA’s new framework and the future of Nigeria’s digital ecosystem, By Shuaib S. Agaka
World.content:
As the country seeks to expand digital public infrastructure, strengthen cybersecurity and position local technology companies for international competitiveness, software quality cannot remain an afterthought. Reliable digital services build public confidence. Secure systems protect national assets. High-quality software enhances economic competitiveness.

Every Nigerian has encountered it at one point or another, an online service that freezes midway through an application, a payment platform that crashes during peak hours, a government portal that disappears just when it is needed most, or a mobile app that works flawlessly one day and inexplicably fails the next. These experiences have become so common that many people have come to accept unreliable software as a fact of life.

But poor software is more than an inconvenience. It wastes time, drains public resources, exposes sensitive data to cyber threats and gradually erodes confidence in digital services. In an economy increasingly dependent on technology, software quality is no longer merely a concern for developers, it is a matter of public trust.

That is why the National Information Technology Development Agency’s (NITDA) newly unveiled National Software Quality Assurance (SQA) Framework deserves attention. While the announcement may appear technical at first glance, its implications extend far beyond programmers and IT departments. It signals an effort to ensure that software serving Nigerians, whether powering government services, financial institutions, healthcare systems or private businesses, is built to be secure, reliable and fit for purpose.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The framework introduces nationally recognised standards covering software design, secure coding, testing, documentation and certification before deployment. For high-risk digital systems, particularly those supporting critical infrastructure, it mandates independent third-party testing before they go live.

The emphasis on quality is timely.

Digital transformation is accelerating across both the public and private sectors. Government agencies continue to digitise services, banks are expanding digital channels, hospitals are adopting electronic health systems, schools increasingly rely on online learning platforms, while startups are building applications that serve millions of users. As society becomes more dependent on software, the consequences of software failure become more severe.

A single vulnerability can expose millions of records. A poorly tested application can halt critical services. Even minor defects can translate into enormous financial losses when multiplied across millions of transactions.

Perhaps the most significant shift introduced by the framework is philosophical. Rather than responding to failures after they occur, it encourages organisations to build quality into software from the beginning. Secure coding practices, structured development processes, rigorous testing and independent validation become integral parts of software development, instead of optional extras added before launch.

This reflects a broader global movement towards “security by design” and “quality by design”, the recognition that resilience cannot simply be patched into software after deployment.

The framework also arrives at a time when questions are increasingly being asked about the quality of Nigeria’s digital public infrastructure.

Investigative reports have repeatedly highlighted government websites that contain outdated information, broken links, inaccessible pages and inconsistent user experiences. Some ministry and agency websites appear to receive attention only when a new leadership assumes office, with updates largely limited to replacing photographs and official profiles, while the underlying platforms remain neglected.

These observations echo concerns raised recently by the Director-General of the Bureau of Public Service Reforms (BPSR), who disclosed that the agency’s ongoing assessment of government websites had found that none evaluated so far had achieved even 10 per cent compliance with established standards.

Although NITDA’s framework is much broader than website management, such findings illustrate why standards matter. Digital transformation is not simply about putting services online. It is about ensuring that the systems citizens rely upon are usable, secure, accessible and consistently maintained throughout their lifecycle.

Yet reducing the framework to government websites alone would miss its wider significance.

Its greatest impact may well be on Nigeria’s broader software ecosystem.

For years, software testing has often been overshadowed by software development itself. Many organisations have prioritised launching products quickly, sometimes at the expense of comprehensive quality assurance. Under the new framework, software testing becomes a recognised discipline with regulatory backing through the accreditation of Licensed Software Testing Organisations responsible for independently evaluating software before deployment.

That could stimulate demand for quality assurance engineers, cybersecurity specialists, penetration testers and software auditors, creating new opportunities for indigenous technology firms while encouraging companies to invest in internationally recognised testing capabilities.

For startups, stronger quality standards may initially appear to introduce additional compliance obligations. In reality, they could become a competitive advantage. Products that meet recognised national and international standards are more likely to gain the confidence of enterprise customers, government institutions and overseas markets. In a global digital economy where trust increasingly determines adoption, demonstrable quality can become a powerful business asset.

The framework’s risk-based classification model also reflects a practical understanding that not all software carries equal consequences. A system controlling financial transactions, managing digital identities or supporting critical infrastructure requires far more rigorous scrutiny than an internal administrative application. By tailoring compliance requirements to operational risk, the framework avoids imposing a one-size-fits-all approach while ensuring that systems with the greatest public impact receive the highest level of assurance.

Implementation, however, will determine whether the framework fulfils its promise.

Standards are only meaningful when consistently enforced. Government institutions must embrace quality assurance as an operational necessity rather than another compliance exercise. Software companies will need to strengthen their engineering practices, while universities and professional training institutions may have to expand programmes in software testing, cybersecurity and quality assurance to meet future workforce demand.

The planned accreditation of testing organisations and stakeholder capacity-building initiatives therefore represent critical early steps.

Perhaps the framework’s most enduring contribution lies in what it says about Nigeria’s digital ambitions.

As the country seeks to expand digital public infrastructure, strengthen cybersecurity and position local technology companies for international competitiveness, software quality cannot remain an afterthought. Reliable digital services build public confidence. Secure systems protect national assets. High-quality software enhances economic competitiveness.

Ultimately, digital transformation is measured not by the number of applications launched or portals created, but by whether people can depend on them when it matters most.

NITDA’s National Software Quality Assurance Framework does not guarantee flawless software overnight. Nor will it eliminate every vulnerability or system failure. But by placing quality, security and accountability at the centre of software development, it establishes an important foundation for a more trustworthy digital future.

In the digital world, trust is earned long before users click “Submit.” It is built into every line of code, every security test and every quality check. By recognising this simple but powerful truth, Nigeria is taking a meaningful step towards designing not just better software, but greater confidence in its digital future.

Shuaib S. Agaka is a tech journalist and digital policy analyst based in Kano.

World.title: FG says no plan to increase electricity tariffs
World.content:
The federal government has said it has no immediate plans to increase electricity tariffs, stressing that its priority is improving power supply, expanding metering and ensuring Nigerians pay only for the electricity they consume.

The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this on Friday during a media interactive session in Lagos.

The clarification came amid concerns over rising electricity costs following previous tariff reviews, particularly for Band A customers, and growing calls for improved power supply before any further pricing adjustments.

“There is no policy by this administration to increase electricity tariffs beyond its current level.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Our priority is not tariff increase in the immediate term. Our priority is service improvement, universal metering and ensuring Nigerians pay only for the electricity they actually consume,” Mr Tegbe said.

He added that the federal government would continue to explore measures to protect vulnerable consumers while improving the financial sustainability of the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry (NESI).

“Indeed, the Federal Government will continue to examine additional mechanisms for protecting vulnerable consumers whilst simultaneously improving the financial sustainability of the market,” he said.

Transformation Agenda

The minister said the power ministry had developed a comprehensive sector transformation agenda aimed at improving electricity generation, strengthening transmission infrastructure, enhancing distribution efficiency and restoring market liquidity.

According to him, the ministry has already commenced several interventions, including the inauguration of the Power Force, a programme that will engage 5,000 youths in electricity meter installation nationwide to accelerate universal metering while building technical capacity in the sector.

He added that progress had been made in resolving long-standing meter procurement challenges, noting that Nigeria had consistently generated over 5,000 megawatts of electricity during the past two weeks through improved coordination across the power value chain.

“Although much work remains, enhanced operational coordination, improved plant availability and better engagement across the value chain are beginning to produce measurable improvements,” he said.

Technical audit

Mr Tegbe also disclosed that the federal government would undertake the first comprehensive technical audit of Nigeria’s national transmission network to identify ageing assets, overloaded substations, weak transmission corridors, protection failures, and other operational vulnerabilities that hinder reliable electricity supply.

He said the audit would guide investment decisions, reduce system failures and improve planning.

He added that the government would strengthen critical transmission infrastructure, improve grid stability and address long-standing liquidity challenges in the electricity market, while advancing a Power Sector Bond initiative to clear legacy debts owed to generation companies, gas suppliers and other market participants.

The minister expressed optimism that the reforms would begin to deliver visible improvements in electricity availability within the next few months, with Nigerians expected to experience a stronger grid, lower technical losses, expanded electricity access and greater operational capacity over the next two to three years.

World.title: Hausa singer Rarara’s new song on Pantami attracts backlash
World.content:
A new political song released on Thursday by popular Hausa singer Dauda Kahutu—better known as Rarara —targeting former Minister of Communications and Digital Economy, Isa Pantami, has sparked severe backlash against the singer over its lyrics.

The song, which accuses Mr Pantami of drug use, praises Gombe State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate Jamilu Gwamna.

Mr Pantami is the governorship candidate of the Wike-backed People’s Democratic Party (PDP).

The track has drawn widespread criticism across social media, with many commentators arguing that the singer misfired.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Rather than damaging Mr Pantami’s reputation to benefit the APC candidate as intended, critics say the song has instead generated public sympathy for the former minister.

Former Minister of Sports and Youth Development, Solomon Dalung, expressed worry over the declining standard of political discourse in northern Nigeria, sharply criticising the use of crude personal attacks in the song.

Commenting on the backlash against the political singer, Mr Dalung lamented that political music, once a tool for education, inspiration, and civic mobilisation in the North, has degenerated into character assassination and public ridicule.

Mr Dalung noted that while political criticism is a crucial aspect of public accountability, public figures should be held to account based on facts rather than personal attacks.

“There was a time when political songs in the North inspired, educated, and mobilised,” Mr Dalung said. “Even the harshest praise singers understood there were lines that decent people simply did not cross. Today, it seems those lines have disappeared.”

He expressed concern that traditional northern Nigerian virtues are being eroded in the pursuit of political point-scoring.

“The North prides itself on adabi (good manners), kunya (modesty), and respect for human dignity,” the former minister stated.

“Those values should not evaporate because someone has taken a political position we disagree with. If Sheikh Pantami is wrong, challenge him with facts. If his politics are inconsistent, expose the inconsistencies. If his public statements deserve scrutiny, scrutinise them.”

The former minister condemned the normalisation of unverified allegations and insult-driven rhetoric on public platforms, warning that double standards threaten the moral fabric of northern political culture.

According to Mr Dalung, the most troubling aspect of the song is the applause the song has received from partisans who would ordinarily condemn similar attacks if directed at leaders they support.

“Principles are only meaningful when they apply equally to friends and opponents,” he cautioned.

“We cannot claim to be defending Northern values while celebrating conduct that erodes the very values our elders taught us.”

Warning of the long-term consequences on northern politics, Mr Dalung urged political actors and commentators to elevate the quality of public discourse.

“Politics will come and go. Governments will rise and fall,” he noted. “But once we normalise indecency as a campaign strategy, rebuilding a culture of respectful disagreement becomes far more difficult. Our disagreements should sharpen our intellect, not coarse our character. The North deserves a higher standard of politics than this.”

Abdulaziz Jauro, from Adamawa state, posted on Facebook that using veiled metaphors to disguise character assassination does not make it art.

Rather than demonstrating creative skill, the piece is presented as a malicious, hollow attack designed purely to ruin a reputation under the guise of symbolism.

Mr Abdulaziz said Rarara leveraged a large public platform to monetise insults, damage societal norms, and degrade civil public discourse.

“Rarara’s latest composition aimed at Professor Pantami exemplifies a troubling descent into artistic insolvency and ethical dereliction. Cloaking insinuations in flimsy allegorical devices does not elevate defamatory rhetoric into sophisticated expression; it merely obscures intellectual vacuity beneath a veneer of performative symbolism. What masquerades as creativity is, in reality, a calculated exercise in reputational vandalism.

“It is profoundly disconcerting that an individual with considerable public reach has chosen to commodify invective, transforming his platform into an instrument of calculated calumny rather than cultural enrichment. Such rhetorical nihilism contributes nothing to public enlightenment; instead, it normalises the corrosion of civic discourse and rewards sensationalism over substance.

“This is not artistic courage. It is an exhibition of moral bankruptcy, discursive delinquency and an astonishing abdication of the ethical obligations that accompany influence. When talent is subordinated to character assassination, the result is neither music nor commentary; it is simply the degradation of both art and public conversation”, Mr Jauro said.

READ ALSO: Fake university disclaims honorary doctorate awarded to Nigerian singer Rarara

Another commentator, Nuhu Dantani, cautioned Gombe APC governorship candidate, Mr Gwamna, over what he described as the erosion of support for APC candidates following the release of the controversial new song.

“I am a supporter of Dr Jamilu Isyaku Gwamna, and I believe he is a good man. However, if he fails in the 2027 Gombe governorship contest, Rarara should be held accountable,” Mr Dantani, a lawyer and rights activist, said.

He warned that the campaign track produced by Mr Rarara inadvertently boosted the profile of former Mr Pantami instead.

“In his song, he only succeeded in raising Prof Pantami’s popularity and enhancing his dignity and respect. On election day, the impact of this mistake will become clear.”

World.title: Liverpool stars Curtis Jones, Szoboszlai clash in heated on-pitch exchange
World.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye

Liverpool midfielders Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai were involved in a heated on-pitch argument following the Reds’ 1-0 pre-season victory over Wrexham in New York.

According to BBC Sport, the pair exchanged words shortly after the final whistle as Liverpool players walked around Yankee Stadium to applaud supporters. Defender Kostas Tsimikas later joined the confrontation, with television footage appearing to show him throwing the captain’s armband onto the pitch during the exchange.

The reason behind the disagreement remains unclear, although BBC Sport noted that Szoboszlai handed the captain’s armband to Tsimikas rather than Jones when he was substituted during the match.

Asked about the incident, Szoboszlai declined to discuss the details but insisted the squad remains united.

We want the best for the club and for each other,” the Hungary international told BBC Sport.

“Now that a couple of guys have left and maybe we are not the oldest in the team but we’ve been here a long time, we are all in the same boat and we want the best for the club and for each other.”

He added that the players are fully behind captain Virgil van Dijk and manager Andoni Iraola as Liverpool continue adapting under their new head coach.

“We have a captain in Virgil [van Dijk] and we will follow him everywhere with what he and the gaffer says and I think I can talk from everybody’s side that we want to be successful this season.

“It’s a long term [project] because obviously we have a new manager and the team has been changed. Maybe not in a couple of months but in the long term, I think it will work out.”

Liverpool sources, however, played down the incident, maintaining that disagreements between teammates are common in elite football and suggesting the exchange only became public because the players were completing a post-match lap of appreciation rather than returning directly to the dressing room.

The incident comes amid continued speculation over Jones’ future after Liverpool rejected a reported £21.7 million bid from Inter Milan earlier this summer.

The England midfielder has one year remaining on his contract, with Iraola recently describing him as “a great, great player” and expressing his desire for him to remain at Anfield.

World.title: Court jails yahoo boys’ middleman four years for money laundering
World.content:
By Innocent Anaba

Justice Akintayo Aluko of the Federal High Court sitting in Ikoyi, Lagos, has convicted and sentenced Sunmonu Olasunkanmi Thaoban to four years’ imprisonment for money laundering offences.

Sunmonu was prosecuted by the Lagos Zonal Directorate 1 of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) on a two-count charge bordering on money laundering.

The EFCC alleged that the convict, while acting as a middleman in 2023, disguised the origin of ₦16 million believed to be proceeds of unlawful activities by converting the funds into a black 2018 G-Wagon Jeep.

The prosecution said the offence contravened provisions of the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act, 2022.

Sunmonu pleaded guilty to both counts.

Following his plea, EFCC counsel, H.U. Kofarnaisa, reviewed the facts of the case and urged the court to convict and sentence him accordingly.

Justice Aluko found him guilty and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, with an option of a ₦1.8 million fine.

The court also ordered the forfeiture of the black G-Wagon Jeep and a mobile device belonging to the convict to the Federal Government.

Meanwhile, the court also convicted and sentenced four Bureau de Change (BDC) operators to 12 months’ imprisonment each for engaging in illegal foreign exchange transactions.

The convicts — Umar Muhammad Lamido, Yusuf Musa Yusuf, Abdulmuhimin Mahmud and Muhammed Musa — were prosecuted by the EFCC on separate one-count charges bordering on illegal foreign exchange operations.

They all pleaded guilty to the charges.

After reviewing the facts of the cases, Kofarnaisa urged the court to convict and sentence the defendants accordingly.

Justice Aluko subsequently convicted the four BDC operators and sentenced each of them to 12 months’ imprisonment, with an option of a ₦100,000 fine.

The EFCC said the convictions reaffirm its commitment to enforcing financial regulations and prosecuting individuals involved in economic crimes.

World.title: Court jails two Chinese nationals 25 years each for illegal mineral export
World.content:
By Innocent Anaba

Justice Akintayo Aluko of the Federal High Court in Lagos has convicted and sentenced two Chinese nationals, Zhang Hong Lin and Gao Pei Hai, to 25 years’ imprisonment each for offences related to the illegal export of Nigeria’s strategic mineral resources.

The judge found the defendants guilty on all five counts filed against them by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), which included conspiracy, unlawful possession and attempted exportation of strategic minerals without lawful authority.

Justice Aluko sentenced each defendant to 25 years’ imprisonment on each of the five counts, with an option of a ₦10 million fine on each count. He also ordered that the sentences take effect from the date of their arrest.

In addition, the court ordered the forfeiture of all the mineral resources involved in the case to the Federal Government.

The defendants were arraigned alongside a third suspect, Gao Pei Yu, who is currently at large.

According to the charge filed before the court on May 28, 2025, the defendants allegedly conspired to defraud the Federal Government of revenue by attempting to export strategic mineral resources without the required authorisation.

The prosecution alleged that the offences were committed in Lagos and contravened the provisions of the Miscellaneous Offences Act, 1983.

The EFCC further accused the defendants of unlawfully possessing mineral resources intended for export without lawful authority.

The minerals listed in the charge included mica minerals such as Muscovite and Lepidolite; lithium-bearing ores including Spodumene and Petalite; and other minerals associated with copper deposits, including Bornite and Cuprite, as well as Anhydrite, Quartz and Magnesite.

After reviewing the evidence presented by the prosecution, Justice Aluko held that the EFCC had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt against the two convicted defendants and accordingly entered judgment against them.

World.title: Naira depreciates to N1,415/$ in parallel market
World.content:
By Elizabeth Adegbesan

The Naira today depreciated to N1,415 per dollar in the parallel market from N1,410 per dollar on Thursday.

But the naira appreciated to N1,368 per dollar in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, NFEM .

Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, showed that the indicative exchange rate for the naira fell to N1368 per dollar from N1368.5 per dollar on Thursday, indicating a 50kobo appreciation for the naira.

Consequently, the margin between the parallel and official markets widened to N47 per dollar from N41.5 per dollar on Thursday.

The interbank turnover at NFEM rose by 1.01 percent to N58.99 million yesterday from N58.4 million on Thursday.

World.title: Canadian citizenship rules changed: 5 things to know
World.content:
Canada has changed its citizenship-by-descent rules following the passage of Bill C-3 on December 15, 2025.

The changes removed the previous first-generation limit for certain people born abroad before that date, potentially allowing more people with Canadian ancestry to claim Canadian citizenship.

However, the changes do not mean everyone with a Canadian connection automatically becomes a citizen.

Here are five things to know about the new rules.

1. The First-Generation Limit Has Been Removed

Bill C-3 removed Canada’s previous first-generation limit on citizenship by descent for people born before December 15, 2025.

This means some individuals born outside Canada may now be recognised as Canadian citizens through a parent or more distant Canadian ancestor.

The change could affect people who were previously unable to claim Canadian citizenship because their connection to Canada extended beyond the first generation born abroad.

2. You Still Have to Prove Your Canadian Citizenship

Being eligible for Canadian citizenship and proving that citizenship are two different things.

People who believe they are Canadian under the new rules may need to apply for a Canadian citizenship certificate, which serves as official proof of their citizenship.

The certificate can then be used when applying for a Canadian passport and accessing other rights and benefits associated with Canadian citizenship.

3. You Need Documents Linking Each Generation

Applicants cannot necessarily rely on a single document showing that an ancestor was Canadian.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) requires evidence establishing the family connection through the relevant generations.

For example, an applicant may need birth certificates, marriage certificates and other official records showing how they are related to their Canadian ancestor.

IRCC has emphasised the importance of providing “proof of parentage and Canadian citizenship for your Canadian parent, grandparent and parental ancestor as applicable.”

The aim is to establish a clear documentary chain between the applicant and the Canadian citizen in their family history.

4. Certain Circumstances Can Affect Eligibility

Having a Canadian ancestor does not automatically guarantee citizenship.

The citizenship chain can be affected by circumstances such as a parent renouncing Canadian citizenship before a child was born.

Another issue can arise where a parent became a Canadian citizen only after their child was born. In such cases, the child may not have acquired Canadian citizenship through that parent at birth.

Because citizenship histories can be complicated, applicants with unusual circumstances may need professional advice before submitting an application.

5. Check Your Family History Before Applying

Anyone who believes they may qualify should first establish their family’s citizenship history.

This includes finding out where each relevant family member was born, when they acquired Canadian citizenship, whether anyone changed their name and whether anyone renounced their citizenship.

Applicants should then gather official documents that establish the connection between the generations.

The new rules could open the door to Canadian citizenship for people who were previously excluded by the first-generation limit, but eligibility still depends on the details of each individual case.

Before applying for proof of citizenship, it is therefore important to understand your family history and ensure that the necessary documentation is available.

World.title: Osun election: IGP deploy Etaifor as Osun commissioner for election
World.content:
By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

In a bid to ensure neutrality of security agencies in the conduct of the August 15 governorship election in Osun State, the Inspector General of Police, Tunji Disu, has deployed CP Election, Mr Erale Samuel Etaifo, to the State to oversee the security architecture for the election.

A statement issued by the Osun Police Command spokesperson, DSP Abiodun Ojelabi, on Friday, stated that CP Etaifo will coordinate election security operations in collaboration with other security agencies and relevant stakeholders to ensure strict compliance with the Electoral Act, the Code of Conduct for Security Personnel on Electoral Duty, and all extant laws guiding the electoral process.

The statement further warned political actors, their supporters, and other stakeholders to conduct themselves peacefully and refrain from acts capable of undermining public order.

It reads partly, “The Osun State Police Command assures members of the public that adequate security measures have been emplaced across the State to protect lives, property, and critical electoral materials before, during, and after the election. All officers and men deployed for election duty have been directed to remain impartial, professional, and respectful of the rights of every citizen, irrespective of political affiliation.

“Electoral violence, vote buying, voter intimidation, the spread of misinformation, and any other form of criminality will be met with the full weight of the law. The command urges residents to remain law-abiding, cooperate with security agencies, and promptly report any suspicious activities through the Command’s emergency channels.

“The Nigeria Police Force remains committed to providing a level playing field for all political parties and ensuring that the will of the people prevails through a peaceful, credible, and transparent electoral process”.

World.title: Bello commends Tinubu’s security gains, meets NSA Ribadu
World.content:
Former Governor of Kogi State, His Excellency Yahaya Bello, CON, on Friday commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for the steady progress being made in the fight against insecurity across the country.

Bello gave the commendation during a meeting with the National Security Adviser, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, at the Office of the National Security Adviser in Abuja.

Speaking after the meeting, the former governor noted that the recent foiling of an attempted abduction of schoolchildren in Kogi State underscored the level of support the state continues to receive from the Federal Government. He attributed the successful operation to the vigilance, professionalism and improved coordination among the nation’s security agencies, describing it as clear evidence that intelligence-driven security operations are yielding positive results.

“I want to use this opportunity to commend Mr President and our leader, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, for his relentless efforts in tackling insecurity across the nation. I also want to commend him and your humble self on the recent foiling of an attempted abduction of schoolchildren in Kogi State, which underscores the level of support the state continues to receive from the Federal Government. I attribute the successful operation to the vigilance, professionalism and improved coordination among the nation’s security agencies, which is clear evidence that intelligence-driven security operations are yielding positive results,” he said.

Bello particularly praised the National Security Adviser for providing strategic leadership and fostering stronger collaboration among the various security and intelligence agencies. According to him, the synergy under Ribadu’s coordination has significantly strengthened the country’s capacity to respond swiftly to emerging security threats.

He also commended President Tinubu for his unwavering commitment to restoring peace and security across Nigeria, noting that the administration’s sustained investment in intelligence gathering, security coordination and operational support has continued to bolster the morale and effectiveness of security personnel working tirelessly to protect lives and property.

Commenting on the recent rescue of the abducted schoolchildren in Oyo State, Bello applauded President Tinubu, the National Security Adviser and the security agencies for their painstaking efforts, professionalism and determination in securing the victims’ safe release. He paid tribute to the brave officers who made the ultimate sacrifice during the operation, describing their courage and selflessness as a testament to their commitment to the defence of the nation.

“Mr President also deserves commendation for the recent rescue of the abducted schoolchildren in Oyo State. I equally commend you, my brother, the National Security Adviser, and, of course, the security agencies for your painstaking efforts, professionalism and determination in securing the safe release of the victims. I also pay tribute to the brave officers who made the ultimate sacrifice during the operation. Their courage and selflessness remain a testament to their unwavering commitment to the defence of our country,” he said.

The National Security Adviser, while thanking the former governor for the visit, stressed that the security of lives and property is everyone’s responsibility and that collective action is essential to overcoming insecurity in Nigeria.

“I want to warmly welcome you to my office this afternoon, my brother. The issue of insecurity concerns everyone in this country, and I believe that if we all play our part at our various levels, we shall overcome insecurity in Nigeria,” he said.

The former governor further urged Nigerians to continue supporting the efforts of the Federal Government and the security agencies by remaining vigilant and providing timely, credible information that could assist security operations. He noted that tackling insecurity requires collective responsibility and sustained cooperation between citizens and security institutions.

Bello expressed confidence that, under the leadership of President Tinubu and with the strategic guidance of the National Security Adviser, Nigeria would continue to record significant gains in the fight against criminality.

He maintained that the ongoing security reforms and strengthened inter-agency collaboration were laying a solid foundation for lasting peace, stability and national development.

World.title: 2027: Vote Tinubu, not Obi, Umahi tells South-East, warns against ‘taking risks’
World.content:

The Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi, has said that he’s not attacking the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) Presidential candidate, Mr. Peter Obi, but asking the South-East people not to vote for him.

He said that he had been proud to work for President Bola Tinubu’s reelection due to his infrastructural projects in Nigeria, especially in the South East zone.

Umahi stated this during an inspection project Trans-Sahara highway and Legacy projects that cut across Cross River–Abuja.

Umahi disclosed that Section One of the Cross River–Abuja Legacy Highway, covering about 125 kilometres, was nearing completion, with more than 30 per cent of the alignment traversing Ebonyi communities.
