Here's what you need to know.

WATCH | FIFA's World Cup profits soar: How FIFA got even richer this World Cup | Duration 2:24 CBC’s Jonathon Gatehouse breaks down how Gianni Infantino doubled profits for the 2026 World Cup, and how much of that money ends up in the hands of organizations like Soccer Canada.

What are FIFA, UEFA and the other soccer confederations?

The Fédération Internationale de Football Association is the international governing body of association football, also known as soccer. Founded in 1904 and headquartered in Switzerland, FIFA today has many stated objectives , including overseeing the development and innovation in the sport, conducting disciplinary matters and organizing international tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cup.

FIFA's membership is currently comprised of 211 national soccer federations (such as Canada Soccer), which are the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law.

Each national federation is also a member of six continental confederations that oversee the sport in their respective regions:

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol (CONMEBOL).

Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF).

Oceania Football Confederation (OFC).

Union of European Football Associations (UEFA).

UEFA is arguably the most powerful of the six, as it counts many of the sport's most successful countries among its 55 members — including France, Germany, Italy and current world champion Spain — as well as the four "home nations" of the United Kingdom, where the sport was formalized.

Infantino, left, stands with Spanish Football Association president Rafael Louzán after the trophy ceremony for the World Cup final on July 19. Spain would be one of the nations involved in a UEFA boycott. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

What is the FIFA plan causing the latest furor?

On Tuesday, FIFA president Gianni Infantino announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup.

Under FIFA's plan, which was pitched as a way to boost the development of soccer around the world, 20 per cent of FFE would be sold off to private investors, including a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, brother of U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

National federations that approve FFE would see their promised $8 million US development funds from FIFA more than doubled to $20 million US for the next four years. It would then increase to $22 million US and $24 million US in the following cycles through 2038, FIFA said.

What was UEFA's reaction?

The continental confederations appear to have been blindsided by Infantino's announcement.

Almost immediately, UEFA called an emergency meeting of its member federations. On Thursday, it released a strongly worded statement saying its members would boycott all the global soccer body's competitions as long as the FEE proposal remains on the table.

UEFA delivered a stinging rebuke of Infantino's plan, saying "the World Cup is not for sale."

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors."

It added that FIFA's plan, under which "commercial return becomes a permanent obligation" and "investor expectations become a daily pressure," would upend the way soccer is governed.

"You're giving undue influence to people that are not going to necessarily be motivated by what's best for soccer but what's best for their bank accounts," said Moshe Lander, a sports economist at Concordia University in Montreal.

Spanish players celebrate after winning the 2023 Women's World Cup at the final in Sydney, Australia. The next Women's World Cup is scheduled to be hosted in Brazil in summer 2027. (Hannah Mckay/Reuters)

Which competitions would be affected by a boycott?

Three FIFA World Cup tournaments are still to be played this year:

The U-20 Women's World Cup in Poland is set to kick off on Sept. 5.

The U-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco is due to get underway on Oct. 17.

The U-17 Men's World Cup in Qatar gets underway in mid-November.

The next senior World Cup, the women's tournament, is scheduled for next summer in Brazil.

UEFA has sent a "powerful message" in threatening to boycott future FIFA events, said Graham Scott, a former English Premier League referee and now a correspondent with The Athletic.

"The withdrawal of UEFA countries from any FIFA tournament effectively renders it worthless," he said.

What about the other confederations?

UEFA's statement blasts FIFA for its lack of consultation with member federations about the FFE plan, a sentiment echoed by both the confederations covering Asia, and North and Central America and the Caribbean.

On Wednesday, a statement by the AFC voiced disappointment "that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it."

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa went further in a letter to member federations, saying "FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football" and warned of risks to their own competitions.

Several hours after UEFA's statement was released Thursday, CONCACAF said its member federations had rejected the proposal to create FFE.

While it didn't go as far as threatening a boycott, a CONCACAF statement called for "greater transparency and proper governance" and raised concerns about "the lack of due process surrounding the proposal."

It also questioned why FIFA deemed that private equity was necessary after what was the most profitable World Cup in history.

The CAF says it will discuss the proposal at a meeting next week, while the OFC said it had begun a consultation process with its members about the proposal. As of late Thursday, CONMEBOL, which covers South America, had not released a statement about the proposal.

The combined votes of the AFC, CONCACAF and UEFA would be enough to defeat the proposal, which requires a majority from member federations to pass.

U.S. President Donald Trump, left, and Infantino stand together during the trophy presentation after the final of the FIFA World Cup 2026, the most lucrative in the tournament's history. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Has Infantino put his position in jeopardy?

Prior to the FFE announcement, it looked as if Infantino would easily win re-election for a fourth term as FIFA president when a vote of member federations is held next March.

That's perhaps less of a certainty now, especially considering the comments from AFC president Sheikh Salman, who has been a staunch ally of Infantino.

It also follows concern over some aspects of the recent World Cup hosted by Canada, Mexico and the U.S., including the high price of tickets, controversies over the video assistant referee, the introduction of hydration breaks during games, and a red card for an American player that was rescinded after the intervention of U.S. President Donald Trump.

FIFA has set a Nov. 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in the vote for the association's next president.

World.title: 'Our house would shake': Shania Twain opens up about growing up in 'violent' home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For a young Shania Twain, home wasn't always a safe place.

Long before she became a global country music superstar, the Man! I Feel Like a Woman! singer, 60, says she spent her childhood in Timmins, Ont., growing up in what she describes as a "very violent" home, caught up in a chaotic cycle fuelled by her mother and stepfather's "volatile relationship."

"They loved each other. They went through so many ups and downs together, but they fought a lot, and they got violent often," Twain revealed on Thursday's episode of NPR's Wild Card with Rachel Martin.

When Martin asked whether she ever got caught in the crossfire of that violence, the five-time Grammy winner replied, "Yeah, with me, too."

"If I was standing in the wrong place at the wrong time, definitely."

Twain, who was born Eilleen Edwards, added that both of her parents were "pretty harsh physically" and that she and her sisters, Jill and Carrie Ann, "definitely got smacked around a lot."

"And kicked around, sometimes literally kicked around."

Still, Twain said it was her parents, Sharon and Jerry Twain, who "hurt each other the most."

"My mom, she would lose clumps of hair, she was bruised often in the face and … it was pretty bad sometimes. Our house would shake. Those walls would shake," Twain recalled, adding that it was "very traumatic."

"It gets loud and scary, like a really bad thunderstorm."

WATCH | Shania Twain on her 'traumatic' childhood:

Twain's mother, Sharon Edwards, divorced her biological father, Clarence Edwards, when the future country music icon was two. She later married Jerry Twain who adopted Shania and her sisters.

Twain said the family grew up poor, often rationing food, and surviving on "stale bread." She says her mother and step father's financial struggles frequently became the source of their fights.

"They would argue over … 'Can't pay the bills. Now we're gonna run out of heat, and now, who's fault is that?'" Twain said.

Twain says her mother tried to leave her stepfather several times, particularly when the violence would reach "its peak" and the "neighbours would call the cops." But they never managed to break completely loose.

"My mother did often try to leave. She did leave — we did leave — but you know, he'd always find us or she'd always give in and go back," Twain said. "It was a cycle."

The couple ended up remaining together until they were both killed in a car accident in 1987 when Twain was 22.

It's not the first time the country singer has spoken publicly about her turbulent upbringing.

The You're Still the One singer opened up about her childhood in her 2011 memoir From This Moment On, where she shared how her stepfather physically, emotionally and sexually abused her for years while she also witnessed him repeatedly assault her mother.

World.title: Permits issued for Alberta coal mine expansion despite environmental opposition
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A sprawling expansion of a massive thermal coal mine has been approved by Alberta’s provincial regulator — clearing the way for the operator to extend the life of the project well into the next decade, despite opposition from conservation groups.

The Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) issued regulatory permits to Coalspur Mines for an expansion of its operation at the Vista Coal Mine near Hinton, Alta., which would turn the largest coal mine in Canada into the largest in all of North America.

The approval will allow the company to expand the open pits of its surface coal mine westward, with new mining operations expected to cover more than 630 hectares of land along the Rocky Mountain Foothills near the gates of Jasper National Park.

Approval was granted for the project by the AER without a regulatory hearing, despite formal objections over the project’s potential environmental impacts.

Conservationists fear the mine will damage local watersheds and at-risk species downstream, including the endangered Athabasca rainbow trout and threatened bull trout.

Excavation plans for the mine cut through headwater streams in the Athabasca drainage basin and environmentalists fear that the expansion will result in the direct destruction of local creeks and leave area watersheds polluted with contaminants such as selenium and arsenic.

Groups including the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society Northern Alberta Chapter had submitted formal statements of concern calling for the application and permits to be denied.

Regulatory documents show approval for the expansion was granted July 20, 2026, when the AER decided a public hearing was not warranted and issued the final permits.

'Extremely disappointing'

Tara Russell, program director for CPAWS Northern Alberta, said the decision demonstrates a lack of regulatory accountability.

The mine’s approval contradicts a federal pledge to phase out thermal coal exports by 2030, Russell said, adding the provincial regulator has “no teeth” to enforce environmental protections and Alberta needs an outright ban on eastern slopes coal mining.

“This is just another great example of the AER moving away from any platforms of public scrutiny on these large, extremely impactful projects,” she said.

“It's extremely disappointing “

In a statement to CBC News, the AER said the operator has met all provincial approval conditions.

The AER said its technical review "considered the environmental, social, economic, and cultural impacts of the proposed activity and assessed Coalspur’s plans to mitigate any resulting adverse impacts.”

Officials with Coalspur Mines have not responded to requests for comment from CBC News.

The green-light for construction comes amid broader debate over regulation of coal production in Alberta’s eastern slopes and federal efforts to phase out thermal exports by 2030.

WATCH | Mine approved without federal impact assessment: Alberta coal mine expansion gets green light without federal impact assessment | Duration 1:18 Planned expansion of the Vista coal mine near Hinton, Alta., would make it the largest mine of its kind in North America. After five months of consideration, the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada says the project can go ahead without a federal study exploring the potential environment and social impacts of it. The CBC’s Acton Clarkin reports.

Federal review considered, quashed

The expansion has faced years of delays as the federal Impact Assessment Agency considered whether the Coalspur project warranted a federal review.

In 2020, then-federal environment minister Jonathan Wilkinson ordered a joint federal-provincial review of both the expansion and the underground test mine. But that review collapsed when the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act was unconstitutional.

In December 2024, the federal Impact Assessment Agency announced the project did not meet the threshold for review.

In 2025, just three months after the Alberta government lifted its moratorium on new coal mine development on the eastern slopes, formal applications to the AER were submitted for the expansion.

In a statement to CBC News, Alberta Minister of Energy and Minerals Brian Jean said he respects the decision of the regulator, noting the Coalspur expansion was an “advanced project” under the rules for reviewing mines .

“Extending the life of an existing operation that employs Albertans and contributes to our energy security is a practical outcome, provided it is meeting all environmental and regulatory requirements," said Jean.

Seepage, reclamation concerns

Coalspur urged regulators to proceed without a hearing, stating in filings that it remains committed to responsible operations and abiding by all regulatory requirements imposed by the AER.

The company cited a mandatory 100-metre buffer along critical habitats to preserve wildlife corridors, alongside ongoing progressive reclamation. The expansion sits above the Athabasca River Valley, in an area of forest home to 22 species at risk.

According to regulatory documents, Coalspur plans to operate the new and old parts of the mine as a single complex. Once expanded, the operator plans to increase production at the mine to 15 million clean tonnes annually and extend the mine's lifespan by 12 years.

The operations of the Vista Coal Mine will include surface open-pit mining, highwall mining and construction of a freshwater pipeline.

Permits allow Coalspur to divert up to 5,406,000 cubic metres of water annually. Wetlands reclamation is expected to take upwards of 20 years.

In letters informing objectors of its decision to issue permits, AER director Steven Van Lingen said a public hearing was unnecessary, maintaining that environmental concerns were adequately addressed through permit conditions.

These conditions include mandatory water release limits designed to safeguard downstream water quality and endangered fish habitat. Among them, an end pit lake, which will be created as part of the mine’s reclamation, was initially estimated to take more than 160 years to fill and become fully functional.

Now, according to approval conditions issued by AER, the company must submit a plan to make that happen within a 10-year timeframe after mining operations come to an end.

Kennedy Halvorson, a conservation specialist with the Alberta Wilderness Association (AWA), which also filed a statement of concern against the project, said those responses have not satisfied her concerns surrounding the project.

She said seeing the project bypass any public hearing is disappointing. Such forums, Halvorson said, bring critical information to light and keep operators accountable.

The AWA remains concerned proposed mitigations will not fully protect local hydrology, peatlands or endangered species, like the Athabasca rainbow trout, Halvorson said.

The mine's plan to divert water from the McLeod River into McPherson Creek also poses serious risks, particularly during dry conditions, she said.

In its own application, the Coalspur acknowledged its operations could completely curtail baseflow at the headwaters of McPherson Creek and said wastewater from the tailings will seep into the creek “approximately 11 to 160 years” after the mine shutters.

"Mitigations — they don't prevent harm, they just reduce harm," said Halvorson. "And sometimes that level of harm is still too much for species at risk or ecosystems to bear."

World.title: Over 1,000 students later, Richmond, B.C., man still teaching English for free as feds cut lessons
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twice a week, the party room of the Mino Club Cafe in Richmond, B.C., is converted into a classroom.

Normally, the café doubles as a children's play space and restaurant. But on Tuesdays and Saturdays, it also becomes a place to learn.

Inside, dozens of people, mostly newcomers to Canada, work hard at one thing.

"I come here want to improve my English," said Meice Xu, an immigrant from Shanghai.

It all happens under the watchful eye of Masih Sabet, who has taught over 1,000 students for free in Richmond since 2017.

Meice Xu, one of the students in Masih Sabet's Richmond English class, explains what she's been learning. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

"We call it [the] English Friendship Corner," said Sabet. “We help them to create friendship between themselves. And they learn that they are not alone in this.”

His lessons have been a vital service amid ongoing federal cuts to English class funding for new permanent residents and refugees.

This September, Ottawa will stop funding intermediate English training altogether.

SUCCESS, a B.C.-based non-profit that helps immigrants, said it has had to close two language centres in Richmond since last year.

"We'll have to reduce the size for the upcoming year as well," said Queenie Choo, CEO of the organization.

WATCH | Masih Sabet teaches English in a café turned classroom: This volunteer is teaching newcomers English for free amid federal cuts to language programs | Duration 2:36 A volunteer in Richmond has taught over 1,000 new immigrants English, all for free. This comes at a time when the federal government is slashing English programs for newcomers, with a new round of cuts coming in September. The CBC’s Steven Chua reports.

The federal class, called Language Instruction for Newcomers to Canada, has been helping people integrate into Canadian society since 1992.

It comes in two distinct packages: Stage 1 focuses on beginner-level English to get people functioning at a basic level in Canadian society, while Stage 2 is intermediate, and often needed for people pursuing white collar work.

Both of these have been strained by funding reductions.

But in September, it’s Stage 2 classes that will be losing all their funding from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).

$234M cut to settlement service

From 2024 to 2027, the federal government anticipates slashing $234 million in overall settlement service provider funding.

This is money given to places like SUCCESS that help new immigrants integrate into Canada. It generally includes cash earmarked for information, employment and language services.

The IRCC said funding is tied to the number of permanent residents coming to Canada, and that it's stopping Stage 2 English funding to prioritize basic language training.

Major immigration cuts began in 2024 when the federal government announced it would reduce the number of new permanent residents by more than 200,000.

During the first quarter of this year, Statistics Canada reported a 20 per cent drop in permanent immigrants compared with the same time last year.

Lessons offer a sense of community

Those working with newcomers say a lack of access to English classes can have consequences.

"There’s a delay in kind of the integration, delay in finding a job or delay in even the overall economic integration into the community," Choo said.

Masih Sabet says his lessons aren't just about teaching English, but about giving people a community gathering space too. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

Sabet, an immigrant himself, said English classes offer an important lifeline.

"It helps them to get … out of their loneliness, helps them to get out of despair," he said.

And it can help them achieve their goals.

Xu said it makes a big difference in accomplishing simple, everyday tasks.

"I want to go to the doctor, go … shopping, even help the people," she said.

Sabet smiles when he hears this. Learning English has given him a way to be generous, and now his student wants to do the same.

World.title: 'It was hell': French communities are on the front lines of Europe's new wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The flames came quick and strong.

Pushed by westerly winds, they'd already devastated Saumos, 14 kilometres away, and in the early morning hours of last Friday, were heading, like a match to gunpowder, through an exceptionally dry forest of pines, in an exceptionally hot summer, toward Le Porge.

When Stéphanie Dhont looked outside her window, sparks were raining down.

"Everything was orange and since it was all so dry, even the smallest bush would instantly burst into flames," said Dhont, whose husband had left only hours before, around 1 a.m. local time, to rescue the couple's 15-year-old daughter from an evacuation order at her summer camp in Biscarosse, south down the coast, where another wildfire had broken out.

Only Dhont and her 18-year-old son, Timothée Collin, a lifeguard and surfer, were left to defend the family's home near the centre of the town in southwestern France against the encroaching wildfire.

Dhont's family is one of many in Le Porge, France, who says they felt abandoned in dealing with a new climate disaster reality.

"So we did what we could to save our house," the 45-year-old mother said of the wood home they built 13 years ago.

The mother and son pulled out the garden hose and started spraying the outside walls, the hedges, the roof, "everything."

Within an hour, Dhont says, the village was surrounded by flames.

Stéphanie Dhont, centre, in white, fought the fire off her home with her 18-year-old son on July 24. Dhont, 45, has been volunteering in her town of Le Porge, France, where the Gironde wildfire destroyed 183 homes. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

There had been no phone alerts, no text messages, "nothing — not even a siren." Instead, neighbours drove by honking, yelling at everyone to leave, she said.

"It was total panic, it was hell."

One hundred and eighty three homes burned in Le Porge in the hours that followed.

"A field of ruins," the town’s mayor, Martial Zaninetti, called it.

The wildfires that have burned in the area near the city of Bordeaux may be smaller than those Canada and the U.S. are used to — totalling over 100,000 hectares — but French authorities and wildfire experts say they are unprecedented in Europe in terms of size, scale and impact.

The small communities that pepper the pine forests around Bordeaux have been left reeling. Many residents stayed behind to help fight the fires, which only began to let up Thursday morning as a light rain fell.

A drone view shows burnt buildings in an area affected by a wildfire in Le Porge, Gironde, amid drought conditions following a heat wave and water shortages across much of France, on Tuesday. (Yves Herman/Reuters)

'We've had to fend for ourselves'

On Wednesday, they'd scrambled, along with firefighters from across the country, in punishing 40-degree heat to tamp out spontaneous re-burns — when heat and dryness cause the smouldering ground to ignite.

But with the emergency out of the way Thursday, and 84,000 out of over 220,000 people allowed to regain in their homes in nine communities — but not Le Porge — resident volunteers there were starting to absorb the extent of their town's destruction and the sense that they’d been left to their own devices.

"We've had to fend for ourselves," said Didier Deyres, 65, a farmer and the vice-president of the local forest fire defence department.

Standing outside Le Porge's party hall, which had been converted into a bustling volunteer and firefighter hub, Deyres decried a lack of resources from the French government he said his town has received since its residents had to flee nearly a week ago.

"We're starting to lose heart," said Deyres. "We need help. We are going to start seeing traumatic shocks, but there's also going to be [health] problems because of the smoke."

Didier Deyres, the vice-president of the forest fire defence department in Le Porge, says his town has been 'abandoned.' (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

A sign at the hall warned of high rates of carbon monoxide in the air and said masks were "mandatory." Few people wore them.

Deyres says he believes that if the French government had been better prepared and had more ressources, including more water bombers, his community would have shouldered far less destruction.

France owns 12 Canadair water bombers, but it can only use five at the moment due to maintenance issues — a fact most people affected by fires in France will mention.

In the back of the party hall, ad hoc health care is underway. Young volunteer health and body workers sit on cots they’d arranged in a corner to treat members of their community.

Emma Jambert, a 25-year-old osteopath from Le Porge, said the solidarity of the town has been motivating, but she, too, wondered aloud when more help would come.

"There’s a lot of fatigue," Jambert said. "The aftermath is going to be complicated."

WATCH | A frontline look a France's fight against wildfires near Bordeaux: Inside France's battle to save Bordeaux from unprecedented wildfires | Duration 2:58 CBC News gets a frontline look at France's pitched fight against unprecedented wildfires in the historic Bordeaux region, where another heatwave is expected to fuel flames that have forced at least 250,000 people from their homes.

'Solidarity,' but questions remain

A group of residents are planning a class action against French authorities who ordered firefighters to leave Le Porge as the fire raged Friday and direct their efforts to Lège-Cap-Ferret, where a wealthy community sits on a nearby peninsula.

The government has justified its actions, saying there is only one route out of Cap-Ferret, making a rapid evacuation nearly impossible.

Dhont and Deyres said the town had been "abandoned" and "sacrificed."

Zaninetti, the mayor, says he "understands their pain."

He prefers to focus on the future, noting he has started gathering local associations and collaborating with nearby communities on a reconstruction plan in an effort he says resembles the response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

"What keeps us going is this solidarity … without it, I think we would have collapsed."

Along with the solidarity, there has been a sense of guilt.

Dhont served meals to a lineup of other volunteers and firefighters at the hall. She, her husband, daughter and son have been working late into the night every day over the past week.

"I’ve been asking myself: why them and not me?"

Timothé Collin, 18, has been volunteering in Le Porge, where he and his family live. It's one of the hardest hit communities by wildfires in southwestern France. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

She hopes all the media attention will result in more help for Le Porge, where she says everyone knows each other cares for each other.

Her home is in the centre of town, where most were spared, but down the road, along the Avenue du Bassin d'Arcachon is a kilometre-long stretch of ashes where homes used to stand.

Blackened trunks reach out of a carpet of cinders. Cars are carcasses and stone walls stand like ancient ruins without roofs without their interiors, their couches, their beds, their curtains. Without shoes in the entryway or homework on the kitchen counter.

'No turning back now'

Timothé Collin, Dhont's 18-year-old, used to drive through down the Bassin every day to get to high school.

Now, it's unrecognizable. Every once in a while, a house, a tree, a shed, or a car is left unscathed.

"It's a lottery," Collin said, while driving through the devastation. "A gust of wind can make the difference."

Collin, fought the wildfire in Le Porge overnight last Friday with his mother. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

In the months and years to come, the residents of Le Porge say they want accountabily — for the warning signs that were missed, the air water bombers that weren't ordered or delivered, the help that didn't come or left, the water the firefighters didn't get enough of to keep flames at bay.

Europe is the fastest warming continent. France has had four heat waves this season alone. These fires were only a matter of time, Collin said.

"There’s no turning back now and it's our fault, humans' fault," he said.

"I try to keep things in perspective; I tell myself that things will change and that all the little things I do — all my small efforts to bring about change — matter. I tell myself that with all these catastrophes, people's mindsets are shifting. I believe in it, I do. We have to, because if we don't, nothing will ever change."

World.title: Police left this survivor feeling blamed, broken. Now they're engaging with her again, and she's worried
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A woman who took part in mediation with the Ottawa Police Service in 2023 after struggling to report an historical sexual assault says the process left her feeling broken down and blamed, then placated and cast aside.

Keara Dean also says the reponse from police leaders after she called out the force at a public meeting in June has reinforced her belief that they're more interested in defending themselves and the institution than acknowledging mistakes, learning from them and repairing harm.

"The revictimization was beyond what I could have ever thought to have prepared for, and I work as a social worker and I've worked in this field," Dean said in an interview.

Recently Ottawa police asked Dean for the second time whether they can use her negative experience to help employees treat trauma survivors with more sensitivity. But Dean said she's worried that, like the first time police asked, it will not go well.

Cold cases break open

Dean's initial frustrations with the force began in November 2022, when she tried to assist with an investigation into a man charged that fall with sexually assaulting two women, murdering one of them and attempting to murder the other.

The alleged offences occurred in 2000 in Quebec City and Jonquière, Que.

Investigators announced there could be more victims. Some details reminded Dean, who lives in Ottawa, of a violent sexual assault she says she endured in Quebec City in the mid-1990s.

Dean called the tip line and said she was passed between police services in Quebec and Ottawa before being directed to report in person to police in Gatineau, Que.

By then, Dean said, she was angry and afraid to proceed, and she told the media about the mishandling of her calls.

An aerial view of the entrance to Ottawa Police Service headquarters at 474 Elgin St. in April. (Michel Aspirot/CBC)

'I was breaking down'

Ottawa police offered Dean mediation in spring 2023, and she said she was escorted into a locked room with two civilian employees of the reporting line and an officer from the professional standards section.

She had not been told she could bring a supporter or lawyer, and Dean said facing the members alone was her first indication that the process would not be trauma-informed.

During the session, Dean said, she was told that Ottawa police had given her the wrong information in 2022 "'because you didn't actually say on the reporting line that you were calling about historical sexual violence.'"

I had not stopped crying. I was in no state or frame of mind to sign anything. I couldn't even think of driving my vehicle. - Keara Dean

Dean said she felt blamed and attacked, and hit by a "flood of emotion" and shock.

She was certain she had used the words "historical sexual violence," she said, and remembered rehearsing them before picking up the phone.

"I was breaking down and crying," Dean said, and she couldn't stop crying after she left the room to use the washroom and returned.

Dean in a photograph taken in November 2022, shortly after she tried to report an historical sexual assault and was directed to contact multiple police forces. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

Flabbergasted

Dean said the two civilian employees left the room, leaving her with the professional standards officer.

The officer slid a piece of paper across the table and asked her to sign it, Dean said.

It was a form withdrawing the complaint Dean had made about Ottawa police to the Office of the Independent Police Review Director, now the Law Enforcement Complaints Agency.

The form had been filled out on her behalf in the first person, as though she had written the responses herself.

Dean was asked to sign this form, titled 'Withdrawal of a Public Complaint Against the Police,' which had been filled out for her. She had not said that she wanted to withdraw her complaint. (Ottawa Police Service/Keara Dean)

"I was, at this point, flabbergasted. I had not stopped crying. I was in no state or frame of mind to sign anything. I couldn't even think of driving my vehicle," Dean said.

She told the officer that asking her to sign the form was unethical, unprofessional and appalling, she recalled.

Dean refused to sign it, kept the document and provided a copy to CBC.

In an emailed statement, Ottawa police declined to answer questions about its mediation process in 2023, how mediation works today, whether it lived up to its own expectations and standards in preparing Dean for mediation, how the force prepares people now, whether the force regularly fills out withdrawal of complaint forms on behalf of people, and whether that's allowed or not.

The force said it "recognizes that Ms. Dean's experience, both when she initially contacted police in 2022 and during the subsequent public complaint process, caused her further distress."

Did say 'historical sexual violence'

A few months after the mediation, in summer 2023, Dean said another professional standards officer called her after listening to her initial call to the Ottawa police reporting line.

Dean said the officer confirmed she had used the words "historical sexual violence."

In September 2023, Dean received a formal letter of apology from Ottawa police, saying "the call taker and supervisor did not make sufficient inquiries of you or seek clarification on the information you provided to arrive at the correct response."

The apology letter ended the complaint process.

Dean said she later learned she could have filed a human rights complaint, but by then she had missed the deadline by one month.

Ottawa police declined to explain why Dean was told during mediation that she had not mentioned historical sexual violence.

The force said "a person reporting sexual violence should not be required to use specific terminology before their disclosure is recognized, properly assessed and responded to with care."

Addressed police board in June

Years later, Dean was among several residents who spoke about police misconduct at an Ottawa Police Service Board meeting this past June. She said she felt compelled to tell the board publicly that police didn't treat her with care, and that she believes the force continues to have difficulty responding appropriately to people reporting trauma.

After Dean finished her delegation, police Chief Eric Stubbs asked whether she would be willing to talk to employees about her experience to help educate them.

Dean said the force had made a similar request after mediation in 2023 but did not follow up, despite her contacting them twice.

I think training is crucial in this — hearing from victims themselves ... And we do that every time we have the opportunity to. - Deputy Chief Patricia Ferguson, later in meeting

"I felt like that was a ploy in mediation to make me feel better. So if you're actually, genuinely asking me to do something, I hope this time you're actually asking me and not … being performative, because last time it was crushing," Dean told Stubbs.

Deputy Chief Patricia Ferguson of the Ottawa Police Service in 2022. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

'Delegate was speaking about November 2022'

Ottawa police said in its emailed statement Thursday that Dean "should have received clearer communication" after the force offered her an opportunity to help train its members.

The force said it was reviewing why the followup did not happen and "what opportunities may remain to learn from her experience."

Later during the June police board meeting, board vice-chair and city Coun. Marty Carr asked what the force was doing to improve how it works with people who have experienced trauma.

"I did note that the delegate was speaking about November 2022. I would say that since then we have made some strides," Deputy Chief Patricia Ferguson replied.

"I think training is crucial in this — hearing from victims themselves, first-hand stories about how the impact of the treatment that they received from our members is very significant. And we do that every time we have the opportunity to, so that we can give that feedback to our officers."

Dean said Ferguson was wrong to characterize the force's handling of her case as an issue limited to November 2022.

She said the lack of a trauma-informed approach continued during the mediation in spring 2023 and after the apology that fall, when police did not respond to her followups about helping with training and later told her all available spots had been filled.

Dean said Ferguson's comments left her feeling "dismissed."

She also said they reinforced her concerns about whether the police force was capable of meaningful change and whether it intended to follow through on its latest request for her help.

The changes made since 2022 do not erase what occurred or lessen the need for [Ottawa police] to continue listening, learning, and improving how it supports victims of sexual violence. - Ottawa police statement

Ottawa police said Ferguson's response to Carr's question was "not intended to minimize Ms. Dean's experience."

"We recognize, however, that the comments did not land that way for Ms. Dean and may have left her feeling that her experience was being dismissed. The changes made since 2022 do not erase what occurred or lessen the need for [Ottawa police] to continue listening, learning, and improving how it supports victims of sexual violence."
