Inside the Grupo Cibest Structure

Both Nequi and Bancolombia remain part of Grupo Cibest, the holding company that controls some of Colombia’s largest financial assets. This is an internal reorganization, not a sale or divestiture.

Bancolombia, one of the country’s largest banks by assets, originally incubated Nequi as a digital-only platform. The spin-off allows each entity to pursue distinct strategies while sharing a common ownership umbrella.

Grupo Cibest’s structure now includes a traditional universal bank and a standalone digital financing company. This dual model mirrors trends in Brazil and Mexico, where legacy banks have carved out agile digital units.

For foreign portfolio investors, the separation could eventually lead to greater transparency in Nequi’s performance metrics. A standalone entity may report its own financial results, offering clearer insights into digital banking adoption in Colombia.

Nequi’s Role in Colombia’s Digital Economy

Nequi is one of Colombia‘s most downloaded financial apps, serving as an entry point to formal financial services for millions. The platform offers savings accounts, payment links, loans, and insurance products without physical branches.

The company competes directly with Daviplata, the digital wallet from Banco Davivienda, and a growing field of fintech startups. Regulation as a financing company could allow Nequi to expand its credit offerings and attract institutional funding.

Colombia’s push for financial inclusion has accelerated digital wallet adoption. Nequi has been a primary beneficiary, particularly among younger users and those outside major banking corridors.

The spin-off arrives as Colombia’s central bank advances its own instant payment system, Bre-B, designed to interconnect all financial institutions. A standalone Nequi could integrate more nimbly with emerging national payment rails.

Investor Context and Market Signals

The spin-off does not involve a public offering or capital raise at this stage. Nequi remains privately held within Grupo Cibest, and no equity is being offered to external investors.

However, the regulatory upgrade lays groundwork for potential future moves. A licensed financing company with its own balance sheet is better positioned to issue debt, securitize loan portfolios, or eventually pursue an IPO.

Latin American fintech valuations have stabilized after a volatile period. Investors are watching Colombia closely as the country implements open banking regulations and modernizes its payments infrastructure.

Nequi’s transition tests whether a digital-first platform can thrive under full regulatory scrutiny while maintaining the user experience that drove its growth. Success would provide a blueprint for other Latin American neobanks seeking formal licenses.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to update my Nequi app or create a new account after September 1, 2026?

No. Nequi confirmed that users do not need to take any action.

The app, login credentials, account details, and all services remain unchanged.

Is Nequi still owned by Bancolombia?

Nequi and Bancolombia are now separate operating companies but both remain under the same parent group, Grupo Cibest. It is an internal reorganization, not a sale.

Will my money in Nequi still be protected?

Yes. As a regulated financing company supervised directly by the Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia, Nequi must meet strict capital and consumer protection requirements.

World.title: Mercado Libre Clothing Brand ‘Balse’ Takes Aim at Shein and Temu
World.content:
Companies · E-Commerce

Key Facts —Trademark Filing Mercado Libre applied to register ‘Balse’ under Class 25 for apparel, including hosiery, underwear, footwear, and outerwear. —Competitive Context The move directly targets Asian fast-fashion rivals Shein and Temu, which have gained significant market share in Latin America. —AI Strategy The company considers artificial intelligence central to its fast-fashion model, leveraging its integrated ecosystem of commerce, logistics, payments, and credit. —Regulatory Action In February 2026, Mercado Libre formally asked Argentina’s Secretariat of Commerce to regulate misleading advertising by Chinese-owned stores. —Ecosystem Moat MELI’s competitive edge relies on its combined AI, proprietary logistics network, and Mercado Pago fintech arm, which no pure-play fashion rival can replicate locally.

Mercado Libre clothing brand ‘Balse’ is the latest weapon Latin America’s largest e-commerce company is deploying to defend its home market from the aggressive expansion of Asian fast-fashion disruptors Shein and Temu.

A logistics warehouse. Mercado Libre is launching a clothing brand to counter Shein and Temu. (Photo: internal archive)

The Homegrown Giant Draws a Line

Mercado Libre (NASDAQ: MELI), founded in Argentina and now headquartered in Uruguay, is far more than an online marketplace for foreign observers to understand. It operates the region’s dominant e-commerce platform, a sprawling logistics network, and Mercado Pago, a fintech arm that processes payments, issues credit, and manages digital accounts for millions of unbanked consumers.

Led by CEO Marcos Galperin, the company has long been the undisputed leader in Latin American digital commerce. Now, it faces a structural threat from Shein and Temu, whose algorithm-driven, ultra-low-cost apparel supply chains have rapidly captured price-sensitive shoppers across Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina.

By filing to trademark ‘Balse’ for apparel, footwear, and accessories, Mercado Libre is signaling it will no longer cede the fast-fashion category to foreign platforms. The move transforms the marketplace operator into a direct competitor, leveraging its own data and infrastructure to produce and sell private-label clothing.

Mercado Libre clothing brand ‘Balse’ and the AI Moat

The company has made it clear that artificial intelligence is the engine behind its fashion offensive. Executives argue that no external player understands the Latin American consumer like Mercado Libre, which sits on a vast repository of search, purchase, and browsing data from its marketplace.

This data allows AI models to predict trending styles, optimize inventory, and personalize recommendations in ways that a foreign entrant cannot easily replicate. The integrated ecosystem combines commerce, logistics, payments, and credit, creating a closed loop that feeds the AI with real-time signals.

For international investors, the strategy mirrors Amazon’s private-label playbook but is tailored to a region where logistics fragmentation and low banking penetration make an all-in-one stack a formidable barrier to entry. The ‘Balse’ trademark application covers everything from hosiery and underwear to outerwear, suggesting a full-category assault.

The company operates Mercado Libre Marketplace, an online commerce platform that can be accessed through mobile app or website; and Mercado Pago, a financial technology solution platform, which offers comprehensive set of financial technology services to users and other users…

The Shein and Temu Threat in Latin America

Shein and Temu have not merely entered Latin America; they have rewritten the rules of engagement. Their direct-from-factory model, gamified shopping experiences, and rock-bottom prices have drawn millions of downloads in Brazil and Mexico, two of Mercado Libre’s most critical markets.

These platforms exploit customs exemptions and lean heavily on targeted social-media advertising to acquire customers at a blistering pace. For a region where disposable income is under constant pressure from inflation and currency volatility, the appeal of a US$5 t-shirt is undeniable.

Mercado Libre’s concern is existential: if these rivals own the apparel category, they could erode the marketplace’s traffic and cross-selling power. The ‘Balse’ brand is a countermeasure designed to offer competitive pricing while keeping transactions, data, and loyalty inside MELI’s ecosystem.

Logistics, Payments, and the Integrated Stack

Mercado Libre's defensive moat extends well beyond AI-driven design. The company has invested billions of dollars in fulfillment centers, last-mile delivery, and its own air fleet through Mercado Envíos, its logistics unit.

This network enables fast, reliable shipping that independent sellers on Shein or Temu cannot match.

Mercado Pago, the fintech division, closes the loop by offering installment plans – a crucial feature in markets like Brazil, where consumers routinely pay in parcels. Neither Shein nor Temu offers a native, region-wide credit infrastructure that rivals Mercado Pago’s reach.

By combining AI trend-spotting with proprietary logistics and integrated payments, Mercado Libre can potentially deliver a fast-fashion experience that feels local. For expatriates and investors watching the region, this stack represents a strategic asset that pure-play apparel platforms lack.

The February Regulatory Complaint

In February 2026, Mercado Libre took its fight beyond branding and logistics by filing a formal complaint with Argentina’s Secretariat of Commerce. The company accused Chinese-owned stores, including Shein and Temu, of misleading advertising and unfair commercial practices.

The regulatory push aims to level a playing field that Mercado Libre argues is tilted by opaque pricing, tax advantages, and consumer-protection gaps. While the complaint was lodged in Argentina, it signals a broader willingness to use legal and policy channels across the region.

Such moves are not uncommon in Latin America, where established players often seek regulatory relief against foreign disruptors. For Mercado Libre, the complaint complements the ‘Balse’ launch, applying pressure on multiple fronts simultaneously.

What ‘Balse’ Means for Investors and Expats

The ‘Balse’ trademark filing is a clear indicator that Mercado Libre is willing to sacrifice some marketplace neutrality to protect its core territory. Private-label apparel carries higher margins but also inventory risk, a factor that analysts will watch closely when the company reports future earnings.

For the expatriate community and international investors following Latin America, the move underscores the region’s growing importance in global e-commerce battles. A homegrown champion is now adopting the tools of its rivals – AI, speed, and private label – to defend a market of over 650 million people.

The outcome will depend on execution. If ‘Balse’ can match Shein’s price points while offering faster delivery and local payment options, Mercado Libre could turn its ecosystem from a defensive moat into an offensive weapon in the fast-fashion war.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Mercado Libre clothing brand?

The Mercado Libre clothing brand is ‘Balse,’ a newly trademarked private-label apparel line covering hosiery, underwear, footwear, and outerwear, designed to compete directly with Shein and Temu in Latin America.

Why is Mercado Libre launching its own fashion brand?

Mercado Libre is launching ‘Balse’ to counter the rapid growth of Asian fast-fashion platforms that are capturing price-sensitive shoppers, using its AI, logistics, and payments ecosystem to offer a competitive local alternative.

How does Mercado Libre plan to compete with Shein and Temu?

The company plans to compete by leveraging artificial intelligence for trend prediction, its proprietary fulfillment network for faster delivery, and Mercado Pago for integrated credit and installment payments that foreign rivals cannot easily replicate.

World.title: Argentina Poverty & Inflation Guide 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Rio Times · Guides

Key Facts —Official poverty rate Q1 2026 INDEC reported 38.1% of urban Argentines lived below the poverty line in the first half of 2026. —June 2026 inflation Monthly CPI decelerated to 1.9%, the lowest figure since mid-2020, confirming a sustained disinflation path. —July 2026 inflation projection Private consultancies tracked by the BCRA expect July CPI to print around 1.8%, extending the cooling trend. —Indigence rate Extreme poverty (indigence) stood at 8.2%, meaning 2.4 million people cannot afford a basic food basket. —Annual inflation outlook The market consensus for end-2026 inflation has dropped to 28.4%, down from 211.4% in 2023. —Key risk A still-fragile exchange-rate anchor and slow real-wage recovery keep millions of families in precarity.

Argentina’s urban poverty rate touched 38.1% in the first half of 2026, while monthly inflation eased to 1.9% in June — the calmest price environment in nearly six years — reshaping the calculations for anyone living in, investing in, or relocating to the country.

Argentina poverty rate 2026

The official urban poverty rate fell to 38.1% in the first semester of 2026, according to the latest release from the national statistics institute, INDEC. That figure marks a sharp improvement from the 52.9% peak recorded in the first half of 2024, yet it still means four in ten Argentines live below the line.

Extreme poverty — indigence, the inability to cover even a basic food basket — dropped to 8.2%. Across the 31 urban agglomerates INDEC surveys, approximately 2.4 million people remain in severe material deprivation.

The human psychogram of Argentina in 2026 is one of cautious, exhausted relief. Families who spent 2023–2024 sprinting ahead of triple-digit inflation are now buying in bulk again.

But the memory of collapse is raw, and the middle class remains psychologically hollowed out by the experience: statistically above the line, yet emotionally scarred.

Argentina inflation rate July 2026 Milei

President Javier Milei’s signature disinflation program has driven the monthly consumer price index below 2% by mid-2026. The June reading landed at 1.9%, and preliminary high-frequency data tracked by the Central Bank’s Market Expectations Survey (REM) points to a July print around 1.8%.

The mechanics behind the cooling are dramatic: a deep fiscal adjustment that flipped a chronic deficit into consistent primary surpluses, a crawling-peg exchange rate of 1% monthly depreciation, and a sterilisation programme that sopped up excess pesos. The cost, felt across 2024, was a brutal recession that slashed consumption and drove poverty above 50% before the late-2025 recovery began.

For foreign investors, the mood contained in these numbers is one of bewildered optimism. Milei’s administration has delivered the most aggressive fiscal correction in modern Argentine history.

The macro numbers are aligning; the street-level reality — still tough — is starting to catch up.

Argentina inflation rate June 2026

June 2026’s 1.9% monthly CPI print confirmed the tenth consecutive month of sub-3% readings. The core component, which strips out seasonal and regulated prices, ran slightly lower at 1.7%, suggesting underlying price inertia is breaking.

The INDEC release shows food and non-alcoholic beverages — the category that most directly affects the poor — rising just 1.2% in June. That deceleration is mechanically reducing the poverty line, allowing more households to cross back above it.

We have tracked this trajectory from its violent beginnings: when The Rio Times reported July 2024 inflation at 4.0% and the central bank rate at 40%, the descent into single-digit monthly prints felt distant. The central bank has since cut its policy rate to 29% nominal in an environment where year-on-year CPI still runs near 35%.

Argentina inflation rate

The annual inflation rate for the 12 months to June 2026 stood at 35.8%, down from an unimaginable year to mid-2025 when it exceeded 80%. The REM consensus expects the 2026 calendar-year figure to settle at 28.4%, a fraction of the 211.4% recorded in 2023.

Core inflation durability matters here. Services inflation has been stickier than goods, a pattern typical of disinflation programmes where wages slowly recover past purchasing power.

Expats earning in hard currency will feel their purchasing power declining from its absurd 2024 peak, while locals in pesos begin to catch a breath.

The exchange rate is the wild card. The official peso depreciates at a controlled 1% monthly crawl, but the parallel ‘blue’ gap has narrowed to roughly 12%.

A sudden unification or realignment would feed directly into short-term CPI, a risk every business continuity plan should bracket.

What changed in 2026

Several structural shifts converged in 2026. First, the government eliminated the remaining import restrictions, allowing goods to flow and disciplining domestic price-setters through competition.

Second, the soybean harvest rebounded strongly after the 2023 drought, bringing export revenue and relieving the reserve position.

Third — and most consequential for the reader on the ground — the real-wage recovery accelerated. After losing nearly 60% of their dollar-equivalent income between 2020 and 2024, registered private-sector workers regained approximately 18% in real terms over the 12 months to mid-2026.

That shift is lifting consumption and, paradoxically, making Argentina feel more expensive to dollarised visitors than it did a year ago.

Politically, Milei’s coalition passed a second wave of structural reforms in the autumn 2026 legislative session, including labour modernisation measures. The governability story — unthinkable in early 2024 when the president held a tiny minority in Congress — has become a market stabiliser in its own right.

Common mistakes

Assuming the poverty number tells the whole story. INDEC’s line uses a basic-basket methodology.

A family dips below if its income cannot purchase a defined set of calories and services. At 38.1%, millions scraping by just above the line are statistically not poor but live one shock away from destitution.

Conflating CPI with dollarised living costs. A 1.9% monthly peso CPI does not mean dollar costs rose 1.9%.

If the exchange-rate crawl lags domestic inflation, dollar costs climb faster. Expats on USD budgets saw local costs surge in 2025–2026 even as peso inflation eased.

Extrapolating the 2026 trend indefinitely. Argentine stabilisations have a record of exhausting themselves when fiscal fatigue or an external shock hits.

The current programme’s durability hinges on commodity prices and the government’s willingness to maintain a primary surplus into an election year in 2027.

Ignoring provincial variation. Poverty rates range from 25% in parts of Patagonia to over 45% in the northern Gran Resistencia and Concordia agglomerates.

Investors targeting regional consumer markets need to disaggregate the national headline.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Argentina’s poverty rate in 2026?

Argentina’s official urban poverty rate was 38.1% in the first half of 2026, measured by INDEC using the income-based basic-basket methodology across 31 urban areas.

What is Argentina’s inflation rate for July 2026?

The official July 2026 CPI figure will be published by INDEC in mid-August 2026, but the Central Bank’s REM survey of private consultancies projects a monthly result of approximately 1.8%.

How does Milei’s programme affect poverty and inflation?

The Milei administration’s fiscal-surplus policy and controlled exchange-rate crawl have slashed monthly inflation from 25.5% in December 2023 to below 2% in mid-2026. Poverty spiked to 52.9% during the 2024 recession as social spending was compressed, then fell sharply to 38.1% as real wages recovered and inflation eased.

Sources: INDEC – Incidencia de la pobreza y la indigencia (First Half 2026 official release), BCRA – Relevamiento de Expectativas de Mercado (REM) July 2026, INDEC – Consumer Price Index June 2026

World.title: US$1 Trillion Africa Trade Opening for Latin America
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio Times · Analysis

Key Facts —East Africa’s Lead East Africa is consolidating as the continent’s fastest-growing sub-region, with projected GDP growth of 5.8–6.1% in 2025–2026, well above the African and global averages. —West Africa’s Rebound West Africa is emerging from post-COVID volatility into more stable growth of roughly 4.1–4.3%, underpinned by reforms in Nigeria and Ghana and new oil and gas production in Senegal and Niger. —A New Continental Arc Together, the two regions form an economic belt from the Gulf of Guinea to the Horn of Africa, reshaping trade corridors, commodity flows, and financial links. —Latin America’s Opening The above-average growth opens space for Latin American exporters of food, fertilisers, construction, and engineering to diversify beyond traditional markets in the US, EU, and China. —Energy and Commodities New energy output in Senegal and Niger, and reform-driven recovery in Nigeria, impact global LNG balances and offer direct links to Brazilian and Mexican energy players seeking African joint ventures. —The Geopolitical Layer As China, Gulf states, and Western powers intensify engagement in the corridor, Latin American governments risk being marginalised unless they actively map and enter this new growth arc.

A quiet but consequential economic realignment is underway across Africa, one that is redrawing the continent’s internal gravity and, with it, the calculus for Latin American governments and businesses that have long treated Africa as a single, distant block rather than a landscape of distinct, fast-moving opportunities.

Shipping containers at the bustling Port of Dar es Salaam, a key gateway connecting East African trade to global markets and increasingly to Latin Ame (Photo internet reproduction)

The Two-Speed Continent Comes into Focus

For years, the standard shorthand for Africa’s economic story was ‘Africa rising’ – a blanket narrative of growth that obscured as much as it revealed. Today, the data paint a far more textured picture, one in which the continent’s eastern and western flanks are pulling ahead in distinct and complementary ways.

East Africa has cemented its place as the continent’s fastest-growing sub-region, with UNECA figures showing average GDP growth holding at around 5.8 to 6.1 percent in 2025–2026. That pace not only eclipses the African average of roughly 3.9 to 4.0 percent but also leaves the global growth rate of around 3.0 percent far behind.

Kenya has emerged as the region’s largest single economy with a nominal GDP of US$147.26 billion, closely followed by Ethiopia at US$121.53 billion. Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, and Djibouti add further momentum, making East Africa a bloc with a combined nominal GDP of about US$512 billion – roughly 18 percent of Africa’s total output.

The drivers are structural, not circumstantial. Diversification into services, technology, and agriculture, coupled with deep regional integration through blocs such as the East African Community and COMESA, has created a self-reinforcing cycle of investment and demand that has proved relatively resilient even through COVID-19, geopolitical shocks, and climate stress.

West Africa’s Hard-Won Stabilisation

West Africa tells a different but equally significant story. The region’s growth decelerated sharply after the pandemic, slipping to 3.8 percent in 2022 from 4.4 percent a year earlier, as inflation, currency pressures, and political instability took their toll on Nigeria, Ghana, and smaller economies alike.

But the latest projections from the African Development Bank and the World Bank point to a meaningful turn. Regional growth is expected to pick up to around 4.1 to 4.3 percent in 2024–2026, with the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) projected to accelerate to 5.3 percent in 2026 and an average of 5.9 percent in 2027–28.

Much of this is being driven by reform governments in Nigeria and Ghana making difficult fiscal adjustments, alongside new oil and gas production coming onstream in Senegal and Niger. These are not merely extractive plays; they are altering the energy infrastructure map in ways that connect West African gas and power markets to global supply chains.

Yet volatility remains a fact of life. UNECA data show average inflation in West Africa running at 19.4 percent in 2024, easing only modestly to 15.8 percent in 2025.

The lesson for Latin American observers is that opportunity here comes with a premium on patience, local partnerships, and currency-risk management of a kind familiar in Buenos Aires, São Paulo, or Mexico City.

Why This Arc Matters for Latin American Exporters

For Latin American trade strategists, the emergence of an East–West African growth corridor is not an academic curiosity. It is a concrete reordering of demand patterns that touches sectors where Latin America is globally competitive.

East Africa’s expanding middle classes and infrastructure boom create demand for food products, fertilisers, construction materials, and agricultural machinery – all areas where Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico have deep export capacity. West Africa’s energy build-out and manufacturing ambitions open doors for engineering services, industrial equipment, and technology platforms.

The numbers are already shifting. South Africa's intra-African exports alone reached R571 billion in 2024, roughly 28 percent of its global exports, with Mozambique, Botswana, Namibia, and Zimbabwe as the top destinations.

As that intra-African trade thickens, the continent becomes a more integrated market that rewards external partners who treat it as a network, not a scattering of isolated national economies.

Latin America's current trade with Africa remains heavily concentrated in a handful of commodity categories. Brazil's flows are dominated by sugar, meat, and iron ore; Argentina's by grains and oilseeds.

The opportunity now is to climb the value chain, exporting not just raw materials but the services, financing, and logistical know-how that a rapidly urbanising Africa wants.

The Energy Bridge: Gas, Oil, and the LNG Connection

One of the most immediate touchpoints between Africa’s new growth arc and Latin America lies in energy. West Africa’s new oil and gas producers – particularly Senegal and Niger – are entering global markets at a moment when LNG trade flows are being redrawn by sanctions, the energy transition, and Asian demand.

Brazil and Mexico are both significant players in the global energy landscape, with Petrobras pursuing deep-water projects and Mexican firms active in gas infrastructure. The prospect of joint ventures, technical partnerships, and offtake agreements with emerging West African producers is increasingly realistic.

On the consumption side, East Africa's fast-growing economies are hungry for reliable power. Kenya, Ethiopia, and Tanzania are investing in geothermal, hydro, and natural-gas generation, often with Chinese and European financing.

Latin American energy firms with experience in complex terrain and emerging-market regulation – from Colombia's EPM to Brazil's construction giants – have relevant know-how to offer.

The competition for these energy partnerships is already intense, with Gulf states, Russia, and China deploying state-backed capital and diplomacy. Latin American firms cannot match the scale of Chinese infrastructure lending, but they can offer something different: a peer-to-peer model based on shared developmental experience and operational agility that resonates with African partners wary of debt-trap diplomacy.

Institutional Lessons for Mercosur and the Pacific Alliance

East Africa’s regional integration is not perfect, but it is instructive. The overlapping memberships of the EAC, COMESA, IGAD, and SADC are messy, yet they have produced real trade facilitation, infrastructure corridors, and policy coordination that Latin American blocs sometimes struggle to match.

West Africa’s ECOWAS and WAEMU have an even deeper institutional architecture, including a common currency for the Francophone states and a long – if uneven – history of free movement protocols. The gap between rhetoric and implementation is still wide, but it is closing, and the direction of travel is toward greater commercial integration.

For Mercosur, which has often been criticised for failing to deepen intra-bloc trade, and the Pacific Alliance, which has focused more on extra-regional ties, Africa’s integration experience offers a mirror. It suggests that ambitious customs unions can work even across economies at starkly different levels of development if the political will and technical infrastructure are sustained over decades.

Latin American diplomats and trade negotiators should be studying East and West Africa’s regional economic communities not as curiosities but as laboratories from which to learn – and as partners with whom to negotiate preferential agreements that could open a hemisphere-sized market for both sides.

The China Factor and the Scramble for Influence

No analysis of Africa’s growth arc is complete without accounting for China, which has spent two decades building deep financial, infrastructure, and diplomatic ties across both East and West Africa. The Belt and Road Initiative, critical-mineral supply agreements, and digital-infrastructure projects have made Beijing the dominant external economic actor in many African capitals.

Western powers have responded with their own initiatives – the EU’s Global Gateway, the US-led Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment – but the gap remains large, and African governments have learned to extract competitive terms by playing external suitors against one another.

Latin America is largely absent from this great-power competition, and that absence is becoming a structural disadvantage. Without a visible economic and diplomatic footprint in the region, Latin American countries risk being sidelined from supply chains, investment opportunities, and standard-setting conversations that will shape African markets for decades.

The antidote is not to mimic China’s scale – an impossibility – but to offer focused, high-quality engagement in niches where Latin America is genuinely competitive: tropical agriculture, bioenergy, medium-scale infrastructure, and digital financial services. A handful of well-executed partnerships would do more for visibility and influence than any rhetorical commitment to South–South solidarity.

South–South Cooperation Beyond Slogans

The language of South–South cooperation has long been a staple of Latin American and African diplomacy, appearing in communiqués from Brasília to Abuja. But the content of that cooperation has often been thinner than the rhetoric, limited to technical exchanges, small-scale projects, and symbolic summits.

The new growth arc in Africa changes the calculus. It creates a commercial logic for engagement that aligns with the diplomatic language, giving Latin American businesses a material stake in Africa's success that goes beyond goodwill.

When Kenyan or Nigerian consumers buy Argentine grain or Brazilian construction services, South–South cooperation ceases to be a slogan and becomes a balance-sheet item.

There are early signs of movement. Brazilian agribusiness firms are exploring East African markets for tropical agriculture technology; Argentine fertiliser companies are eyeing West Africa's expanding farming sector; and Chilean renewable-energy developers are scoping opportunities in the Rift Valley.

But these are still exceptions, not the rule.

Scaling this requires deliberate government action: trade missions, export-credit facilities, bilateral investment treaties, and – crucially – a sustained diplomatic presence in African capitals. The countries that do this work now will be the ones that benefit when Africa’s growth arc matures into a full-blown economic corridor.

Scenarios for the Next Five Years

The baseline scenario is steady divergence: East Africa continues to grow at 5 to 6 percent, West Africa stabilises at 4 to 4.5 percent, and Latin America engages fitfully, capturing some commodity-driven gains but leaving higher-value opportunities on the table. The status quo is comfortable but leaves strategic value unclaimed.

A more ambitious scenario envisions a Latin American–African partnership agenda built around energy, agriculture, and digital services. This would involve not just bilateral deals but trilateral frameworks that link Latin American capital, African markets, and European or Asian technology and distribution networks.

The risk scenario is neglect. If Latin American governments and firms treat Africa as an afterthought while China, the Gulf states, and Europe deepen their positions, the region will find itself locked out of one of this century's most important growth stories.

That is not a neutral outcome; it is a slow-burn competitive loss.

For The Rio Times' readers – policymakers, investors, and business leaders across Latin America – the message is straightforward. Africa's new growth arc is not a distant abstraction.

It is a trade map being redrawn in real time, and the question is whether Latin America decides to be a cartographer or a spectator.

The Rio Times Read-Through: Why This Matters Now

The Rio Times has long argued that Latin America’s global positioning depends on looking beyond the traditional triad of the United States, Europe, and China. Africa – and specifically the East–West growth corridor – represents the most underexplored piece of that global puzzle.

The data are clear, the trends are structural, and the window is open. What remains to be seen is whether Latin American decision-makers have the strategic imagination and institutional patience to move before the window narrows.

This is not about charity or solidarity. It is about recognising that the fastest-growing economic bloc in the world over the next decade lies not in Asia or the Global North but along a corridor stretching from the Gulf of Guinea to the Horn of Africa.

The partners Latin America builds there now will define the region's place in the global economy for a generation.

For a publication committed to covering the intersections that others miss, this story is not optional. It is the kind of deep, cross-regional analysis that defines authority and serves a readership that needs to see the full board, not just the nearest pieces.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are East and West Africa growing faster than the rest of the continent?

East Africa benefits from diversified economies, strong regional integration through the EAC and COMESA, and investments in services and technology. West Africa is rebounding due to reforms in Nigeria and Ghana, new oil and gas production in Senegal and Niger, and recovering domestic demand after years of macroeconomic volatility.

What specific opportunities does this create for Latin American companies?

Latin American exporters of food, fertilisers, construction materials, and agricultural machinery can find expanding demand in both regions. Energy firms can explore joint ventures in West African oil and gas, while fintech and logistics companies can partner with East Africa’s rapidly growing tech hubs.

How does China’s presence affect Latin America’s ability to enter these markets?

China’s dominance in infrastructure and finance makes it a formidable competitor, but African governments are actively seeking to diversify partnerships. Latin America’s advantage lies in peer-to-peer models based on shared developmental experience, operational agility, and niche expertise in tropical agriculture, bioenergy, and medium-scale infrastructure.

World.title: Cyanide on Tomato Farms Kills 15 Elephants in Kenya’s Amboseli
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

KENYA · CONSERVATION

Key Facts —The toll: Fifteen elephants died in the Amboseli ecosystem over about a month, the Kenya Wildlife Service said on 29 July. —The cause: Preliminary laboratory analysis of samples taken from the carcasses detected cyanide, pointing to agricultural chemicals. —The source: The agency attributes the poisoning to pesticides sprayed on tomato farms neighbouring the park. —The worst-hit place: One herd in the Kimana Wildlife Sanctuary lost six animals in a short period, including adult females and calves. —The pattern of death: Ten animals showed partial paralysis and died within two days; five were found dead, their carcasses partly taken by scavengers. —Who died: Most of the dead were females and calves, with a single male among them.

The Amboseli elephant deaths were caused by cyanide, the Kenya Wildlife Service said on 29 July, after fifteen animals died over roughly a month from pesticides sprayed on tomato farms beside the park. Nobody has been accused of poisoning them deliberately.

What caused the Amboseli elephant deaths

The Kenya Wildlife Service said on 29 July that preliminary laboratory analysis of samples taken from the carcasses had detected traces of cyanide. Its director general, Professor Erastus Kanga, pointed to agricultural chemicals as the likely source.

The elephants had ingested pesticides sprayed on tomato farms bordering the Amboseli ecosystem. Post-mortem examinations linked the deaths to poisoning from chemicals believed to have come from those neighbouring farms.

The deaths were first noticed late in June, when rangers began seeing elephants fall ill, collapse and die. Fifteen animals died over roughly a month.

Where the farms meet the herds

The worst-affected area was the Kimana Wildlife Sanctuary, where a single herd lost six elephants in a short period, among them adult females and calves. Kimana sits in Kajiado County and is one of its main tomato-growing areas.

That is the whole problem in one sentence. Amboseli’s elephants move constantly between protected land and farmland in search of food and water, and the boundary exists on maps rather than on the ground.

Kenya has spent years building conservancies and corridors precisely to manage that movement. A sprayed field on the edge of one of them can undo a great deal of that work in a fortnight.

How the animals died

Ten of the elephants showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days, according to reporting on the agency’s findings. The other five were simply found dead, their carcasses partly consumed by scavengers.

Most of the dead were females and their calves, and only one male was among them. Dr Isaac Lekoolol, who heads veterinary and capture services at the agency, said the animals had shown similar clinical symptoms.

Farmers in Kenya have in the past been suspected of poisoning elephants deliberately to keep them out of crops. The Kenya Wildlife Service has made no such accusation in this case, and has not said who sprayed the fields.

The economics under the story

Amboseli is one of Kenya’s best-known parks, and its elephants, long studied and photographed against Kilimanjaro, are among the most recognisable in Africa. They are also, in plain commercial terms, an asset.

Wildlife tourism ranks among Kenya’s biggest earners of foreign exchange, and Amboseli is one of the handful of places international visitors ask for by name. Losing fifteen elephants in a month is a conservation event and a balance-sheet event at once.

The tension is not between tourism and farming in the abstract. It is between a horticulture sector that depends on pesticides and a tourism sector that depends on the animals those pesticides killed.

What the wildlife service is doing now

Kanga said the agency has contained the situation and warned communities around Amboseli and the neighbouring conservancies to take care with pesticides and other agricultural chemicals. It says it is working with others to prevent a repeat.

Rangers and researchers have stepped up surveillance across the ecosystem and are monitoring herds while investigations continue. The agency has not said whether anyone faces prosecution.

On human health it has been careful. It says there is currently no evidence that the contamination poses a risk to people, while cautioning that livestock also graze in the affected area.

A regional herd, a national problem

Amboseli’s elephants cross into Tanzania and back, which makes a poisoning on the Kenyan side a regional matter rather than a local one. The Rio Times reported in June on a Kenya and Tanzania agreement to jointly manage exactly those shared herds.

The case also lands in a difficult period for East African conservation generally, with sanctuaries elsewhere on the continent losing populations to habitat pressure rather than poison. Amboseli’s problem is closer to home and, in principle, easier to fix.

What makes this episode unusual is that nothing malicious has been established. Fifteen elephants may have died because a tomato crop was protected in the ordinary way, on land that a herd happened to walk across.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the Amboseli elephant deaths? Preliminary laboratory analysis of samples from the carcasses detected cyanide, which Kenya Wildlife Service traced to pesticides sprayed on tomato farms next to the park. Post-mortem examinations linked the deaths to those agricultural chemicals. How many elephants died and where? Fifteen elephants died within the Amboseli ecosystem over roughly a month. The worst-affected area was the Kimana Wildlife Sanctuary, where a single herd lost six animals in a short period. Is the contamination dangerous to people? Kenya Wildlife Service says there is currently no evidence that the contamination poses a risk to human health. It has cautioned that livestock also graze in the affected area. Has anyone been accused of poisoning the elephants? No. Kenya Wildlife Service has not accused anyone and has not said who sprayed the fields, and investigations are continuing.

World.title: 34 Dead as 49,000 Migrants Storm Spain’s Ceuta Enclave
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MOROCCO · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —At least 34 dead: Ceuta’s regional president, Juan Jesús Vivas, put the death toll at 34 by Friday, up from nine on Thursday evening. —Tens of thousands in a day: Estimates of arrivals in 24 hours range from about 49,000 to around 60,000, the higher figure equal to roughly 70% of the city’s usual population. —Spain calls it an attack: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, visiting on Friday, described the events as a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity. —Who he blames: Sánchez pointed at human smuggling networks rather than at Rabat, and both governments have reinforced the border. —The legal trigger: Spain’s Supreme Court ruled this month that people intercepted at sea cannot be returned to Morocco without due process. —The 2021 echo: More than 8,000 people entered Ceuta in two days in May 2021, during a diplomatic rupture over Western Sahara, according to the Associated Press. —Europe’s only land border with Africa: Ceuta and Melilla are the two points at which the European Union touches the African continent by land.

The Ceuta migrant crossing has killed at least 34 people and brought tens of thousands into the Spanish enclave in a single day, by the estimates available on Friday. Spain has sent soldiers, and its prime minister has called what happened a violation of the country’s territorial integrity.

How the Ceuta migrant crossing escalated

The first crowds came over on Thursday 30 July, most walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach and onto local roads, and Spain’s government delegation reported nine dead that evening. By Friday the toll given by Ceuta’s regional president, Juan Jesús Vivas, had reached at least 34.

The scale moved just as fast. What began as an estimate of 1,500 to 2,000 arrivals over ten days became, within a day, figures of between about 49,000 and 60,000 people in 24 hours.

At the upper end that is close to 70% of the city’s normal population. No European territory absorbs that in a day.

Madrid’s response, and its careful choice of words

Spain first refused Ceuta’s request for a national emergency, arguing that its legislation does not treat migration flows as a national-security risk, and sent 60 soldiers to reinforce the Civil Guard. By Friday the prime minister was on the ground.

“A violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” was how Pedro Sánchez described the events during his visit. It is the language of a border incident rather than a humanitarian one.

He was careful about who he blamed. Sánchez pointed at human smuggling networks that he said deceive young people and lead many of them to their deaths, rather than accusing the Moroccan government of opening the gates.

A court ruling that travelled faster than the law

Spain’s Supreme Court ruled earlier in July that people intercepted at sea on their way to Ceuta or Melilla cannot be pushed straight back without due process. Those who climb the land fence can still be returned immediately.

Sánchez said that interpretation had spread through smuggling networks over a matter of hours, which is his explanation for why a slow increase became a mass movement. Moroccan activists have been sceptical that a judgment in Madrid is what drew a crowd to a beach at Fnideq.

Both readings can be true. A legal change creates an opening, and organised networks are what turn an opening into a queue.

What Rabat has done, and not said

Morocco’s interior ministry did not respond to requests for comment as the crossings began. By Friday, Spanish and Moroccan forces were reinforcing the border together.

Spain’s interior ministry has said throughout that Rabat was cooperating closely and that Moroccan police were stopping large numbers of people on their side. Both governments have agreed to work towards returning everyone who entered illegally.

That cooperation is the diplomatic fact worth holding onto. This is not being handled as a rupture, whatever the rhetoric about territorial integrity suggests.

The shadow of 2021

The scenes recalled May 2021, when more than 8,000 people entered Ceuta within two days, according to the Associated Press. Spain had allowed Brahim Ghali, leader of the pro-independence Polisario Front, to be treated in a Spanish hospital, and Morocco was widely accused of easing its border controls in response.

That episode ended in a full diplomatic rupture, which is why every surge here is now read as a possible signal. No evidence has been produced that the same thing happened this week.

What is beyond dispute is the leverage. Morocco polices the approach to two European cities, and both capitals understand what that is worth.

Why a small enclave matters to the whole continent

Ceuta has been Spanish since 1580 and sits on a narrow isthmus, with a mixed population of Spanish and Moroccan residents and daily cross-border workers. Together with Melilla it forms the European Union’s only land frontier with Africa.

That makes it the place where Europe’s migration politics and Africa’s labour market meet most directly. Interior ministry figures put arrivals in Ceuta at close to 3,000 for the whole year as of 15 July, a number this week has made meaningless.

The pressure travels. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was ready to suspend the Schengen arrangement with Spain to protect Italian borders, even though the two countries share none.

Spain’s next official migration report is due on 3 August, and it will be the first audited measure of the past week. Until then every number in circulation is an estimate from a city that ran out of beds days ago.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people have died in the Ceuta migrant crossing? At least 34, according to Juan Jesus Vivas, president of the autonomous city of Ceuta. The toll rose through Thursday and Friday from an initial figure of nine. How many migrants have entered Ceuta? Estimates range from about 49,000 to around 60,000 in 24 hours. The higher figure is roughly 70% of Ceuta’s usual population. What has Spain said about it? Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, visiting Ceuta on Friday, called the events a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity. He blamed human smuggling networks rather than Morocco. Why did so many people cross at once? Spanish authorities link the surge to a Supreme Court ruling this month that people intercepted at sea cannot be returned without due process. Sanchez said that interpretation spread rapidly through smuggling networks.

Connected Coverage This story belongs to our running coverage of the contest for influence across the continent, gathered in Africa: The New Scramble. For the economic side of the same relationship, see how Morocco built Africa’s car and battery powerhouse on the strength of its access to European markets, and how Rabat has positioned itself as a security partner after it foiled a network of Sahel plots.

World.title: Tyla Drops Lagos Concert After Xenophobia Backlash
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

NIGERIA · MUSIC

Key Facts —The date is gone: Tyla’s 22 December Lagos show no longer appears among the listed dates of her A*POP World Tour, TVC News reported on 31 July after checking the schedule. —It was advertised: The Lagos performance had been carried on the tour’s promotional flier. —The trigger: Nigerian commentators had called for a boycott over xenophobic attacks on Nigerians living in South Africa. —The names: The content creator Solomon Buchi and the broadcaster known as Dotun were among those urging fans to stay away. —The flashpoint: Much of the anger centred on Chidimma Adetshina, the former Miss Universe Nigeria of Nigerian descent, reported to be facing deportation proceedings in South Africa. —No explanation: Neither Tyla nor her management has commented on the removal or given a reason for it. —The tour goes on: She is still billed to close the tour with shows in Cape Town and Johannesburg in January.

The Tyla Lagos concert scheduled for 22 December has disappeared from the South African singer’s official world tour dates, days after Nigerian public figures called for a boycott. Nobody in her camp has explained why, and the rest of the tour is unchanged.

What happened to the Tyla Lagos concert

TVC News reported on Friday 31 July that the 22 December date no longer appeared among the performances listed for Tyla’s A*POP World Tour. The show had previously been carried on the tour’s promotional flier.

There was no announcement, no statement and no refund notice reported alongside the change. The date simply stopped being there.

The rest of the itinerary is intact. Tyla is still scheduled to finish the tour in Cape Town and Johannesburg in January.

Why Nigerian audiences turned on a South African star

The boycott campaign built through the last week of July, driven by anger at renewed xenophobic attacks on Nigerians and other African migrants in South Africa. The content creator Solomon Buchi and the broadcaster known as Dotun were among the public figures who called on Nigerians not to attend.

Their argument was not about the music. It was that a South African artist should not collect Nigerian ticket money while Nigerians in South Africa were being attacked.

Much of the feeling attached to one case in particular. Chidimma Adetshina, the former Miss Universe Nigeria who is of Nigerian descent, is reported to be facing deportation proceedings in South Africa.

Nigerian opinion was not unanimous. Several Nigerian outlets described a split audience, with some fans arguing that punishing a performer for her government’s failures changes nothing.

The backdrop had been building for weeks. The Rio Times reported earlier this month that more than 53,000 migrants had left South Africa under pressure, and Nigeria’s government formally accused Pretoria of complicity in the violence on 29 July.

The silence that became the story

Tyla did not address the controversy publicly before the date came off the schedule, and she has not addressed it since. Neither she nor her management has confirmed that the boycott was the reason.

That silence is itself part of the complaint. The original criticism was that a performer with a global platform had said nothing about attacks on other Africans in her own country.

It leaves the removal open to two readings. Either it was a commercial decision about a show that would have struggled, or a quiet withdrawal from a fight the artist never chose.

What a cancelled date costs

Lagos is not a symbolic stop on an African tour. It is the commercial centre of one of the continent’s most important music markets, and losing the date removes a real revenue line and a promotional anchor for West Africa.

Nigerian promoters have spent years building an international touring circuit in Lagos, and a headline slot in late December is peak-season business. Removing it at this stage is costly for the local promoters and venues that had planned around it.

It also cuts against a decade of Afrobeats and amapiano cross-pollination, which has depended on artists moving freely between Lagos and Johannesburg. That traffic is what turned two national scenes into one export industry.

Promoters elsewhere will read the episode carefully. A tour date can now be lost to a diplomatic row that has nothing to do with the artist on the poster.

The row is bigger than one show

The politics around it moved quickly in the same week. South Africa’s envoy said around 80 people had been arrested over the attacks, and Pretoria pushed for a continental conversation on migration.

The Pan-African Parliament adopted a resolution on the violence, and President Cyril Ramaphosa called for African cooperation on migration. Nigeria had already accused South Africa of complicity in the attacks.

Cultural boycotts are a blunt instrument and rarely change a government’s behaviour. What they do reliably is make a private dispute visible, which is roughly what has happened to a December concert in Lagos.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has the Tyla Lagos concert been cancelled? The 22 December Lagos date no longer appears among the performances listed for her A*POP World Tour, TVC News reported on 31 July. Neither Tyla nor her management has confirmed a cancellation or given a reason. Why did Nigerians call for a boycott? The campaign followed renewed xenophobic attacks on Nigerians and other African migrants in South Africa. Critics argued that a South African artist should not take Nigerian ticket money while Nigerians in South Africa were being attacked. Who led the boycott calls? The content creator Solomon Buchi and the broadcaster known as Dotun were among the public figures who urged Nigerians to stay away. Nigerian opinion was divided, and several local outlets reported a split audience. Is the rest of Tyla’s tour affected? No. She is still billed to close the A*POP World Tour with performances in Cape Town and Johannesburg in January.





Sources: TVC News.

World.title: FDLR Disarmament Deal Fails to Sway Rwanda
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

DR CONGO · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —The protocol: Kinshasa announced on 28 July that the FDLR had signed an agreement to disarm, demobilise and move into cantonment sites away from combat zones. —The dissolution clause: FDLR leaders committed to dissolving the organisation, and accepted that fighters facing evidence of criminal responsibility answer in court. —The conditions: The group asked that no combatant be repatriated to Rwanda by force, with relocation to unnamed third countries as the alternative. —Rwanda’s answer: Kigali’s foreign minister called the protocol a non-event and said it is not part of the Washington Accords. —The territorial problem: Congo’s own monitoring identified six main FDLR zones in North and South Kivu, and says five of them are held by AFC/M23. —The verification plan: Biometric registration and individual identification are meant to stop demobilised fighters simply rejoining armed groups.

FDLR disarmament is back on the table: DR Congo said on 28 July that the militia had signed a protocol to disband, hand over its weapons and move into cantonment. Rwanda dismissed the deal within a day, which tells you how far apart the two governments remain.
