What the FDLR disarmament protocol actually says

Congo’s government announced the signing on national television on Tuesday 28 July, at a press conference given by Regional Integration Minister Floribert Anzuluni and government spokesman Patrick Muyaya. The FDLR agreed to disarm its fighters, demobilise them and move them into secure cantonment sites away from combat zones.

Its leaders also committed to dissolving the organisation and taking part fully in the process, and accepted that fighters against whom there is evidence of criminal responsibility will face the courts. The group is made up of remnants of Rwanda’s former army and of militias responsible for the 1994 genocide.

In return, the FDLR asked for guarantees. It wants demobilised combatants returned to Rwanda only voluntarily, arguing that conditions there are not yet safe, with relocation to third countries as the alternative.

Kinshasa says several countries have already signalled a willingness to receive them. It has not named any of them.

Why Kigali says it changes nothing

Rwanda’s foreign minister described the protocol as a non-event and said it bore no relation to the Washington Accords signed in 2025 or to their implementation framework. On that reading, Kinshasa still owes the dismantling of the FDLR as an obligation rather than a negotiation.

The dispute is not really about paperwork. Rwanda has for years cited the FDLR to explain its security posture in eastern Congo, and Congo has for years replied that the group is a residual force whose danger has been inflated.

Congo accuses Kigali of backing the M23 rebellion, which took large areas of the east in a rapid advance last year. Rwanda denies that, and denies having troops on Congolese soil, while occasionally describing its actions as defensive measures against the FDLR.

The map problem: five zones out of six

Technical work under the Joint Monitoring Mechanism identified six main FDLR areas of operation across North and South Kivu. That is where the protocol meets geography.

“Five of these areas are currently outside the control of the Armed Forces of the DRC and are under the control of the AFC/M23,” Anzuluni told reporters.

A disarmament programme that cannot physically reach five of its six target zones is, for now, a document rather than an operation. Whoever holds that ground controls the timetable.

How Kinshasa got here

Under the Washington agreements and the accompanying concept of operations, two mechanisms were foreseen for the FDLR: an awareness campaign to secure voluntary surrender, and military neutralisation if that failed. Rwanda, within the same framework, is expected to withdraw its troops.

Campaigns ran from last October with support from the UN mission and community leaders, and Kinshasa judged the results insufficient. From March it deployed army units to Walikale territory in North Kivu in preparation for possible operations.

According to Anzuluni, that deployment is what accelerated talks, and the FDLR’s political and military leadership eventually asked to negotiate terms. Between 10 and 27 July he took a progress report to the European Union, France, Belgium, South Africa, Angola, Tanzania, Uganda, Burundi, Togo and Equatorial Guinea.

Fingerprints instead of promises

A regional committee of international partners and experts is to be created to give the process credibility. Implementation falls to Congo’s Disarmament, Demobilisation, Community Recovery and Stabilisation Programme, with support from the UN mission and others.

Combatants are to be registered biometrically, including fingerprints, and identified individually. The purpose is blunt: earlier repatriation programmes lost track of fighters who then rejoined armed groups.

What it means for the minerals

Kinshasa’s own explanation for Rwanda’s presence is not security at all. It says the real motive is control of eastern Congo’s mineral resources, an argument that has hardened as coltan and tin from the region have been traced into global supply chains.

For anyone exposed to that supply chain, the FDLR file is the hinge. If it closes, Rwanda loses its stated reason to be there, and the argument moves to the harder question of who profits from the mines.

Nothing about this week guarantees that outcome. It does put a decades-old dispute onto paper for the first time in a long while.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the FDLR disarmament protocol commit the group to? The FDLR agreed to disarm its fighters, demobilise them and move into secure cantonment sites away from combat zones. Its leaders also committed to dissolving the organisation and accepted that fighters facing evidence of criminal responsibility will answer in court. Why does Rwanda reject the deal? Kigali’s foreign minister called the protocol a non-event and said it bears no relation to the Washington Accords or their implementation framework. Rwanda’s position is that Congo owes the dismantling of the FDLR as an obligation, not something to be negotiated. What is the biggest practical obstacle? Congo’s own monitoring identified six main FDLR zones across North and South Kivu, and says five of them are outside government control. Those five are held by the AFC/M23 rebellion. How will Congo verify who has demobilised? Combatants are to be registered biometrically, including fingerprints, and identified individually. The stated aim is to stop demobilised fighters from quietly rejoining armed groups, as happened in earlier programmes.

Sources: Regional Integration Minister Floribert Anzuluni; government spokesman Patrick Muyaya; Kigali's foreign minister.

World.title: Costa Rica Suspends Florencio del Castillo Toll Due To Romería
World.content:
Those brave enough to drive towards Cartago during Costa Rica’s annual Romería will receive a temporary break from toll payments on the Florencio del Castillo Highway this weekend. The National Roadway Council, known as Conavi, will suspend toll collection at the Tres Ríos station for 12 hours, beginning at 6 p.m. on Saturday, August 1, and ending at 6 a.m. on Sunday, August 2.

The measure is intended to keep traffic moving during the busiest period of the pilgrimage, when large numbers of people travel on foot and by vehicle toward the Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels in Cartago. The Romería is one of Costa Rica’s largest religious traditions. Pilgrims from across the country walk to the basilica to honor Our Lady of the Angels, our patron saint, whose feast day is celebrated each year on August 2.

The Florencio del Castillo Highway is the main connection between the San José metropolitan area and Cartago. The combination of pilgrims, support vehicles, buses and regular weekend traffic can create significant congestion along the route, particularly around Tres Ríos and the entrances to Cartago.

Authorities expect that allowing vehicles to pass through the toll station without stopping to pay will reduce delays during the overnight period when pilgrim traffic is expected to reach its peak. However, Conavi warned drivers that the temporary suspension does not mean they should pass through the station at high speed.

The toll booths, barriers and other structures will remain in place throughout the night. Motorists should reduce their speed when approaching the plaza, follow posted limits and remain alert for traffic officers, temporary controls and pedestrians near the roadway.

Drivers should also expect heavier-than-normal traffic even while toll collection is suspended. Authorities are urging motorists to plan ahead, allow additional travel time and follow instructions from traffic police operating along the route.

Pedestrians participating in the pilgrimage should use designated walking areas whenever possible, remain visible after dark and exercise caution when crossing streets or walking near moving traffic. Regular toll collection at the Tres Ríos stationwill start again at 6 a.m. Sunday.

The temporary suspension is part of the wider traffic and public safety operation organized each year for the Romería. Authorities may introduce additional road controls depending on the number of pilgrims and traffic conditions approaching Cartago.

World.title: Novak Djokovic Returns to Cincinnati With US Open History at Stake
World.content:
Novak Djokovic will return to the Cincinnati Open in August, choosing one final hard-court tournament before resuming his pursuit of a record 25th Grand Slam singles title at the US Open. The 39-year-old Serbian is part of the Cincinnati field after withdrawing from the Canadian Open in Montreal to manage his workload. His decision gives him additional recovery time following Wimbledon while still providing an opportunity to test his form before the season’s final major.



The Cincinnati Open runs from August 8 through August 23. The US Open begins August 23, with the singles main draws starting August 30 in New York. Djokovic’s appearance will mark his return to a tournament where he has produced some of the most memorable tennis of his career.

He is a three-time Cincinnati champion, winning the event in 2018, 2020 and 2023. His most recent title came after a remarkable final against Carlos Alcaraz that lasted three hours and 49 minutes. Djokovic saved a championship point before defeating Alcaraz 5-7, 7-6(7), 7-6(4). The match remains the longest best-of-three-set final in ATP Tour history.

Cincinnati now carries a different kind of importance for Djokovic. He remains capable of reaching the closing stages of the sport’s biggest tournaments, but winning them has become increasingly difficult as Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have taken control of the men’s game.

Djokovic reached the Australian Open final in February after defeating Sinner in a five-set semifinal. Alcaraz then denied him the title in four sets, becoming the first player to defeat Djokovic in an Australian Open final.

At Wimbledon, Djokovic survived a five-hour, 15-minute quarterfinal against Félix Auger-Aliassime before losing to Sinner in the semifinals. It was another strong Grand Slam run, but it also illustrated the physical challenge facing Djokovic when he must defeat several leading players over two weeks.

“It’s good, but not good enough,” Djokovic said after his Wimbledon exit. His reduced schedule reflects that reality. Djokovic has increasingly avoided tournaments that might leave him physically depleted before the Grand Slams, preferring longer training periods and carefully selected appearances.

That strategy allows him to arrive rested, but it can also leave him short of competitive matches. Cincinnati offers a compromise. It gives Djokovic a high-level hard-court test against many of the same players he could face in New York, while leaving time to recover before the US Open singles competition begins.

The tournament will feature a deep men’s field led by Sinner, Alcaraz and several other leading contenders. Alcaraz won the Cincinnati title in 2025, while Sinner captured the championship in 2024. Djokovic enters the event ranked No. 5, meaning his path could include an earlier meeting with one of the tournament’s leading seeds.

The expanded Cincinnati format also makes recovery between matches and management of the summer heat important parts of any title run. The immediate objective will be finding his timing on outdoor hard courts. The larger question is whether he can still defeat Sinner or Alcaraz late in a major after navigating several demanding rounds.

Djokovic has not won a Grand Slam singles title since the 2023 US Open, when he collected his 24th major. He has continued reaching finals and semifinals since then, but the record-breaking 25th title has remained out of reach. Cincinnati will not settle that pursuit. It will, however, provide the clearest indication yet of whether Djokovic is ready for another serious challenge in New York.

World.title: Costa Rica Cuts 2026 Growth Forecast as El Niño Raises Cost Risks
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Central Bank has lowered its economic growth forecast for 2026 as weaker exports, slower household demand and the expected effects of El Niño increase pressure on agriculture, electricity generation and consumer prices. The bank now expects the Costa Rican economy to grow 3.4% this year, down from the 3.5% forecast issued in April and the 3.8% projected in January. Growth is expected to reach 3.5% in 2027, also one-tenth of a percentage point below the previous estimate.

The revision does not point to a recession, but it confirms that the economy is losing momentum after expanding 4.6% in 2025. Economic growth slowed from 4% during the first quarter of this year to 3.4% in the second quarter. Household spending and construction remain the main sources of support. Household consumption is forecast to grow 2.9% in 2026, while investment in buildings, equipment and other fixed assets is expected to rise 5.3%.

Construction grew 8.9% year over year during the second quarter. Financial and insurance services expanded 5.9%, while information and communications grew 4.4%. Exports present a more uneven picture. Total exports are expected to rise 2.4% this year, but that figure masks a projected 5.3% increase in goods exports and a 1.7% decline in services exports.



The slowdown reflects weaker international demand and reduced activity in business and manufacturing-related services. Costa Rica’s free trade zone economy is still expected to grow 4.6% during 2026, compared with 3.2% for businesses operating under the domestic tax system.

El Niño adds another layer of uncertainty. Current projections call for significantly below-average rainfall in the Pacific, Central Valley and parts of the Northern Zone, alongside higher temperatures across much of the country. Rainfall could fall as much as 60% below normal in the North Pacific and about 40% below normal in several other affected regions. The Caribbean and parts of the Northern Zone may experience the opposite pattern, with rainfall above historic averages.

Drier and hotter conditions could reduce yields for crops such as coffee and pineapple while limiting water and pasture available for cattle. Higher temperatures may also increase the spread of certain fungi and plant diseases. The outlook has already led to lower expectations for the agricultural sector. The Central Bank projects that agricultural production could contract in 2027 as weather damage combines with higher fertilizer and operating costs.

The risks extend beyond farms. Costa Rica depends heavily on hydroelectric plants, and lower water levels in reservoirs could force the Costa Rican Electricity Institute to generate more power using imported fuel. Thermal generation is substantially more expensive than hydropower. Greater reliance on fuel-powered plants could eventually raise electricity rates for homes and businesses, particularly if international oil prices remain elevated.

The Central Bank estimates that hydrocarbon prices will increase by an average of 28.2% during 2026. Fuel prices were already 15.5% higher in June than a year earlier. Those pressures are expected to gradually lift inflation after an extended period of unusually low or negative price growth. Average inflation should rise above 2%, though it is expected to remain below the bank’s 3% target.

Food and electricity represent the clearest risks for consumers. Lower agricultural production can push up grocery prices, while more expensive power generation can raise household bills and operating costs for hotels, restaurants, manufacturers and other businesses. The exchange rate continues to complicate the picture. The colón’s appreciation has helped limit the local cost of imported goods, but it has also placed pressure on tourism companies, exporters and other businesses that earn dollars while paying many expenses in colones.

The Central Bank reported purchasing $944.8 million in the foreign exchange market for stabilization purposes through July 30. International reserves stood at approximately $20.8 billion on July 28, equal to 18.1% of gross domestic product. The bank lowered its monetary policy rate to 3% in July, continuing a series of cuts that began in March 2023. Lower policy rates can eventually reduce borrowing costs, although the decline has only partially reached the interest rates offered by commercial banks.

Public finances remain another concern. Central government debt reached 61.1% of GDP in May, placing it above the 60% threshold that triggers stricter spending limits under Costa Rica’s fiscal rule. The government maintained a primary surplus, meaning revenue exceeded spending before interest payments, but the surplus fell from 0.7% of GDP in May 2025 to 0.6% a year later. The overall financial deficit increased from 1.1% to 1.3% during the same period.

Costa Rica’s economy is still growing faster than many developed countries, and strong construction, financial services and goods exports provide some protection against a sharper slowdown. However, the revised forecast shows that the country is entering the second half of 2026 with less room for error. A stronger-than-expected El Niño, further increases in fuel prices or weaker demand from major trading partners could place additional pressure on growth and household costs.

World.title: Boston Scientific Confirms Costa Rica Layoffs in $800M Plan
World.content:
Boston Scientific has confirmed that its Costa Rican operation forms part of a global restructuring program that sets aside as much as $300 million for employee termination benefits, though the company has not disclosed how many workers it will cut in Costa Rica, in which of its local sites, or on what timeline.

The medical device manufacturer’s board of directors approved the plan, which the company calls its 2026 Restructuring Plan, on July 21. It was disclosed publicly six days later in a Form 8-K filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing estimates total pre-tax charges of between $700 million and $800 million, broken down into $300 million to $350 million to move production lines between facilities, $275 million to $300 million in employee termination benefits, and $125 million to $150 million in other costs including consulting fees, contract cancellations, program management and asset write-offs.

Between $600 million and $700 million of the total is expected to result in cash outlays. The company projects the program will reduce gross annual pre-tax expenses by roughly $500 million once its benefits are realized, and says those savings will be reinvested into growth initiatives. The plan began this year and is expected to be substantially complete by the end of 2029.

In the filing, Boston Scientific stated that it anticipates some headcount reductions while continuing to create positions in areas of growth. It provided no figures for total job losses and no country-level breakdown. Asked afterward about the Costa Rican operation, the company confirmed that the country is included in the reorganization but declined to specify numbers or the areas affected. In a written position, Boston Scientific said Costa Rica has been an important part of its global organization for more than 25 years and that it maintains a commitment to its long-term future in the country.

The scale of that operation is substantial by any measure, though the company’s own public figures for its Costa Rican workforce have not been consistent. Boston Scientific has previously stated through its vice president of operations that it employs 10,000 people in Costa Rica, a figure it has also characterized as 16.9 percent of a global workforce of 59,000. In a separate response to questions this week, the company put its local payroll at approximately 12,000 across San José, Alajuela, Cartago and Heredia. The two figures have not been reconciled by the company, and no explanation has been offered for the difference.

Against those numbers stand the commitments Boston Scientific filed with the state. The record of free trade zone benefits granted to the company, published in La Gaceta, shows a projected investment of more than $850 million together with 9,531 direct jobs beginning in January of this year and a further 200 positions by September 2029. Boston Scientific has not confirmed whether it will maintain those projections following the restructuring announcement. Those figures are the terms on which the company received its tax and tariff exemptions, and they represent the clearest public benchmark against which the plan’s local effect can eventually be measured.

Evidence that the cuts have already begun in Costa Rica comes from workers themselves. A research and development engineer who was let go and spoke on condition of anonymity described being notified without warning after three years supporting product review work for one of the company’s local divisions. The engineer said reductions of one to two people had occurred across several different teams and that layoffs of this kind had not previously been seen at the Costa Rican operation, in contrast to the United States. That account has not been independently confirmed by the company or by labor authorities.

The government has acknowledged it does not yet know the domestic impact. Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos said information on Boston Scientific remains in development and that the global plan has not specified its effects in Costa Rica. The administration of President Laura Fernández has announced preliminary measures in response.

The announcement lands on a free trade zone regime already under strain. More than 600 companies operate under the regime, and together they generated 67 percent of the $11.722 billion in goods Costa Rica exported in the first half of 2026. Medical device manufacturers accounted for $5.382 billion of that total, with the United States as the principal destination. Costa Rican exports to the United States now face a 12.5 percent tariff imposed on July 24 following a Section 301 investigation into the enforcement of prohibitions on goods produced with forced labor, a rate higher than the 10 percent applied to Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

Boston Scientific has operated in Costa Rica since 2004, manufactures more than 1,800 types of medical devices in the country and opened an additional plant in Cartago earlier this year. It ranked as the country’s leading medical device exporter in 2024 and the first half of 2025. What remains unknown is the only question that matters locally: how many of those jobs, and which of those plants, fall inside the $300 million the company has now set aside to pay people to leave.

World.title: Costa Rica Investigates Jaguar Pelt Seized in Heredia Raid
World.content:
An apparent jaguar pelt found inside a home during raids against a violent criminal group has opened a separate wildlife investigation alongside an organized crime case involving drugs, weapons and homicide. The Judicial Investigation Organization (OIJ) carried out eight raids early this morning in Heredia, Aserrí and Desamparados. Ten suspects were detained, including alleged members of a group operating primarily from the La Gran Samaria neighborhood in Heredia.

Investigators believe the organization carried out tumbonazos, a term used in Costa Rica for armed robberies in which criminals steal drugs, money or other contraband from rival trafficking groups. Some groups pose as police officers to enter homes or intercept shipments.

Agents seized an apparent jaguar pelt inside one of the properties. Michael Soto, interim director of the Judicial Investigation Organization, said the discovery is now being examined as a possible violation of Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law. Authorities have not determined where the pelt originated, how it reached the house or whether the animal was killed in Costa Rica. It is also unclear whether the pelt was being kept as a trophy, offered for sale or moved as part of a wildlife-trafficking operation.

Investigators will also need to formally confirm that the skin came from a jaguar. The jaguar, known scientifically as Panthera onca, is classified as an endangered species under Costa Rican wildlife regulations. National law allows wildlife officials to confiscate animals, skins, body parts and other products linked to suspected illegal hunting, transport or trade.

The discovery could therefore produce an additional criminal case separate from the drug and homicide investigation. Any charges will depend on what authorities establish about the pelt’s authenticity, origin and chain of possession.

The criminal group targeted today is also suspected of involvement in the September 2025 killing of a man in Barreal de Heredia. Investigators believe the homicide followed a dispute involving drugs and that the group hired gunmen from southern San José neighborhoods to carry it out.

A pistol recovered during the raids could be connected to the killing and will undergo forensic testing. The suspects are also believed to have links to another organization dismantled during raids in Santa Bárbara de Heredia on July 9. Six people were detained in that operation, where authorities found counterfeit OIJ vests and high-caliber weapons allegedly used during armed home invasions.

The ten people detained today were transferred to prosecutors, who will determine what precautionary measures to request while the investigation continues. The jaguar pelt remains one of the operation’s most unusual pieces of evidence. What began as a raid focused on violent drug-related crime could now expand into an investigation involving the illegal possession, hunting or trafficking of one of Costa Rica’s most protected wild animals.

World.title: National Emergency Management Organization supports Hurricane Preparedness Simulation Exercise
World.content:
National Emergency Management Organization supports Hurricane Preparedness Simulation Exercise

By Zoila Palma: Today, the National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO) Southern Region is supporting the Three-Phase Hurricane Preparedness Simulation Exercise for Fisherfolk and Fishing Cooperatives in Dangriga Town.

The simulation exercise conducted by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in collaboration with the Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation is designed to strengthen hurricane readiness by testing warning dissemination, communication protocols, fisher and vessel accountability, vessel and equipment protection, evacuation procedures, and continuity arrangements for the fisheries sector under a simulated tropical cyclone scenario.

NEMO noted that these exercises help identify strengths, expose operational gaps, and ensure that communities and critical sectors are better prepared to respond when severe weather threatens.

World.title: BELTRAIDE meets with Belize Tourism Industry Association to strengthen Tourism collaboration
World.content:
BELTRAIDE meets with Belize Tourism Industry Association to strengthen Tourism collaboration

By Zoila Palma: On July 30, 2026, BELTRAIDE met with the Belize Tourism Industry Association (BTIA) to explore opportunities for collaboration in support of Belize’s tourism industry and tourism-related businesses.

The meeting was led by BTIA President, Efren Perez, and Executive Director, Lynette Canto.

BELTRAIDE was represented by Executive Director, Ishmael Quiroz, Deputy Executive Director, Monique Usher, Jorge Gentle, Manager of SBDCBelize, and Sarita Bejerano, Manager of Belize Training & Employment Centre (BTEC).

Discussions included hospitality training, business development support, digital marketing, the wedding and destination tourism market, destination planning initiatives (including the World Bank Tourism Corridor Project), and the creation of a referral system to connect BTIA members with BELTRAIDE’s services.

BELTRAIDE also highlighted support available through BTEC, SBDCBelize, BelizeINVEST, and EXPORTBelize—offering training, advisory services, investment facilitation, export development, and market access.

World.title: Government of Belize launches development of Electronic Single Window for Trade
World.content:
Government of Belize launches development of Electronic Single Window for Trade

The Government of Belize has officially launched the development of its Electronic Single Window (ESW) for Trade, marking a significant milestone in the country’s ongoing efforts to modernize trade administration, strengthen border efficiency, and improve the ease of doing business.

Supported through financing from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and the European Union (EU), the ESW will establish a secure, digital platform that enables traders to submit import and export documentation electronically through a single entry point. By replacing multiple paper-based processes with an integrated online system, the ESW will simplify regulatory procedures, reduce processing times and administrative costs, and enhance transparency and predictability across Belize’s trade environment.

The development of the system will be undertaken by Concepto SAS, a Uruguay-based technology firm with extensive experience in implementing electronic single window solutions throughout the region. The implementation phase will span 24 months, which commenced with the official vendor kick-off meeting held on July 29, 2026.

The first phase of implementation will integrate five key regulatory agencies: the Customs and Excise Department, the Chief Pharmacist Office, the Supplies Control Unit, the Belize Agricultural Health Authority, and the Belize Fisheries Department. These institutions will work collaboratively to redesign business processes, digitize permit and licensing procedures, and strengthen inter-agency coordination. The Central Executing Unit and the Directorate General for Foreign Trade are coordinating the initiative.

Once operational, the Electronic Single Window is expected to strengthen Belize’s competitiveness, support exporters and importers, attract investment, and contribute to sustainable economic growth by making trade faster, more transparent, and more efficient. As implementation progresses, additional border regulatory agencies will be incorporated into the platform, ultimately creating a fully integrated national trade facilitation ecosystem that benefits government, the private sector, and consumers alike.

World.title: Ministry of Rural Transformation launches Digital platforms to modernize trade licensing and rural development
World.content:
Ministry of Rural Transformation launches Digital platforms to modernize trade licensing and rural development

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government has launched two new digital platforms aimed at modernizing local governance and strengthening evidence-based rural development across Belize.

The Trade License Management and Administration System (TRALMA) and the Community Profile Information System (CPIS) were officially unveiled as part of the country’s ongoing transition toward more efficient, transparent and technology-driven public administration.

TRALMA is designed to digitize the trade licensing process across Belize’s municipal and rural authorities in accordance with the Trade License Act 19 of 2024. The system features separate portals for the public and government staff, allowing business owners to apply for trade licenses, track applications, make payments and download QR-coded, verifiable licenses online, reducing the reliance on manual and paper-based procedures.

Meanwhile, CPIS provides a centralized, publicly accessible platform containing demographic, economic and infrastructural information on rural communities. The data is collected using KOBO technology by rural community development officers and is intended to provide planners and policymakers with reliable baseline information to help guide targeted and equitable development initiatives.

The launch ceremony was attended by Minister of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government Oscar Requena, Chief Executive Officer Valentino Shal and key stakeholders, municipal representatives, rural officers and government partners.

Guest speaker Giacomo Sanchez, President of the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also participated in the event.

The Ministry said the introduction of TRALMA and CPIS represents a major step in bridging technology and public service while improving access to transparent and efficient governance for businesses and rural communities across Belize.

World.title: International News: ICE Airport arrests raise alarm as Immigration Enforcement intensifies across US
World.content:
International News: ICE Airport arrests raise alarm as Immigration Enforcement intensifies across US

By Zoila Palma: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests at US airports are reportedly becoming more frequent, raising concerns among immigration attorneys who say travelers are increasingly being detained while attempting to board flights.

The arrests come as the agency faces pressure to advance President Donald Trump’s deportation agenda, including a stated goal of approximately 2,000 arrests per day, CNN reports.

Attorneys say the enforcement actions are increasingly targeting people with expired visas and others involved in immigration proceedings. In one recent case, a woman who had entered the United States legally and was seeking asylum was detained at a Washington, DC-area airport while traveling home to Texas for her father’s funeral. Another client represented by attorney Joe Moravec was reportedly detained at a Chicago airport despite also being legally present in the country.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has defended its enforcement approach, saying the administration is working to prevent undocumented immigrants from flying unless they are leaving the country voluntarily.

Immigration attorney Jeff Joseph, president of the American Immigration Lawyers Association, said the level of enforcement and cooperation between TSA and ICE at airports is unlike anything previously seen.

Former acting ICE Director John Sandweg said airports provide agents with a secure environment where travelers’ information and movements are already known, making arrests easier to carry out with fewer personnel.

World.title: Police Youth Cadet summer camp highlights discipline, leadership and youth talent
World.content:
Police Youth Cadet summer camp highlights discipline, leadership and youth talent

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department continued its youth-focused programming on Thursday, July 30, with Day 4 of the National Police Youth Cadet Corps Summer Camp 2026, featuring a day of competition, leadership development and talent showcases.

The activities included a Foot Drill Competition, where regional teams demonstrated discipline, teamwork, precision and coordination while performing various drill movements and reciting the Belize Police Youth Cadet Corps Pledge. The Northern Region emerged as champions, while the Eastern Region placed second.

The competition was adjudicated by Dangriga Town Mayor Robert Mariano, retired Police Inspector Matthew Lopez and Commander of the Community Oriented Policing Unit, Senior Superintendent Gerald Jones.

The Police Department said the event sought not only to test the cadets’ ability to perform drill movements accurately and in synchronization, but also to instill values including respect, responsibility, perseverance, leadership, compassion, morale and good sportsmanship.

The day’s activities concluded with the Cadet Glamorous Pageant Night, celebrating the creativity, confidence and talents of Belize’s youth. Cadets competed in segments including casual wear, talent showcase, formal No. 1 cadet uniform and evening wear, with Athena Azueta of Roaring Creek, representing the Western Region, crowned the winner.

The summer camp is a flagship initiative of the Community Oriented Policing Unit aimed at strengthening trust and positive relationships between young people and police officers while developing skills in leadership, teamwork, communication and problem-solving.

World.title: Taiwan’s Medical students conduct clinical placement in Belize
World.content:
Taiwan’s Medical students conduct clinical placement in Belize

By Zoila Palma: Taiwan Ambassador to Belize Amino Chi met recently with Taiwanese medical students from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University—Bo Jang Chiou, Tian Qi Wang, and Yi Chan.

The medical students are conducting their clinical placement under the guidance of Antonio Coyoc, Regional Hospital Administrator of the Western Regional Hospital.

During the meeting, they shared their experiences working alongside local healthcare professionals, caring for patients, and learning from Belize’s healthcare system.

Ambassador Chi commended the students for their passion for public service and their dedication to improving the health and well-being of the Belizean people.

The Taiwan Embassy pledged to continue to promote medical cooperation with Belize and deepen bilateral partnership.

World.title: International News: Spain says mass migrant surge into Ceuta reversed as thousands return to Morocco
World.content:
International News: Spain says mass migrant surge into Ceuta reversed as thousands return to Morocco

By Zoila Palma: Spain says a massive surge of migrants into its North African enclave of Ceuta has been brought under control, with thousands of those who crossed the border reportedly returning voluntarily to Morocco.

Spanish authorities estimated that about 50,000 people entered the territory by land and sea since Thursday, while local officials put the figure as high as 60,000.

At least 19 bodies were reportedly recovered from the water, while Ceuta’s local government said the death toll could be as high as 34, Reuters report.

Moroccan security forces used batons and tear gas to disperse crowds gathered near border gates as authorities sought to prevent further crossings. Water cannon were also deployed, while the charred remains of vehicles could be seen following clashes. Spanish military vehicles were positioned along sections of the border, as several hundred migrants were seen returning through official checkpoints and openings in the fence, with some saying they lacked food and shelter in Ceuta.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited Ceuta on Friday and described the mass crossing as a “violation of Spain’s territorial sovereignty.” He said authorities were accelerating the repatriation of migrants who entered illegally, with Morocco cooperating in the process.

Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres suggested that a recent Supreme Court ruling restricting the summary return of migrants intercepted at sea may have contributed to the surge.

World.title: Wheatley granted injunction barring IC charges until judicial review
World.content:
Andrew Wheatley

The Supreme Court has granted an injunction preventing the Integrity Commission (IC) from charging Cabinet Minister Dr Andrew Wheatley until the hearing and determination of an application by his lawyers for judicial review.

Wheatley had applied for leave to pursue judicial review against the IC’s recommendation that he be charged with illicit enrichment.

Observer Online understands that the Supreme Court on Friday granted Wheatley’s application, recommending that the judicial review be heard by a panel of three judges.

Before granting the injunction, presiding Judge Justice David Batts had suggested that the IC consider an undertaking not to charge Dr Wheatley until the hearing and determination of the judicial review.

The commission said it could not give an undertaking at this time. The judge then granted the injunction.

It is understood that the IC’s application for leave to appeal the ruling was denied.

The Integrity Commission had alleged that there is a disproportionality in Wheatley’s assets when compared to his income to the tune of $164 million.

Wheatley rejected the allegation and accused the IC of failing to take into consideration $168 million in rental income accumulated over a decade.

He is being represented by a high powered legal team including King’s Counsel Ransford Braham, Abe Dabdoub and Neco Pagon.

The Integrity Commission is being represented by King’s Counsel Kevin Powell.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.
