World.title: Albanian Graduates Hit Hardest by ‘Outdated’ North Macedonia Ranking System
World.content:
In early 2025, when Emine Haxhiu Memishi applied for the post of Junior Associate at North Macedonia’s Ministry of Economy and Labour, she did so armed with a degree in economics from Istanbul Commerce University, an average grade of 9.88, a year of professional training behind her, and a readiness to return to her homeland when so many like her do not.

There was another grade, however, that Haxhiu Memishi hadn’t factored in, one that did not feature on her diploma, in her grade average, or the recommendation letters written by her professors – 0.5, the coefficient assigned by North Macedonia to any foreign university that does not feature on the three big international rankings lists.

Haxhiu Memishi fell at the very first stage of the recruitment process.

“I felt disappointed and treated unfairly,” the 31-year-old told BIRN.

World.title: Money the Greatest Challenge Facing Serbia’s Small, Independent Media
World.content:
For Serbia’s small independent newsrooms, pressure comes not only in the form of intimidation, spurious lawsuits, or physical assault. Increasingly, it is financial.

The Serbian media landscape is sharply divided between outlets close to the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and independent newsrooms.

Research has found that media loyal to the ruling party are the primary beneficiaries of co-financing and advertising from public bodies. Independent media are starved of such funds.

This helps explain why pro-government outlets can operate without the same financial pressures, while independent newsrooms struggle to cover basic overheads and remain vulnerable to political and economic pressure.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Danube Falls to Lowest Levels in 30 Years
World.content:
Suspected Russian missile lands in Poland; extradition of former justice minister sought

A cruise missile crossed into eastern Poland early on Thursday, striking a field and apparently exploding on impact, during another large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland’s Operational Command said radar detected an unidentified object moving west at 03:40 and dispatched an F-16 to identify and intercept it. Six minutes later, the object disappeared from radar. A Mi-24 helicopter traced its probable impact point to an uninhabited area near Tarnawa-Kolonia in Lublin province. Police arriving at the site found fragments spread around a crater approximately 10 metres across, some 2 kilometres from the nearest homes. No one was injured and no buildings were damaged. The area was checked for explosive and radiological hazards before investigators began examining it. Speaking to reporters, PM Donald Tusk said the preliminary evidence pointed to a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, but stressed that this still had to be confirmed. He said there was no reason to believe Poland had been the intended target, and that Polish forces were prepared to shoot the missile down had it continued flying. “This war is full of surprises, and we must learn very quickly from new situations and possible new threats,” Tusk said. “For now, the reports – particularly the military ones – indicate that everything worked as it should.” Maksymilian Dura, a retired naval commander and Defence24 expert, said it was possible that the Russians had deliberately directed the missile over Poland. “Given Russia’s desperation and the difficult situation it is now in, they may simply be probing us. Such incidents will happen again,” he told PAP. The episode adds to a growing record of the war crossing Poland’s border. In September 2025, 19 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in a single night, prompting allied NATO aircraft to intervene.

Poland this week formally requested the US detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted over alleged abuses of the Justice Fund under the previous Law and Justice government. Spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office Anna Adamiak said the request, submitted through diplomatic channels on Monday, covers 19 of the 26 offences prosecutors have attributed to Ziobro. Prosecutors accuse him of directing a criminal group, exceeding his powers and steering grants towards selected organisations. Ziobro, in the US since May, has not been questioned in the investigation and denies fleeing Poland. He had previously received protection in Hungary, but the new government there later withdrew his refugee status and invalidated his travel documents. The US Justice Department will first assess whether Poland’s request meets the treaty’s formal requirements. A federal judge would then rule on whether extradition is legally permissible, before the final decision passes to the US secretary of state. Polish prosecutors say the process could take anywhere from several months to several years. Responding on X, the former justice minister said he trusted the independence of American institutions and expected them to examine what he called the case’s political context. “Donald Tusk, Adam Bodnar and Waldemar Zurek repeatedly publicly prejudged my guilt before any independent court had examined the case,” he claimed.

World.title: Bosnia’s Mainly Serb Entity Ramps Up Lobbying Outlay under Trump
World.content:
In 2021, under the Democrat administration of President Joe Biden, lobbyists hired by the Republika Srpska authorities were focussed mainly on forwarding messages from Banja Luka to US senators, including Marco Rubio, now US Secretary of State.

In early 2022, however, the focus shifted to direct conversations with, for example, Robin Brooks, the then director of the Department of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs at the US State Department and Republican congressman Robert Aderholt.

“Our goal is a network of relevant interlocutors who share key principles: respect for Dayton, appreciation of reality, and readiness for rational cooperation,” said Ana Trisic Babic, director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republika Srpska.

Trump’s return to office in January 2025 brought a significant hike in spending by the Republika Srpska in the US. Since then, the entity has hired four new lobbying firms: Zell & Associates International Advocates, Stokes Strategies, GS2Law and Continental Strategy.

Zell & Associates International Advocates was paid around a million euros, though almost half of that went to an Israeli subcontractor called Gilad Government Relations and Lobbying.

One of the most influential lobbying firms in Israel, Gilad is co-owned by Ariel Sender, who headed Trump’s campaign among US citizens in Israel during the 2016 and 2020 elections; in 2012, the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, temporarily revoked the entry passes for Gilad staff amid an ethics scandal.

Zell & Associates did not respond to a request for comment.

Republika Srpska also paid around half a million euros to Stokes Strategies, whose submissions to FARA show it focussed on building relations with conservative organisations and meetings in Congress.

Stokes paid Christine Czerjenewski of Firefly Communications some 50,000 euros for research work. Czerjenewski has connections in US conservative circles and the Republican Party and is a former fellow of the conservative public policy group The Heritage Foundation, described by The New York Times this week as a “bastion of American conservatism”.

Neither Stokes Strategies nor Firefly Communications responded to requests for comment.

A month before the US lifted sanctions on Dodik & Co, Republika Srpska authorities hired GS2Law to the tune of 130,000 euros.

According to their FARA report, GS2Law was tasked with legal research and preparation of a lawsuit “in connection with the previous listing of certain citizens and entities of Republika Srpska on the OFAC [sanctions] list”.

GS2Law did not respond to a request for comment.

Continental Strategy was hired earlier this year, on a contract worth around 660,000 euros. The firm is led by former Trump adviser Carlos Trujillo.

World.title: Serbian Feminists Expect Boost From Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law
World.content:
Serbian women’s rights organisations say they feel encouraged by developments in neighbouring Montenegro, which has adopted law changes introducing two paid days of “menstrual leave” per month for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea, or severe menstrual cramp.

“It has generated considerable enthusiasm among women. It feels like a very progressive idea and a major step forward, especially if we take into account that no country in the wider region has a law introducing such measures,” said Ljiljana Todorovic Jovanovic, founder of the FemIn Collective, a women’s rights NGO from Pozarevac.

The news from Montenegro has been hailed by Serbian women’s rights groups but criticised by some of the general public, activists said.

“Part of the general public welcomed the move and expressed hope that something similar would be introduced in Serbia. However, another part interpreted the news as meaning that women had been granted some kind of privilege,” Ana Mirkailo, an activist from Befem, a Belgrade-based feminist cultural centre and NGO founded in 2009, told BIRN.

She added that this divided reaction didn’t surprise her but “served as a reminder of how much work still needs to be done in this area”.

Spain was the first country in Europe to introduce paid “menstrual leave” in 2023, followed by Portugal, which has allowed up to three consecutive paid days off per month since 2025 for people experiencing disabling pain caused by diagnosed endometriosis or adenomyosis.

The Montenegrin measure applies to women suffering from serious conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace, and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

Todorovic Jovanovic said women in Serbia with menstrual health problems can already take ordinary sick leave, during which they receive 65 per cent of their salary. The problem, however, is that employers do not always respond well when employees request sick leave.

“On paper, the law allows workers to take sick leave simply by visiting a doctor, but there are employers and workplaces where taking leave is effectively impossible – whether to care for a child, because of illness, or due to menstrual health problems,” Todorovic Jovanovic said, adding that even if a similar law as Montenegro’s were adopted, the question of implementation in practice would remain.

For years there have been attempts in Serbia to address menstrual health issues as part of women’s general health, and put them up for discussion.

Last year, a Menstrual Justice Initiative was established in Serbia, bringing together researchers and several women’s organisations from across the country. The initiative was created to advocate for greater recognition of menstrual health and related rights.

The latest law changes in Montenegro have given Menstrual Justice Initiative fresh momentum.

“Women’s organisations actively monitor and listen to the communities they work with, and it is important to respond to that momentum. Legislative initiatives of this kind should originate from women’s organisations and be developed in cooperation with political actors who demonstrate a genuine willingness to support them,” Mirkailo said.

Both Todorovic Jovanovic and Mirkailo agreed that menstrual leave is not a “privilege” and that the question of menstrual leave is not only a question of health but of obtaining work-based rights for those who need them.

Todorovic Jovanovic, from Femin Collective, which is a member of the Menstrual Justice Initiative, explains that two main advocacy models are being pursued in the region. The first focuses on reducing VAT on menstrual products, while the second concerns the introduction of “menstrual leave”, as in Montenegro.

North Macedonia currently has the lowest VAT rate on menstrual products in the region, at 5 per cent, compared with 20 per cent in Serbia and 21 per cent in Montenegro.

“What we have been considering is initially directing our advocacy efforts towards reducing VAT, based on research conducted by the Gender Knowledge Hub, which reported in 2023 that women needed about 8,300 dinars (70 euros) a year to cover the cost of menstrual products,” Todorovic Jovanovic said.

She explained that this becomes particularly significant when it is considered how many women come from socially disadvantaged groups and cannot afford these essential products.

World.title: Live From Manhattan: Bosnia’s Republika Srpska and a Selective View of the Past
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

In late July, Denis Bojic, the director of the Republika Srpska Memorial Centre, told the Serbian daily newspaper Politika: “The politics of memory is a means of survival.”

Bojic was commenting on the Centre’s recent campaign in New York, in which billboards bearing photographs and accounts testifying to the ‘suffering’ of the Serb people travelled through Manhattan.

Bojic’s words offered perhaps the clearest explanation of the campaign’s political significance. If Republika Srpska, the predominantly Serb-populated entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were denied the right to tell the world about Serb suffering, he said, it would mean “the end of the existence of Republika Srpska”.

‘Learn About Serbian Suffering’ was presented in New York on July 10 and 11 by the Memorial Centre, a public institution established by the Republika Srpska government in 2024.

According to the organisers, the exhibition appeared at a number of prominent locations in the city, including near the headquarters of the United Nations. A QR code was displayed, directing interested passers-by to a digital collection of testimonies and archival material.

Even the timing of the exhibition was political.

World.title: Croatia–US Economic Relations: Tax Changes Open Doors for Diaspora Business
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Croatia-US economic relations have seen a new chapter in the (apparently very long) book penned, opening doors for diaspora business.

These new and upcoming tax changes will open doors for businesses operating between the two countries, as well as for the Croatian diaspora who might need another more concrete reason to seek citizenship.

For very many decades, the relationship between Croatia and the United States has been built on more than diplomacy. It has been shaped by migration, family ties, investment, and the millions of people of Croatian heritage who have made the United States their home. Now, a brand new step in that relationship could reshape how Croats and Americans do business, invest, and maintain connections across the pond.

the old double taxation hurdle…

A long-awaited agreement on avoiding double taxation between Croatia and the United States is finally moving closer to implementation, bringing the possibility of greater financial certainty for individuals and companies operating between the two countries. Until relatively recently, this all seemed to move at a glacial pace, with many in both Croatia and the diaspora forgetting about much movement at all on the issue.

For Croatian citizens living abroad, especially the large Croatian-American community, the changes represent more than a technical tax issue. They are part of a broader trend: Croatia is becoming increasingly connected economically, legally, and professionally with its diaspora. For a great many descendants of Croatian emigrants, that renewed connection may raise an important question about whether or not now be the right moment to formally reconnect with Croatia and gain citizenship.

croatia and america, a story of immigration, migration and struggle

Ancient Croatia and the very new United States have a relationship that extends far beyond modern state diplomacy that we see all countries at least attempting to engage in in the modern day. From the waves of Croatian migration that took place back during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, to the creation of strong Croatian communities across major US cities such as Chicago, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, and New York, generations of Croatian-Americans maintained cultural and family links with their ancestral homeland.

During Croatia’s struggle for independence in the 1990s, the diaspora played a significant role in raising awareness of Croatia’s position internationally. Since Croatia gained independence back during the 1990s, relations with the United States have expanded into security cooperation, tourism, technology, investment, and trade. Looking at the situation as it is today, this relationship is entering a new economic phase, one where easier movement of capital, business opportunities, and legal certainty are becoming increasingly crucial.

Why this Tax Agreement Matters (in more ways than one)

Obviously, the primary goal of the Croatia–US income tax agreement is to reduce uncertainty for people and companies that have financial ties to both countries. Currently, individuals and businesses operating across borders often face complicated questions about where exactly any income actually be taxed, and how this problematic double taxation can be avoided.

They’re the basic questions. It becomes more complex as you delve deeper, with questions about what rules apply when investing, opening a company, receiving dividends, or earning income abroad often becoming too much for many. Understandably so.

The agreement aims to provide clearer rules and reduce situations where the same income could potentially be taxed twice. It includes measures related to withholding taxes, information exchange, dispute resolution, and mechanisms designed to create a more predictable environment for cross-border activity. A protocol signed in 2026 further addressed outstanding issues and is intended to support the treaty’s progress toward US Senate consideration.

For businesses, this could mean greater confidence when investing between Croatia and the United States. For individuals, especially those with connections to both countries, it could simplify financial decisions and encourage closer economic links.

A New Opportunity for americans with croatian ancestors who might want croatian and eu passports

The Croatian diaspora has always been one of Croatia’s greatest assets. Indeed, there are now more ethnic Croats born and living outside of Croatia than there are living in it. Millions of people around the world have Croatian roots, but many have never formally explored their legal connection to Croatia. There are a wide array of reasons for that. For descendants of Croatian emigrants, being granted Croatian (and as such EU) citizenship can represent more than a passport. It can be a practical bridge to easier access to life, work, and property ownership in Croatia and the European Union, much stronger connections with family heritage, new business and investment possibilities and the ability to participate more directly and concretely in Croatia’s future.

For many Americans with Croatian ancestry, the gap between loving dida’s war stories or enjoying Dalmatian gregada was comfortable, but there wasn’t enough of an urge there to try to get a Croatian passport. America is a country filled with people who value economic success and the grind in a way few in Europe do. For many, pursuing citizenship would need an extra push wrapped in a more economic bow.

As Croatia becomes more economically integrated with countries such as the United States, citizenship can become increasingly valuable for those who want to maintain a meaningful connection with their ancestral homeland, all while seeking business opportunities without getting ravelled up and ultimately strangled in red tape. Many members of the diaspora already visit Croatia every year. Some invest in properties, start businesses, or consider spending more time in the country. Formal citizenship can be the next step in turning a cultural connection into a legal and practical one, all without the threat of Croatia’s infamous bureaucracy on steroids.

From Tourism to Investment: Croatia’s Changing Image Abroad

For decades, Croatia’s global reputation was primarily connected to tourism. It would be a lie to say that is no longer the case, but things are altering. Now, the country is increasingly positioning itself as a place for investment, entrepreneurship, technology, and international cooperation. A more predictable tax environment with the United States could encourage additional economic activity, particularly among Croatian-Americans who already understand both markets. The massive Croatian diaspora has a unique advantage: many already have knowledge of American business culture while maintaining personal ties to Croatia. That combination can create opportunities in areas ranging from technology and renewable energy to tourism, manufacturing, real estate, and services.

What Comes Next and what does this all really mean?

In practical terms, the implementation of the Croatia–US tax agreement will depend on completion of the necessary procedures in both countries. There are still a few hurdles to jump, but the direction is clear and the track is getting shorter. Croatia and the United States are moving toward a closer economic relationship, and the Croatian diaspora is positioned at the centre of that connection.

For descendants of Croatian emigrants who have always felt connected to Croatia but never explored citizenship, this may be a moment worth genuinely considering. As Croatia strengthens its global economic position, those with Croatian heritage are increasingly asking not only where their ancestors came from and exploring their origins for emotional reasons, but what concrete, economic and business opportunities their Croatian identity can provide today.

croatianbydescent – turning heritage into opportunity

Croatian by Descent has helped many Americans pursue their interest in gaining Croatian citizenship, as it goes without saying that few know where to even begin. For the vast majority of the Croatian diaspora, the connection to Croatia has always existed through family traditions, language, memories, and annual visits to the coast and islands. However, as Croatia’s role in the European and global economy continues to grow, more descendants of Croatian emigrants are exploring what it means to make that connection official.

Obtaining Croatian citizenship is increasingly viewed not only as a way to preserve family heritage, but also as an opportunity to strengthen personal and professional ties with Croatia and the European Union. For those who qualify, citizenship can open the door to greater mobility, easier long-term stays, investment opportunities, and a deeper relationship with the country their ancestors once called home.

Navigating the Croatian citizenship process, however, can involve complex documentation, historical records, and legal requirements, especially for descendants whose families left Croatia generations ago. The attitude you’re likely to receive as you attempt to do all this is also a bit of a culture shock for many Americans used to smiles and client-facing service. This, is, let’s say… not so common in Croatia!

It’s precisely why many choose to work with the likes of Croatian by Descent, who understand both Croatian regulations and the unique challenges faced by applicants living abroad. They have noted an uptick in those seeking their services and help as more and more of the diaspora look to Croatia as more than just sunshine and sea in their ancestral village each summer. As Croatia and the United States enter a new era of economic cooperation, reconnecting with Croatia through actual citizenship may become an increasingly valuable step for a new generation of Croatian-Americans looking to turn their heritage into a permanent, unbreakable connection cemented with (another), stronger blue passport.

World.title: Svetac: The Remote Island Where History and Nature Meet
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Svetac is a very remote Croatian island where abandoned history and wild, untamed nature come together in perfect harmony without any interference from humanity.

Hidden far out in the Adriatic Sea, just west of the far-flung island of Vis, the small island of Svetac is one of Croatia’s most isolated destinations. Also known as Sveti Andrija, the small offshore island is renowned for its dramatic cliffs, fascinating past, unique wildlife and complete and utter absence of permanent residents.

Located around 30 nautical miles from the mainland, Putni kofer writes that Svetac belongs to the Vis archipelago and lies just 2.5 kilometres from the volcanic islet of Brusnik. Throughout history it has been known by several names, including Sant’Andrea during Venetian rule and the local name Štondrija.

“a place for dreamers and madmen”

The island’s rugged coastline makes landing difficult. Towering cliffs surround much of the shore, leaving Slatina Bay on the southeastern side as the only practical place for boats to come ashore. Above the coast rises Kosa, the island’s highest peak at 316 metres, while strong sea currents and open waters add to its reputation as one of Croatia’s most challenging islands to reach. Croatian poet Tin Ujević famously described it as a place “for dreamers and madmen.”

Svetac also stands out for its climate. It is considered the warmest location in Croatia, with temperatures never falling below freezing. The island’s average annual temperature is around 17.4 degrees Celsius, comparable to Mediterranean locations such as Malta.

uninhabited since the year 2000…

Despite its isolation, Svetac has a long history of human settlement. Archaeological discoveries include ancient anchors, Roman remains and the ruins of a Byzantine fort. Benedictine monks lived on the island during the 15th and 16th centuries before ownership later passed to the Zanki family, who arrived from Italy’s Gargano Peninsula in the mid-18th century. The family originally settled there to harvest pine resin, leading many people to refer to Svetac as “the island of the Zankis.”

The island’s harsh environment has always made life difficult. There is no natural source of drinking water, strong winds frequently batter the coast and powerful southerly storms have claimed lives over the centuries. For generations, fishermen provided the islanders’ only connection to the outside world, sometimes becoming stranded themselves when rough seas prevented them from leaving. The final permanent resident died in January 2000, leaving the island uninhabited ever since.

wildlife and nature – svetac’s greatest treasures

Nature remains one of Svetac’s greatest treasures. Carob trees grow across the island, while it provides habitat for Eleonora’s falcon and Europe’s largest owl species. Mediterranean monk seals once frequented its shores, and the surrounding waters were historically rich in lobsters.

The island also carries a darker legend. Its pine forests were once heavily exploited for resin used in shipbuilding, while shepherds grazing church-owned sheep were said to have killed English shipwreck survivors. According to local tradition, this earned Svetac the nickname “Devil’s Island” among British sailors, reinforcing its reputation as a mysterious and forbidding place.

Today, although no one lives permanently on Svetac, its untouched landscapes, remarkable history and remote location continue to fascinate travellers looking to discover one of Croatia’s last truly wild islands.

World.title: Croatia Plans Taxi Fare Caps to End Excessive Charges
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Croatia is planning to finally deal with the taxi fare issue with caps and a hope to end excessive charges and frequent tourist rip-offs during summer.

Croatia is preparing to introduce a new set of rules for the taxi industry that will allow the government to cap fares, aiming to protect passengers from excessive prices while ensuring drivers can continue operating sustainably. Poslovni reports that the measures form part of amendments to the Road Transport Act, which have already been approved by Parliament and are expected to reshape the country’s taxi market.

Under the new legislation, the Minister of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure will be authorised to set maximum fares for all key components of a taxi ride, including the starting fare, per-kilometre rate, waiting time, and per-minute charges. The goal is to prevent extreme price spikes that have generated negative publicity, particularly in tourist destinations.

The reform follows several high-profile incidents in which passengers, including foreign tourists, were charged hundreds or even thousands of euros for relatively short journeys. Those cases prompted calls for stronger consumer protection and greater transparency across the industry.

The government says the new framework is intended to strike a balance between protecting customers and ensuring taxi drivers receive fair compensation. Officials have been working with representatives of the taxi sector, digital ride-hailing platforms and consumer groups to develop a pricing model that avoids both unreasonably low fares and excessive charges.

The legislation also introduces several additional changes designed to improve oversight of the sector. Every taxi vehicle will require its own operating permit, while specially designated TX licence plates will make licensed taxis easier to identify. Authorities are also strengthening checks on drivers and expanding enforcement powers to police, customs officers and municipal inspectors.

Digital ride-hailing platforms will face tighter regulation as well. They will be required to work only with properly licensed operators and maintain records that allow authorities to verify compliance with Croatian transport regulations.

The government believes the reforms will create a more transparent, competitive and reliable taxi market, improving confidence among both residents and the millions of visitors who use taxi services each year. The new rules are expected to take effect following the implementation of the amended Road Transport Act.

World.title: €20 Million Investment Aims to Transform Continental Croatian Tourism
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – A massive investment is aiming to totally transform continental Croatian tourism, with the majority of the focus on the overlooked Daruvar Spa.

Croatia has officially unveiled the fully renovated and expanded Daruvar Spa, a €20 million project that the government says marks a major step in strengthening the country’s continental tourism and positioning it as a leading European destination for health and wellness travel.

Poslovni reports that Prime Minister Andrej Plenković attended the opening ceremony, describing the project as one of 15 major investments designed to reshape Croatia’s tourism offer beyond the Adriatic coast. He noted that €13.2 million of the investment was financed through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), while the overall goal is to create a year-round tourism industry with high-quality facilities that attract visitors throughout all seasons, not just the summer months.

The renovation has transformed one of Croatia’s oldest spa resorts, whose history stretches back nearly 2,000 years, into a modern wellness and rehabilitation destination. The project included the complete reconstruction of 77 existing accommodation units and the construction of 13 new rooms at the Hotel Termal.

Guests can now enjoy newly renovated thermal pools featuring massage zones, an expanded sun deck, and a modern pool bar. The investment also introduced a new recreational and tourism centre with a multifunctional sports hall that will be used by both spa visitors and Croatian war veterans staying at the nearby Veterans’ Centre.

Among the new wellness facilities are beer baths, oak baths, salt rooms, cryotherapy chambers, and hyperbaric chambers. Spa director Ratko Vuković described the beer and oak baths as unique products that reflect Daruvar’s local identity and wellness tradition.

Local officials called the redevelopment a turning point for the region. Daruvar Mayor Damir Lneniček said it is the city’s largest investment in the past 45 years, adding that it will stimulate not only tourism but the broader local economy. Bjelovar-Bilogora County Prefect Marko Marušić said the upgraded spa has the potential to become the “locomotive” of Croatia’s health tourism sector by setting new standards in quality and visitor experience.

The project also focused on sustainability and digitalisation. Alongside modernising the facilities, the investment included a digital transformation of operations, the installation of photovoltaic power systems, and electric vehicle charging stations to improve energy efficiency and reduce environmental impact.

According to Plenković, the Daruvar project is part of a broader national strategy involving 15 spa and health tourism developments, with 10 located in continental Croatia and five along the coast. The wider programme is backed by a €356 million tourism investment package, of which €320 million comes from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan.

Other destinations included in the programme are Veli Lošinj, Stubičke Toplice, Lipik, Varaždinske Toplice, Topusko, Terme Bjelovar, Biograd na Moru, Makarska, Crikvenica, and the island of Korčula. The government says the investments are intended to diversify Croatia’s tourism offer, reduce seasonal dependence, and strengthen the country’s position in the growing European health and wellness tourism market.

Although continental Croatia currently accounts for less than five percent of the country’s total tourism traffic, officials believe projects such as the redevelopment of Daruvar Spa will help unlock its significant growth potential by attracting domestic and international visitors throughout the year while creating new economic opportunities for local communities.

World.title: Croatia Airlines Welcomes World’s First Airbus A220 in Star Alliance Livery
World.content:
July the 31st, 2026 – Croatia Airlines has welcomed the world’s very first Airbus A220 to wear the official Star Alliance livery, making it a unique edition to the global fleet.

As Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni, Croatia Airlines has received its tenth Airbus A220, marking another major milestone in the largest fleet renewal programme in the airline’s history. The new Airbus A220-300 is also the first aircraft of its type in the world to wear the official Star Alliance livery.

The aircraft, registered 9A-CAS and rather aptly named Velika Gorica, arrived in Zagreb directly from Airbus’ assembly facility in Mirabel, Canada. Configured with 149 passenger seats, it is the third of seven new Airbus A220s scheduled for delivery to Croatia Airlines during 2026.

Croatia Airlines President and CEO Jasmin Bajić described the arrival of the aircraft as another important step in the transformation of the national carrier and the implementation of its historic fleet renewal project.

He said the airline is especially proud that Velika Gorica is the world’s first Airbus A220 in Star Alliance colours, making it a visible symbol of Croatia Airlines’ long-standing membership in the world’s largest airline alliance. Bajić added that the new generation of A220 aircraft will serve as the backbone of the airline’s future development, allowing it to provide passengers with greater comfort and service quality while improving operational efficiency and sustainability, benefiting both Croatian tourism and the wider economy.

Renato Ramos, Vice President for Corporate Strategy at Star Alliance, said Croatia Airlines has been a valued member of the alliance for more than two decades, connecting hundreds of thousands of passengers each year to its global network.

He noted that the Star Alliance livery represents far more than branding, describing it as a symbol of cooperation, global connectivity, and the alliance’s commitment to making multi-airline journeys as seamless and enjoyable as possible. According to Ramos, the new aircraft reflects the strength and longevity of the partnership between Croatia Airlines and Star Alliance.

As part of the airline’s ongoing fleet renewal, Croatia Airlines has now received eight Airbus A220-300 aircraft, each with 149 seats, and two Airbus A220-100 aircraft, each configured with 127 seats.

The airline expects to receive four more Airbus A220-300s before the end of 2026. The complete fleet renewal programme is scheduled to conclude in 2027, when Croatia Airlines will operate 15 Airbus A220 aircraft, 13 A220-300s and two A220-100s.

World.title: How Can Sweden Have Cheaper Petrol Than Croatia With No Domestic Production?
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Sweden produces almost no domestic oil, yet drivers there usually have access to much cheaper petrol than Croatia. How is that possible? The answer is more complex than you might realise.

The answer to the question posed above is that fuel prices are not simply determined by whether a country has oil reserves. Slobodan Mufic explained for Index that the final price at the pump depends on a combination of factors, including taxes, government decisions, competition between fuel companies, transport costs and market conditions.

Sweden imports the oil that it needs, but it has an incredibly highly developed energy market and strong purchasing power. The country has also introduced policies that influence the cost structure of fuels and energy, meaning the absence of domestic oil production does not automatically lead to higher prices. Croatia, meanwhile, also relies heavily on imported oil, but fuel prices are shaped by different economic conditions. The Croatian government has repeatedly intervened in the fuel market by setting maximum retail prices and adjusting measures such as excise duties to protect consumers from price increases.

Another important factor is the difference in wages. A litre of petrol may cost a similar amount across Europe, but what matters for citizens is how much of their income goes towards filling up their cars.

The comparison between Sweden and Croatia shows that having domestic oil production is not the only factor that determines fuel prices. Countries without their own oil can still have cheaper petrol if their tax systems, markets and economic conditions create lower costs for drivers. So while Croatia and Sweden both depend on imported energy, the price drivers behind the pump are much more complicated than simply asking: “Who has oil?”

World.title: Croatia’s Greatest Strength is Outstanding English Skills Says Global Study
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Croatia’s greatest strength is the outstanding English skills of its population, according to a recently commissioned global outsourcing study.

Croatia’s strongest competitive advantage on the global outsourcing market is its exceptional command of the English language, according to the 2026 Global Talent Index for Outsourcing published by the U.S. consulting company Ataraxis. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that the study assessed 193 UN-recognised countries using five key criteria: labour costs, English proficiency, talent availability, digital infrastructure and political stability.

The report highlights Croatia as one of the emerging success stories in Europe’s outsourcing industry, which is worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually and is no longer dominated solely by traditional outsourcing hubs such as India and the Philippines. Eastern European countries are becoming increasingly competitive, with Croatia standing out as a “hidden gem” in the European market.

croatia’s english skills see it receive 100 out of 100

According to the study, Croatia is one of only two countries in Eastern Europe, alongside Romania, to achieve a perfect score of 100 out of 100 for English proficiency. This places Croatia alongside native English-speaking countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States and South Africa, giving it a significant advantage when competing for international business.

The report notes that strong English skills are only part of Croatia’s appeal. The country also scored 90 out of 100 for digital infrastructure and 84 out of 100 for labour costs, creating a balanced profile that is attractive to companies looking to outsource high-value work. Croatia is home to almost 70,000 technology professionals, providing a solid foundation for further growth in the sector.

500 new croatian ict companies are established yearly

The country’s technology industry is also expanding rapidly. According to HUP-ICT, around 500 new ICT companies are established in Croatia every year, making it one of the most dynamic parts of the national economy.

Croatia’s digital infrastructure also compares favourably with the rest of Europe. The country has 82.7% coverage of very high-capacity broadband networks, 77.9% fibre-to-the-premises coverage, and 97.8% 5G network coverage, placing it above the European average in several key categories. These factors strengthen Croatia’s position as an attractive destination for international companies seeking outsourcing partners.

The Ataraxis report concludes that Croatia’s combination of excellent English proficiency, competitive labour costs, strong digital infrastructure and a growing technology sector gives it a unique opportunity to attract more international outsourcing projects and strengthen its position in the global digital economy.

World.title: Taxi Fares Vary Across Croatia as New Rules Aim for Price Transparency
World.content:
July the 30th, 2026 – Taxi fares vary wildly across Croatia as new rules aim to further increase price transparency and end the practice of ripping off customers.

Poslovni reports that the cost of taking a taxi in Croatia differs significantly depending on the city, with some destinations charging more than double the starting fare of others. According to data from the international cost-of-living platform Numbeo, Pula is among the most expensive Croatian cities when it comes to the average price per kilometre, while Osijek remains the cheapest.

the highest starting fare isn’t in dubrovnik…

The data show that the highest starting fare is found in Rijeka and Šibenik, where the average base price is 5 euros. In Dubrovnik and Opatija, the average starting fare is 4 euros, while it is 3.32 euros in Split. Zagreb and Osijek actually have the lowest average starting fare at just 2 euros.

When it comes to the cost per kilometre, Pula, Dubrovnik and Zadar top the list at an average of 2 euros per kilometre. Split follows at 1.60 euros, while Rijeka, Opatija and Šibenik average 1.30 euros per kilometre. In the City of Zagreb, the average is 1.25 euros, and Osijek has the lowest average price at just 1 euro per kilometre.

The figures are based on user-submitted data collected by Numbeo and represent average prices. Actual fares may vary depending on the taxi company, time of day, traffic conditions and any additional charges applied during the journey.

the road transport act seeks to increase transparency

Meanwhile, the Croatian Parliament has adopted amendments to the Road Transport Act aimed at making taxi pricing more transparent. Under the new rules, passengers must be shown the maximum fare and the planned route before the journey begins. The legislation also allows a future regulation to set maximum permitted prices for the starting fare, price per kilometre and waiting time.

The changes are intended to improve consumer protection and reduce the risk of unexpectedly high taxi bills, particularly during the busy summer tourist season, while bringing greater transparency and consistency to Croatia’s taxi market.

World.title: Bear cub encounters near homes prompt safety warning from experts
World.content:
Bear cubs appearing close to human habitation are not cute cuddly toys, experts have warned, and it may only be a matter of time before such incidents end up with someone being harmed, Maaleht reported .

The cautions come following several incidents, including one filmed earlier this month which went viral and which showed three bear cubs strolling around the yard of a Harju County farmhouse in full view of people.

"The truth is that even a one-and-a-half-year-old bear has claws, fangs and considerable strength, enough to inflict very serious injuries on a person if necessary. An attack by a mother bear would most likely be fatal," said Ruttar Roht, a representative of the Ardu Hunting Society – a society member had put up the original bear cubs video, adding wild animals are always unpredictable.

"The truth is that even a one-and-a-half-year-old bear has claws and fangs and quite a lot of strength, which, if necessary, can cause quite serious injuries to a person. An attack by a female bear would most likely end fatally for a person," Roht went on.

Marko Vinn, advisor to the national hunting society, said while encounters with bears in Estonia have so far ended happily for all involved, with large predators increasingly venturing into human settlements, sooner or later that happy situation may change.

How the three cubs came to be separated from their mother is unknown, with speculation including she had come to harm, had temporarily abandoned her cubs for their safety, or they had escaped from her – Vinn said this could happen if an adult male had attempted to kill the cubs in order to mate with the mother with a view to producing his own cubs, a not unheard-of scenario with bears in the wild.

While the cubs in the video are too young to viably survive without their mother over the long term, this does not mean feeding them and giving them water is an option – the animals might then become reliant on human aid, which is also unnecessary given the abundance of freshwater bodies, small and large, in Estonia.

Estonians, Vinn noted, have lost their rural roots and have become so urbanized that they have lost a clear picture of nature red in tooth and claw, tending to see the animals more as cute cuddly toys.

Roht and Vinn disagreed on the rise in bear numbers being down to clear-cutting of forests – clearing away trees wholesale – with Roht saying if anything the practice provides more opportunities for them to hunt, and so does not drive them out of the forest as has been claimed; it is simply the numbers, around 1,100 and counting, which have led to more bears, often weaker individuals, ending up nearer to human habitation than before, he said.

As omnivores, bears will happily feed on berries and fruit found in bogland and open areas, and even on agricultural produce.

The viral video shared by the Estonian Hunters' Society on July 23 showed cubs later confirmed to have returned to the forest, though one is thought to have later raided a chicken coop in Paide, prompting the Rescue Board and the Environmental Agency to relocate it.

Over the past 20 years, the bear population has almost doubled, indicating a very favorable conservation status, Maaleht reported, adding the low point in the thousands of years they have been resident in the area – since the end of the last ice age, in fact – came in the 1920s, when only around 30 animals were living in the country, and even in the 1950s the figure was below 100.

Hunters' lobby groups have been calling for an expansion to the annual bear cull, claiming numbers are now too high.

Worldwide, brown bears (Ursus arctos) number around 200,000, with an estimated 130,000 of these being in the Russian Federation. Grizzly bears are a subspecies of the brown bear.

If you see bear cubs apparently separated from their mother, you should call the national information hotline on 1247.

The Estonian Hunters' Society advises staying calm, never feeding bears, making noise while walking in forests, and avoiding bear cubs, carcasses and roaming alone. If a bear is seen near homes as in the recent events, scare it away with loud noise rather than approaching or photographing it. Keep dogs leashed, back away slowly if threatened, never run or climb a tree, and if attacked by a brown bear, lie on the ground, protect your head and neck, and play dead.

World.title: Finland to work with Estonia to stop migrants, interior minister says
World.content:
Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said the Finnish authorities will assist their Estonian counterparts in stopping illegal immigrants who are trying to reach the Nordics after crossing the Belarusian-Latvian border.

Over the past two weeks, over 80 migrants have been detained in Estonia, most likely after entering the European Union illegally via the Belarusian-Latvian border, as part of what authorities say is a hybrid attack orchestrated by the Minsk regime. This is a significant increase, as the total number stands at 128 detained so far this year.

The migrants have been caught in hotels, Tallinn city center, and around the port. The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) said they are mostly trying to reach Finland, as routes to Germany have become more difficult due to checks on the Polish borders.

Taro said the Estonian and Finnish authorities have reached an agreement that the Finns will come to help Estonia at ports and airports.

"Then we have a few more eyes and pairs of hands at transport hubs, and we free up a little resources to deal with hotels and accommodation facilities. Since people have been caught in shopping centres here, our Police and Border Guard Board personnel can deal with them more outside ports and airports as well," he told the "Uudis+" on Friday.

Minister of the Interior Igor Taro. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

He said the Finnish forces can arrive in a matter of hours.

"We need this kind of additional force. We discussed all kinds of possibilities for carrying out some kind of joint operation so that illegal immigrants would not be able to continue onwards through Finland. It would be a very bad message if they managed to get to Finland – it would mean that it is possible to go through Estonia," Taro said.

The minister added that Estonia wants to send a clear message.

"It is very important that we can catch everyone and that they do not move onwards from Estonia, so that nobody gets the impression that Estonia is a suitable transit corridor through which one can get to wherever they want to go. These are not simply migrants; things must be called by their proper names here – these are illegal immigrants. They are trying to get to Europe illegally and they have no right to do so," he stressed.

Migrants sent back to Latvia

The migrants detained in Estonia will be returned to Latvia, following EU rules, Taro said. New rotations of border guards will also be sent to assist their Latvian counterparts on the Belarus border for the next two months.

"First, we are going to help on Latvia's external border. Second, Latvia itself has been very reasonable in its approach throughout this situation, and everyone whom we have detained and who has apparently come from that direction will indeed be sent back through Latvia," Taro said.

"For our detention centres not to become overcrowded and for us not to deal with lengthy procedures here in Estonia, it is in fact very important to send all these people back," the minister added.

The Latvian-Belarusian border. Source: Latvian Border Guard.

The identification of the migrants and their country of origin will be carried out in Estonia, while further procedures take place in Latvia. The minister said there is no point in Estonia duplicating a system that already exists in Latvia.

He added that there is no reason why illegal immigrants should be allowed to remain in the European Union.

"If a person has crossed the border illegally and has also come from a safe country, I do not see any argument that we or Latvia should offer them international protection. They have not come directly from a war zone, but have travelled through safe countries," Taro said.

As of Thursday, Estonian authorities had caught five smugglers. The minister added that this number will increase.

Tense months ahead

Yesterday, more than a dozen migrants staying at a short-term rental property in the Nõmme suburb of Tallinn were detained by the PPA. The interior ministers said smugglers use both cheaper hotels and private accommodation.

"I would urge people to keep an eye on what is happening in these accommodation places. These latest detentions have all happened thanks to attentive citizens who have reported that something is wrong," Taro said.

The minister stressed that those placing the orders and those who later use the accommodation may not be the same people.

Police operation on Tallinn's Nõmme district on Thursday. Source: Private collection

"They have smugglers or helpers of illegal migrants who can arrange certain things. They book accommodation for them and afterwards completely different people come in, so it is worth keeping an eye on things," Taro said.

He called on Estonian residents to be vigilant.

"I have repeatedly said that if Estonian residents see some strange group of foreigners who look lost and do not know exactly where they are going. They are clearly not cruise tourists, then such people should definitely be reported," he said.

"I cannot be ruled out that more will be caught somewhere again. I predict that perhaps for up to a couple of months we may have a very tense and difficult period," Taro said "Uudis+".

World.title: Kuressaare begins chlorinating water after E. coli found in routine tests
World.content:
Kuressaare Water Utility has begun chlorinating the city's water supply after routine drinking‑water tests showed, based on preliminary lab results, E. coli and other coliform bacteria at the ends of local pipelines.

Saarte Hääl reported that the samples were taken on 30 July and that, according to Kuressaare Water Utility, the information is preliminary and the official analysis protocol has not yet been issued.

The utility recommends that residents in the Upa area boil drinking water as an additional precaution before use.

According to the company, a coli‑like bacterium is an indicator that may appear at pipeline ends during warm weather and stagnant water, and its presence mainly signals the need to flush the system.

More attention is required for the E. coli bacterium found at the end of the Upa pipeline, which has not been detected in Kuressaare's water over the past three years. The utility says that a single E. coli finding does not in itself mean the city's drinking water is widely contaminated, but it does require immediate action.

World.title: Tech firm Nebius hiring push fuels speculation over Estonia data center plans
World.content:
The international technology company Nebius, which develops artificial intelligence infrastructure, is recruiting employees in Tallinn, but the company's exact plans in Estonia are not known.

Nebius, an international technology company born from the restructuring of the Russian tech giant Yandex and headquartered in Amsterdam, is hiring in Estonia. The company is offering positions for a data centre IT manager, IT technician, IT support unit manager, IT infrastructure engineer and senior IT technician, and is also looking for a warehouse and logistics specialist.

Both Estonia's largest data centre Greenergy Data Centers and Sunly, which is building a data centre in Läänemaa, believe that if one major international client can be attracted to Estonia, others will gradually follow.

Since it became known this week that Greenergy Data Centers in Hüüru is building additional IT capacity to install artificial intelligence computing power and expand its client base beyond Estonia, journalists asked Greenergy whether they had struck a deal with Nebius.

Greenergy andmekeskus Hüürus. Autor/allikas: Tõnu Tunnel/Greenergy

Greenergy Data Centers' large‑client segment manager Martin Rungi did not wish to comment on the assumption, but noted that Greenergy has so far built out only a small part of its resource and that there is still a long way to go to reach the full potential of up to 300 megawatts.

"We are targeting all the names you hear in the public information space – Amazon, Microsoft, Google, they are all welcome clients. But who and when and in what volume will move here, that will be clear when the time is right. I cannot answer this question otherwise, but our ambition is to serve everyone operating in this field," Rungi said.

He added that the international market is highly supply‑constrained and Estonia has resources to offer. However, concrete agreements in this business are often not discussed publicly.

"A lot of things in our business are confidential until the parties themselves disclose them," Rungi said. "Since most clients are listed companies, they have their own rules for disclosure, and we cannot say anything until they are able to comment."

Nebius also did not provide clarification on its plans in Estonia.

Some data centre clients in Estonia will remain unknown to the public. For critical infrastructure, clients aim to keep the location of their data strictly hidden. Rungi said Greenergy is negotiating with many clients simultaneously and work is very active.

"There are always all kinds of speculations," Rungi said, adding that in this industry it is normal that information is disclosed only when a major client announces something.

Sunly kavandab Eestisse Baltimaade suurimat andmekeskust. Autor/allikas: Sunly

Sunly also actively seeks major clients

Commenting on Nebius hiring in Estonia, Rungi said that there are several development projects in Estonia, including Greenergy, Sunly and Evecon. "There is more than one bride at this wedding," he added.

Sunly, a renewable energy company planning to build the largest data centre in the Baltics in Läänemaa, did not wish to speculate on whether Nebius might target Greenergy's Hüüru data centre as a location.

Sunly's energy centre development manager Kaarel Aus said the sector is developing rapidly. He said Sunly is also actively negotiating with potential partners.

"The need for new data centres among major technology companies is large. A few years ago, Scandinavia and Finland were not preferred destinations for data centres. Since Western and Central European electricity grids have no short‑term capacity left for new data centres, attention has shifted to Scandinavia and Finland. Now those grids are also filling up, and data centres are looking for new locations," Aus explained.

According to Rungi, the moment when Greenergy can announce the addition of a major client may come very soon, but it may also take time.

"Sometimes where there is smoke, there is no fire, but sometimes there is," he said, adding that more than one good piece of news is coming. "Our industry is such that first we lay the egg and then we cackle."

Nebius' origins are linked to Yandex

Nebius may raise questions due to its connection to the Russian technology company Yandex, as Nebius emerged after Yandex came under sanctions following Russia's full‑scale invasion of Ukraine.

In 2024, the company sold its Russian business units and adopted the name Nebius Group, headquartered in the Netherlands. Nebius CEO Arkady Volozh is one of Yandex's founders, but he has since renounced Russian citizenship.

Rungi said Nebius is being labelled with things that are not true and that it is likely the most thoroughly scrutinised organisation in the entire chain.

"Because they were once connected to Russia, their burden is so heavy that it is even harder to gain trust. Yet they have earned trust from Meta, Microsoft, the US government, Nvidia and the New York Stock Exchange," he said. "I do not understand why this labelling continues."

Shared data hall equipment racks. Source: Tõnu Tunnel/Greenergy

Greenergy has operated for ten years, the first five spent on preparation, and has since offered services to the Estonian market while also investing in international expansion. A concern is Estonia's proximity to Russia, which causes hesitation among many potential foreign clients.

"At the same time, Finland has gained clients from this world and is also a neighbour of Russia (Nebius will build one of Europe's largest AI data centres in Finland by 2028). It is also about reputation, reliability, being known and trusted," Rungi said, adding that Greenergy has held hundreds of client meetings and practically all technology companies targeted by market players have visited them.

Aus said geopolitics is always part of negotiations with potential partners, but Estonia's membership in NATO and the European Union reduces risks for foreign partners.

Data centers could make a strong contribution to Estonia's GDP

If one major international client can be attracted to Estonia, finding additional clients will become much easier, Rungi said.

"This is a gravity business. If one comes, others follow. That is how it goes internationally; I have seen this pattern in many new markets. First come some crazy guys like us with an ambitious plan to do something that supposedly can never happen. Until the first breakthrough comes and the market develops," he said.

Aus agreed: once one major player establishes itself in the Baltics, validating the region as a data centre location, others will start looking more seriously, as has happened in Scandinavia and Finland.

"If we delay too long, until Western Europe's electricity grids catch up with demand, we will lose the opportunity to attract data centres here," Aus said.

Success, however, is hard‑won. Rungi said other countries offer tax incentives for such businesses, but Estonia does not, and there is no support from the export promotion system. He said established players are supported, but new ones do not qualify even when their ambitions are large and they have invested significant capital.

Data centres could bring substantial benefits to the state as a new economic sector. Rungi said that if Estonia's full potential were used, consuming local electricity and adding value through expertise, it would mean billions of euros annually in additional revenue for electricity companies and rental income for data centres, contributing a significant share to Estonia's GDP. The prerequisite is public acceptance.

Rungi said AI tends to be demonised, and although there are contexts where criticism is justified, accusations that data centres are to blame for energy consumption are unfair. He stressed that they do not consume energy for nothing – demand arises when people pay with a bank card or watch a film on Netflix.

"Just as a landfill is not to blame for the creation of waste, but people are, the same applies in the digital information space," he said. "We have a long way to go to make this clear."

He added that high water consumption in data centres is true in hot climates, but at Estonia's latitude, cooling is needed only for a small number of hours per year, which is a competitive advantage.

"The climate allows for much more efficient business, and in the end that means money," Rungi said.

Aus noted that Estonia currently has practically no energy‑intensive industry. For example, electricity consumption per capita in Norway is nearly four times higher than in Estonia, and in Sweden and Finland it is twice as high.

World.title: Estonian FA boss on FIFA privatization plan: The sport should be for football people
World.content:
Pohlak and EJL secretary general Mihkel Uiboleht took part in a UEFA online meeting held on an extraordinary basis on Thursday afternoon to form a common position on FIFA's plans.

"For Europe's football associations, FIFA's plan raises three main concerns. First, governance – decision-making in football can only be in the hands of football people. Second, the process – not a single association, confederation or other stakeholder was involved in developing the plan. Third, money – there is no need to involve private investors to provide additional support to members, thereby opening the door to money flowing out of football. FIFA has already earned this money by organizing various competitions and will continue to do so in the future. At today's meeting, we fully supported what was set out in UEFA's joint statement," Pohlak said after the meeting.

In the official statement issued after the meeting, UEFA unequivocally rejected FIFA's proposal to allow private investors to acquire stakes in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions.

An official statement followed, in which FIFA said the World Cup "is not for sale."

Statement on behalf of UEFA and its 55 National Associations — UEFA (@UEFA) July 30, 2026

"UEFA and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA's proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors," the statement read.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams, and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale," the statement went on.

FIFA says it will continue consulting member associations on its proposal to sell up to a 20 percent stake in a new company that would manage the World Cup and other major tournaments. UEFA has threatened to boycott FIFA competitions over the plan, arguing it risks the future of football, while other confederations have also raised concerns. FIFA insists no decision will be made without member approval and denies it is "selling football."

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino says the process will represent the "democratization" of football. Many of the private investors are reportedly connected to associates of US President Donald Trump, whose close relationship with Infantino was extensively reported on during the recent World Cup in North America.

World.title: EDF intel: Shipping from Ukraine's ports halted after Russian attacks
World.content:
Shipping from Ukraine's ports in the Odesa region has come to a "complete halt" after Russian attacks, as owners are not willing to let their vessels enter ports, the Estonian Defense Forces Intelligence Center has said.

The main developments of the war this week have been the worsening of relations between Ukraine and Iran after a Ukrainian drone hit an Iranian cargo ship, as well as intense mutual medium- and long-range precision strikes between Ukraine and Russia, the Estonian Defense Forces Intelligence Center said in its weekly overview.

Worsening relations between Ukraine and Iran

The intelligence Center said a noteworthy development was Iran's statement following a Ukrainian drone attack on an Iranian merchant vessel in the Caspian Sea.

While tensions were reduced during a phone call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, he still said that Ukraine must compensate for the damage caused by the attack.

During the war, Iran has supplied Russia with drone technology, missiles, ammunition and other equipment, and together with Russia, North Korea and China is among the countries that are highly interested in dismantling the current world order, the Intelligence Center said.

"Iran's missile arsenal makes it capable of attacking Ukraine," it emphasized.

Ukraine ports at a standstill after Russian strikes

The agency also highlighted Russia's attacks on Ukraine's ports in the Odesa region, which have brought shipping to a "complete halt" since July 22. Ukraine has raised the situation at a meeting of the UN Security Council.

"The situation is serious because Ukraine exports 90 percent of its agricultural products through Black Sea ports. Officially, shipping has not been suspended, but many shipowners do not allow their vessels to enter Ukrainian ports," the intelligence agency's statement said.

"As ships are not transporting grain out of the ports, Ukraine has also restricted the movement of grain-loaded trains to Odesa. To offset the disruption of maritime transport, Ukraine is implementing measures to export agricultural products by rail, but its lower capacity does not fully compensate for the halt in maritime transport."

Fuel shortages reach Russia's front line

The overview also touched on Ukraine's long-range strikes on the Wildberries warehouses and fuel infrastructure across Russia, as well as the Avitek military plant in the Kirov region.

"According to various estimates, Ukraine's attacks on Russia's fuel industry have reduced Russia's oil refining capacity by 20–40 percent, and reports have also emerged publicly of fuel shortages in Russian Armed Forces units fighting in Ukraine," the intellegence center said.

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy has presented plans to further increase the range of long-range strikes and to attack targets that have so far remained beyond reach but are important for Russia's continuation of the war against Ukraine, it added

World.title: Narva‑Jõesuu begins demolition of local ghost town
World.content:
In Ida‑Viru County, demolition has begun on the derelict apartment blocks of Viivikonna village, Estonia's best‑known ghost town. Narva‑Jõesuu plans to turn the abandoned mining settlement into a district of neat residential homes. Tourism operators, however, hope at least some of the old buildings will be preserved.

Just a few years ago, Viivikonna attracted tourists, musicians and filmmakers who used the empty buildings as shooting locations. Today, most houses along the main street have already disappeared.

Viivikonna was transferred to Narva-Jõesuu from Kohtla‑Järve during the administrative reform. Narva‑Jõesuu began tearing down the derelict blocks with the aim of transforming the area into a respectable neighbourhood of private homes.

"The next stage is cleaning up the plots, dividing them and selling them. The area has entirely new potential," said Narva‑Jõesuu Mayor Maksim Iljin.

Maksim Iljin. Autor/allikas: ERR

Tourism operators in Ida‑Virumaa are divided. Some say the region still has plenty of Soviet‑era heritage; others see the destruction of Ida‑Viru's uniqueness.

"We're losing the distinctive, sometimes extreme sights that define Ida‑Virumaa. What's happening now is simply erasing a chapter of history. Soon we'll have only empty lots that quickly become overgrown," said Marko Kaldur, guide at avastaEesti.ee.

Kaldur noted that a film studio complex is currently being built in Ida‑Virumaa, but by the time it is ready, potential filming locations may already be gone.

The mayor acknowledges receiving requests from tourism operators and filmmakers to preserve Viivikonna's ghost buildings, but none are willing to take responsibility for safety and maintenance.

"Of course, for us it's a constant headache, and honestly — from the beginning we saw no real future for these apartment blocks. In my view, demolition is the most sensible option," Iljin said.

Narva‑Jõesuu estimates that clearing Viivikonna of derelict buildings will cost around €1 million, most of which will be covered by state support.

World.title: Turnover volume of grocery stores up in June after long decline
World.content:
Retail sales turnover rose to €950 million in June – an increase of 1 percent on year – bucking a more than two-year negative trend, data from Statistics Estonia shows.

Johanna Linda Pihlak, a leading analyst at Statistics Estonia, pointed out that the turnover volume of retail trade enterprises, which had declined in May, began to grow again in June.

The increase in turnover volume in June was driven by grocery stores, which saw turnover volume grow after more than two years of decline.

"The last time the turnover volume of grocery stores grew was in March 2024," she said.

Turnover volume index. Source: Statistics Estonia

The turnover volume of both enterprises engaged in the retail sale of automotive fuel and stores selling manufactured goods remained at the level of June 2025.

"In the case of enterprises engaged in the retail sale of automotive fuel, it is worth noting that the data covers not only the sale of motor fuels but reflects total sales, including income from food service and provision of other goods and services," the analyst added.

Compared with May, the turnover volume of retail trade enterprises increased by 2 percent in June. According to seasonally and working-day adjusted data, turnover volume was up by one percent compared to the previous month.

In the first half of this year, the retail trade turnover increased by three percent compared with the same period of the previous year.
