World.title: Iraq denies launching strikes from its territory against neighboring nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The military spokesperson for the Iraqi commander-in-chief, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed on Thursday that neither a foreign nor local body has presented proof that recent regional drone attacks were launched from Iraqi territory.

In a statement to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), al-Numan urged accusing parties to submit reliable proof, saying that Baghdad has yet to receive such data.

The development comes following statements made by the Saudi Ministry of Defense, alleging that drone attacks targeting key oil infrastructure in the past few days originated in Iraq.

The Iraqi official indicated that the government will neither tolerate unilateral military acts from within its borders nor accept foreign violations of its territorial sovereignty.

Al-Numan’s remarks come a day after the United States and Saudi Arabia launched coordinated airstrikes targeting several bases of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing and injuring many fighters.

The joint operation targeted several logistical and weapons storage locations in different provinces in Iraq, escalating the current regional battle.

The PMF described the joint US-Saudi strike as a dangerous escalation and a clear breach of Iraqi sovereignty.

World.title: Iraqi oil flows to continue via Turkey’s Ceyhan as renewal deal is discussed
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish sources told Reuters that crude oil shipments from northern Iraq to the Turkish port of Ceyhan will continue while the two countries seek an arrangement to extend the pipeline’s operation for another 12 months.

On July 27, a bilateral agreement that had been in place for decades ended. Despite expectations, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi did not sign a 12-month renewal deal during his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Tuesday.

According to a Turkish official, oil flows via the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, which is Baghdad’s only operational export pipeline, will continue while negotiations for a renewal deal are still in progress.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar recently announced a 12-month extension agreement between the two countries.

During a joint press conference in Ankara, Erdogan stated on Tuesday that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible.

An extension is intended to provide additional time for discussions on a complete accord. Turkey aims to fully utilize the 1.5 million barrels per day pipeline and consider expanding it to oil fields in southern Iraq.

Turkish data suggests that the pipeline currently transports approximately 170,000 barrels per day.

World.title: Turkey seeks comprehensive energy cooperation deal with Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stated that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement with Iraq following discussions with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Ankara.

Erdogan said that Turkey’s state-owned oil and gas company, TPAO, will operate at Iraq’s Kirkuk oilfield, which is now being developed by British Petroleum (BP), during a joint press conference following a signing ceremony that had been expected to extend the Kirkuk-Ceyhan oil pipeline deal for another year, according to Reuters.

The agreement to renew the decades-old pipeline contract, which regulates shipments along the strategic route, expired on Monday.

After signing three agreements, Erdogan noted that additional deals were anticipated. However, his ministers promptly briefed him on stage, and the two leaders continued with their statements without announcing any further agreements.

The agreement between Iraq and Turkey regarding the crude oil pipeline expired on July 27.

“Our goal is to complete an energy cooperation deal that benefits both parties as quickly as possible,” Erdogan said.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said in a statement on X that TPAO has bought a 15 percent stake in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk Limited (BPECKL), enabling the Turkish business to operate in the sector.

Bayraktar explained the TPAO will cooperate with BPECKL to raise oil production at the Kirkuk field, which has reserves estimated at three million barrels.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports to India fall as New Delhi diversifies import sources
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi oil exports to India fell in the first half of 2026, as Indian refineries diversified their crude import sources to minimize the geopolitical risks associated with shipping via the Straits of Hormuz.

According to officials at Indian refining companies and the Indian Ministry of Petroleum, the goal of this measure is to improve supply security.

The drop in Iraqi supplies to India comes at a time when the global oil market is under increased pressure due to security worries along critical maritime routes. This pressure is causing consumers in Asia to split their purchases among many producing countries.

Iraqi oil remains a vital resource for India due to supply security and the high quality of Basra crude.

Indian refiners confirmed they have secured their crude oil requirements until the end of September and have begun arranging purchases for the fourth quarter of the year, despite persistent concerns about the impact of any interruptions to shipping routes on global supply chains.

Meanwhile, Russia remained India’s top crude oil supplier in the first half of the year, while imports from the UAE and Brazil increased.

India’s purchases from Iraq and the United States fell as New Delhi attempted to diversify its supply sources and reduce the risks associated with reliance on a single source.

Indian refiners have warned that increased shipping risks and higher insurance costs, along with declining discounts on Russian oil, are affecting profit margins.

Experts anticipate that continuing instability in the Middle East will raise oil prices and pose new hurdles for Asian oil-importing countries.

World.title: Six Iranian advisors killed in US-Saudi attack on Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A joint US-Saudi attack on targets in Iraq killed six Iranian advisors on Wednesday, according to two Iraqi officials who spoke to the Associated Press (AP).

A meeting that was set for Thursday in Saudi Arabia between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was called off due to recent attacks by armed groups targeting Saudi Arabia.

Al-Zaidi ordered an emergency meeting of Iraq’s National Security Council following the coordinated attacks on the country.

The Iraqi Security Media Cell said in a statement that the meeting was ordered in response to the evolving security situation and the airstrikes that targeted several Iraqi provinces early on Wednesday.

The US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Wednesday that US forces, in cooperation with Saudi armed forces, carried out precision airstrikes targeting sites linked to Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

The coordinated airstrikes were in retaliation for a series of drone attacks targeting US interests and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

CENTCOM said in a statement that the strikes, carried out on July 28, targeted logistics sites and weapons depots allegedly used by Iranian-backed groups. It added that these groups were directed by the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to attack US forces and Saudi oil facilities.

US and Saudi fighter jets carried out the strikes, an operation described by CENTCOM as a strong response to more than 30 drone attacks that the IRGC had conducted in the past few days.

Headquarters and sites belonging to the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in several Iraqi provinces were targeted by the US-Saudi airstrikes in the country.

World.title: US-Saudi strikes test Iraq’s fragile security balance
World.content:
Baghdad – US-Saudi strikes on Iraq killed at least 20 militants, including several Iranians, on Wednesday, according to the Hashed al-Shaabi, an armed Iraqi alliance that includes pro-Iran groups.

The United States and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed armed militants in Iraq in response to attacks on US forces and Saudi oil facilities.

Washington and Tehran are Iraq’s main allies, but their enmity has long turned the country into a proxy battleground and left successive governments struggling to maintain a delicate balance between the foes.

The Hashed al-Shaabi, also known as the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), said that at least 20 fighters “were martyred and another 32 wounded according to a preliminary toll”.

Two Hashed officials told AFP that five Iranian advisors were among those killed in a strike in the central province of Diyala.

AFP correspondents saw coffins wrapped in Iranian flags during a funeral organised by the Hashed al-Shaabi in Baghdad for those killed.

The Hashed alliance was created in 2014 to fight jihadists before it was formally integrated into the Iraqi armed forces.

It now includes brigades belonging to Iran-backed groups reputed for acting unilaterally.

US President Donald Trump said the strikes were coordinated with the Iraqi government, according to Fox News.

They follow growing US pressure on Baghdad to disarm pro-Iran armed groups, which have frequently targeted US facilities in the country and have long called for the withdrawal of US troops.

Iraq’s new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who came to power this year with Washington’s blessing, vowed to ensure those groups would hand over their weapons, but has faced pushback from some powerful factions.

Earlier this month, Zaidi visited both the United States and Iran.

– ‘Inevitable response’ –

The strikes came after Riyadh said its forces had intercepted drones targeting oil facilities, blaming the Iran-backed groups in Iraq.

The most active pro-Iran armed groups are united under an alliance known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, which has acted in support of Tehran during the Middle East war, claiming hundreds of attacks against US bases in Iraq and across the region.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq said “our response to the American enemy is inevitable, and may target its tools in Saudi Arabia”.

But the group added that it would only retaliate after the Arbaeen day of pilgrimage, which falls on Tuesday.

The Arbaeen marks one of the most significant events in the Shia Muslim calendar, during which pilgrims, many from Iran, flock to Iraq to visit the holy shrines.

The pro-Iran groups denied attacking Saudi Arabia and they haven’t claimed any attacks since the US-Iran war resumed earlier this month.

– Violation –

Iraq denounced the US-Saudi strikes and said it rejects “all acts of aggression, regardless of the party responsible or the justifications presented.”

The Ministerial Council for National Security said it would “confront any violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, and prevent any source from using Iraqi territory to threaten neighbouring states”.

It reaffirmed its commitment to ensure the state’s monopoly over weapons.

Zaidi’s government has given those groups that Washington designates as terrorist organisations until September 30 to disarm.

Oil-rich Iraq has been trying to move past decades of war and unrest, but it remains vulnerable to regional and internal flare-ups.

World.title: Iraq condemns US-Saudi strikes, vows tighter control over armed groups
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq condemned U.S.-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday that targeted Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) sites, calling the attacks a violation of its sovereignty, and announced new measures to tighten state control over security and prevent Iraqi territory from being used to threaten neighboring countries.

Following the attacks, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over an emergency meeting of the Ministerial Council for National Security, which the government said killed and injured many Iraqis.

As regional tensions rose, Al-Zaidi cancelled a planned visit to Saudi Arabia on Thursday.

In a statement published after the meeting, the council said that the strikes happened when Baghdad was already in talks with US and Saudi authorities over suspicions that Iran-aligned armed organizations operating from Iraq committed drone assaults on Saudi land.

“The government was actively engaging with the relevant parties to verify and address the concerns raised by both the Saudi and US sides,” the statement stated, adding that the military action hampered such efforts.

The council authorized a comprehensive security strategy aimed at strengthening state authority across Iraq, combating breaches of Iraqi sovereignty, and prohibiting any party from exploiting Iraqi territory to threaten neighboring nations.

The steps reflect Baghdad’s efforts to guarantee that no armed organization may launch assaults from Iraqi soil that could pull the nation into larger regional wars, while also confirming the government’s goal of bringing all security actions under state control.

The council also directed the Foreign Ministry to take legal and diplomatic measures under international law and the United Nations Charter to record the attacks and protect Iraq’s legal rights.

The government condemned the attacks but emphasized that responding to security threats and enforcing the law is solely the responsibility of Iraq’s constitutional institutions.

“The government rejects all acts of aggression, regardless of the party responsible or the justifications presented,” the statement read.

The council underlined Baghdad’s commitment to addressing regional conflicts via diplomacy while maintaining efforts to keep all armaments under state control.

It also restated Iraq’s commitment to carrying out the security agreement guiding the departure of the US-led international coalition by the end of September 2026.

The emergency conference occurred hours after US President Donald Trump claimed that the midnight attacks were coordinated with the Iraqi government, something Baghdad has not officially verified.

Iraqi authorities have openly opposed the operation, emphasizing the political sensitivity of the attacks.

The events highlight Al-Zaidi’s increasingly precarious situation, as he seeks to boost Iraq’s connections with the US and Gulf Arab governments while retaining relations with Iran.

His decision to cancel the Saudi visit underlines the gravity of the problem, as Baghdad seeks to temper regional tensions while preventing Iraqi land from becoming a battlefield for opposing forces.

The government’s current security strategy also suggests a renewed desire to prevent armed groups from operating outside official control, as Baghdad wants to reassure neighboring nations that Iraq will not be used as a springboard for assaults that endanger regional peace.

World.title: Uptime Institute partners with T964 to expand Iraq’s digital infrastructure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Uptime Institute, based in the United States, and Iraqi digital infrastructure company Tech964 Holding Limited (T964) have formed a strategic partnership to help develop Iraq’s digital infrastructure, marking the latest technology agreement to result from Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s investment-focused visit to Washington.

The agreement, signed earlier this month at the U.S.-Iraq Business Summit hosted by the US Chamber of Commerce, names T964 as Uptime Institute’s business partner in Iraq to promote international data center standards, professional training, and the development of resilient digital infrastructure.

The agreement is part of Baghdad’s larger effort to diversify its economy beyond oil by increasing digital infrastructure, attracting technological investment, and bolstering industries including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, financial technology, and cybersecurity.

T964, one of Iraq’s major private digital infrastructure businesses, has announced that it would collaborate with the Uptime Institute to implement internationally recognized standards for the country’s expanding network of data centers, as well as increase technical competence and operational best practices.

The partnership is anticipated to help establish carrier-neutral data centers, telecommunications infrastructure, cloud services, and AI-ready digital platforms, all of which the government believes are important to modernizing public services and stimulating private-sector investment.

The pact follows a series of technological ties announced during Al-Zaidi’s tour to the United States, during which Iraq inked more than 50 agreements totaling more than $60 billion in the energy, banking, infrastructure, industrial, and technology sectors.

Improving digital infrastructure has become a key component of Iraq’s long-term economic plan, as the country strives to lessen reliance on oil earnings and establish a knowledge-based economy capable of attracting foreign technology businesses while also encouraging homegrown innovation.

The alliance also underscores increased US private-sector interest in Iraq’s digital economy, especially as demand for secure data centers, cloud computing capacity, and AI infrastructure in the Middle East grows.

Iraq has increasingly prioritized digital infrastructure for foreign investment alongside energy and transportation, with officials claiming that internationally certified data centers and modern telecommunications networks will be critical to supporting e-government services, digital banking, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence, as well as strengthening Iraq’s role as an emerging regional technology hub.

World.title: 'Abuses never solve anything': PM Modi posts late night video amid row over Noida woman's remarks
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra

on Friday night shared a video carrying a message against abusive language and hate, saying that "abuses never solve anything", amid the controversy over alleged derogatory remarks made against him by a Noida woman during a

in Delhi.

Sharing the video on X, PM Modi wrote, "Abuses never solve anything. Letâs guide the misguided. Letâs work together. Letâs work for Bharat."

The post comes a day after Ruchika Singh, a 25-year-old woman from Noida, was booked for allegedly making abusive and objectionable remarks against the PM Modi during student protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.

In the video, PM Modi also spoke about the government's efforts to strengthen India's examination system following Parliament's passage of a stringent anti-paper leak law.

"Friends, we are continuously taking one step after another to build a trustworthy examination system. Whether it is creating fast-track mechanisms or incorporating suggestions from the states, we are working in that direction."

The Prime Minister said paper leaks had affected governments across the country for decades and jeopardised the future of students.

"For several decades, every state government and every central government has faced the challenge of paper leaks.





Because of this, the future of our children has also been put at risk."

He said reforming the education system and expanding the use of technology had become essential to tackle the menace.

"Keeping all this in mind, it has become essential to reform the education system across the country, both in the states and at the Centre. The extensive use of technology has become a necessity."

PM Modi reiterated that the government would act firmly against those involved in paper leak rackets.

"At the same time, paper leak mafias, gangs involved in leaking examination papers and gangs that play with the future of the nation's children will not be spared. Strict laws are also necessary."

Referring to the legislation recently passed by Parliament, he said:

World.title: Delhi riots: Convicts' kin to challenge life sentence in HC, deny links to Tahir Hussain
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The family of two convicts sentenced to life imprisonment in the Ankit Sharma murder case, along with former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain, on Friday said they would challenge the trial court's verdict in the Delhi High Court.

Speaking to ANI, Mohammad Asif, the brother of convicts Nazim and Kasim, claimed that his brothers had been falsely implicated in the case and denied any connection with Tahir Hussain.

"We will appeal in the High Court. One of my brothers, the younger one, Kasim, lived in the village. The other one too had gone to the village two days before the incident. Tahir Hussain's house is very far away; we had no connection at all," Asif said.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Alleging police misconduct, he added, "The police brought them in and filed a case against them."

Meanwhile, speaking to ANI over the phone, Ankit's brother, Ankur Sharma, said, "Our demand was that the court should treat this case as a 'rarest of rare' case, and that the guilty should receive the harshest possible punishment. They should have been given the death penalty; that is what we wanted."

"As the case moves to the Delhi High Court or the Supreme Court, we want my brother to get justice there as well, and the guilty should receive the severest punishment. An example should be set so that such an incident never happens to anyone else," he added.

The court has awarded life imprisonment to all five convicts. The prosecution had argued that Sharma suffered 51 injuries and was brutally assaulted before his body was dumped into a drain.

World.title: 'Pak-trained Mujahideen have turned their guns inwards': India slams Islamabad over PoK crackdown
World.content:
The MEA criticized Pakistan's harsh crackdown on protesters in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. (PTI images)

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India on Friday slammed Pakistan of making an open admission of state-sponsored terrorism after a senior aide to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif acknowledged that Islamabad had trained and armed Mujahideen who have now turned against the Pakistani state.The ministry of external affairs (MEA) also condemned Pakistan's crackdown on anti-government protesters in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK), alleging that more than 40 civilians had been killed.Addressing the weekly media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Pakistan's handling of the protests had exposed its treatment of civilians in the region."As you and all of us have witnessed, the Pakistani establishment continues to unleash ruthless force against peaceful civilians in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. This crackdown has resulted in the tragic death of over 40 innocent people, and many more have been seriously injured. It's the establishment's absolute disdain for the innocent people of Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir that was laid bare when their Defence Minister branded the protesting civilians as enemies," Jaiswal said.Referring to recent remarks by Pakistan Prime Minister's Special Assistant on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Jaiswal said the statement amounted to a public acknowledgement that Pakistan had trained, funded and armed militants who were later sent into India."The Special Assistant of the Prime Minister [of Pakistan] on Political Affairs has openly admitted that the very Mujahideen that the Pakistani establishment trained, funded, armed, and sent to India have turned their guns inwards, weaponising themselves against the state," Jaiswal said.The remarks came after Sanaullah, in an interview with Geo News, said: "are the same people we once trained as Mujahideen. We sent them to fight, and today they are hanging around our necks."India has long accused Pakistan of sponsoring cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad has consistently denied.Jaiswal also criticised the recently held elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, calling them a rejection of Pakistan's establishment."The so-called elections stand as a humiliating rejection of the Pakistan establishment. Facing a violent regime, the people have requested international organisations for an independent investigation into the unlawful killings. We urged that the international community should scrutinise Pakistan's actions and hold it accountable for its atrocities," Jaiswal said.According to ANI, widespread protests have erupted across PoJK over allegations of electoral rigging, political interference and suppression of democratic rights.The United Kashmir People's National Party (UKPNP) has appealed to the United Nations and the international community to intervene over what it described as a worsening human rights situation in the region.In a statement posted on X, the organisation urged international institutions, governments and human rights organisations to take immediate steps to protect civilians, ensure accountability and uphold international human rights law.The group specifically appealed to the United Nations, the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, Russia and China, as well as international human rights organisations and global media, to respond to the reported escalation of violence in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir.India has consistently maintained that Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of India and has repeatedly raised concerns over Pakistan's support for cross-border terrorism and its treatment of civilians in the region.

World.title: Assam floods: Death toll rises to 80; state shifts focus to rehabilitation, announces loan relief
World.content:
Two more deaths in Sivasagar pushed Assam's flood toll to 80 on Friday, even as more than 2.12 lakh people across eight districts continued to grapple with the deluge.

The latest figures mark an improvement from the previous day's situation, when the flood toll stood at 78, over 3 lakh people across seven districts were affected, and floodwaters had inundated 551 villages and more than 21,500 hectares of crop area.

21 revenue circles and 437 villages remain inundated across Golaghat, Sivasagar, Biswanath, Charaideo, Kamrup (Metropolitan), Jorhat, Dhemaji and Nagaon. Charaideo remains the worst-hit district with nearly 80,000 affected people, followed by Sivasagar (71,000) and Jorhat (40,000), PTI cites.

Floodwaters have also caused extensive damage to embankments, roads, bridges and other public infrastructure.

Rescue teams continue relief operations

According to the recent data shared by the government, relief operations are continuing across Assam, with 216 relief camps and 1,788 relief distribution centres supporting flood-affected communities. The camps are currently sheltering 71,416 people, while authorities continue to provide food, drinking water, medicines and other essential supplies. Sarma said rehabilitation efforts remain the government's top priority as floodwaters recede.





The Army, NDRF, SDRF, Fire and Emergency Services, police and civil administration remain engaged in rescue and relief efforts.

In an X post, CM Himanta wrote, "Our teams are working 24*7 while we are formulating policies to directly benefit the affected."

With floodwaters receding, Sarma said the administration has expanded relief work to include debris clearance, doorstep healthcare, disposal of animal carcasses, disinfection drives, restoration of electricity and other essential services.

Government announces loan relief package

Chief minister

on Thursday also announced a six-month moratorium on repayment of loans availed by flood-affected people in Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat and Golaghat districts. The decision was taken at a special meeting of the State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC), attended by representatives of the RBI, NABARD, SBI and other commercial banks.

Banks have also agreed to extend loan tenures by one to seven years, depending on the type of loan, he informed. The Assam government has sought a special relief package from the Centre and urged the Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT) to classify the Upper

as an "atypical, high-intensity, rapid-onset event" for more flexible relief norms.

Meanwhile, Assam ministers flagged off 30 trucks carrying food, clothing and other essential supplies for flood-hit districts.

Assam minister Atul Bora, talking to ANI, said the government was continuing relief operations on a war footing and highlighted the Rs 15,000 financial assistance announced for each affected family, in addition to food supplies and other necessities.

Cloudburst triggered unprecedented flooding: CM

Earlier, chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma had attributed the devastating floods to an intense cloudburst in the upstream states of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

In a post on X on July 22, he said Arunachal Pradesh received 141% above-normal rainfall, while Nagaland recorded 181% above-normal precipitation, resulting in an unprecedented discharge of floodwaters into Assam.

Sarma said the sudden surge inundated several districts that had witnessed little or no flooding in recent history.

World.title: Explained: India's first urban ropeway is almost here. Can Varanasi's sky-high commute change how Indian cities travel?
World.content:
For centuries, getting around Varanasi has been part of the city's experience.

Its narrow lanes, bustling bazaars, temples and ghats are integral to the spiritual capital's identity.

But as one of India's oldest continuously inhabited cities welcomed millions of pilgrims and tourists every year, those same streets also became one of its biggest infrastructure challenges.

The stretch between Varanasi Cantonment railway station and Godowlia, the gateway to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Dashashwamedh Ghat, often witnessed bumper-to-bumper traffic.

During festivals or the peak pilgrimage season, a journey of less than four kilometres could easily take 40 minutes or more.

Building wider roads was never a practical solution. Much of the corridor passes through densely populated neighbourhoods and heritage areas, where large-scale demolition would not only be expensive but also risk altering the city's centuries-old character.

Instead, policymakers looked upwards.

Later this year, Varanasi is expected to become home to India's first urban public transport ropewayâa project that promises to ferry commuters and pilgrims above the city's congested streets in gondola cabins suspended nearly 45-50 metres above the ground.





Unlike the ropeways familiar to tourists in hill stations, this one is being built as part of the city's everyday mass transit network.

Officials say it will cut travel time between Cantt and Godowlia from around 40-45 minutes by road to roughly 15 minutes, while reducing pressure on one of the city's busiest traffic corridors.

The project is also a global rarity. Urban ropeways are still uncommon worldwide, with only a handful of cities integrating them into their public transport networks.

Indian officials have frequently described the Varanasi project as among the first of its kind globally to use ropeway technology for mass urban commuting rather than tourism.

Beyond offering a faster ride for pilgrims heading to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple, the project is being viewed as a test case for whether aerial mobility can solve transport problems in India's densely populated and heritage-rich cities, where conventional infrastructure often faces severe space constraints.

If successful, it could influence similar projects planned in cities ranging from Guwahati and Shimla to Dehradun and beyond under the Centre's broader ropeway expansion programme.

That makes Varanasi more than just another infrastructure project, as it could become the template for a new model of urban transport in India.

So, what exactly is India's first urban ropeway? Why has the government chosen cable cars over roads or metro lines? And can this technology genuinely become part of India's future public transport network?

What exactly is the Varanasi Urban Ropeway?

The Varanasi Urban Ropeway is India's first ropeway designed primarily as an urban mass transit system rather than a tourist attraction.

The project is being implemented by the National Highways Logistics Management Limited (NHLML), a wholly owned company of the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Swiss ropeway manufacturer Bartholet Maschinenbau AG has supplied the cable transport technology for the project.

Once operational, the ropeway will connect Varanasi Cantonment railway station with Godowlia Chowk, one of the busiest intersections in the city and the main access point for pilgrims visiting the Kashi Vishwanath Temple.

Stretching approximately 3.75-3.85 kilometres, the corridor will include stations at Cantt, Vidyapeeth, Rath Yatra and Godowlia, linking the railway station with major commercial, residential and religious hubs.

The project was conceived after authorities concluded that expanding roads through Varanasi's congested core would be extremely difficult because of the city's dense urban fabric and heritage structures.

Instead of competing for road space, the ropeway will operate entirely above existing traffic, offering commuters a predictable travel time regardless of congestion below.

According to the government, the system will use 148 modern gondola cabins, each capable of carrying 10 passengers. Gondolas are expected to arrive every one-and-a-half to two minutes, allowing the system to transport nearly 3,000 passengers per hour in each direction, or about 6,000 passengers every hour in total.

Official estimates suggest the network could eventually handle close to 96,000-1 lakh passengers daily, depending on operational schedules and demand.

Passengers boarding at Cantt Railway Station will be able to reach Godowlia in about 15-16 minutes, less than half the time the journey often takes by road during busy hours.

The Uttar Pradesh government has also finalised passenger fares. The minimum ticket has been fixed at Rs 10, while travelling the entire stretch from Cantt to Godowlia will cost Rs 50.

Holders of the Kashi Smart Pass will receive a 20% discount, reducing the end-to-end fare to Rs 40. Premium gondolas have also been planned for tourists and group bookings.

Modern passenger facilities, including lifts, escalators, CCTV surveillance, digital ticketing, fire safety systems and dedicated infrastructure for senior citizens and persons with disabilities, have been incorporated at stations to position the ropeway as a full-fledged public transport system rather than simply another tourist attraction.

The project, estimated to cost over Rs 800 crore including long-term operation and maintenance, has already completed trial runs and is expected to begin commercial operations after receiving the necessary regulatory clearances.

Why is the government betting on ropeways?

The Varanasi project is not an isolated experiment. It is part of the Centre's much larger strategy to introduce ropeways as an alternative mode of transport in places where building conventional roads, metro lines or rail corridors is either too expensive, technically difficult or environmentally disruptive.

This vision took shape in 2022 with the launch of the Parvatmala Pariyojana, the National Ropeways Development Programme announced in the Union Budget. The scheme aims to develop ropeways in hilly regions as well as congested urban areas through public-private partnerships.

Traditionally, ropeways in India have been associated with tourist destinations such as Gulmarg, Auli, Mussoorie or pilgrimage centres.

Under the new policy, however, the government wants them to become part of mainstream public transport.

Officials argue that ropeways offer several advantages over conventional infrastructure. They require significantly less land acquisition than roads or metro systems because towers occupy relatively small footprints.

Construction is also faster since there is little need for tunnelling, large flyovers or extensive utility shifting.

Since the cabins are electrically operated, ropeways also produce lower emissions than conventional road traffic, making them an attractive option for cities trying to reduce congestion and pollution.

The Varanasi project perfectly fits this philosophy.

The city's historic core leaves almost no room for widening roads without affecting heritage structures and densely populated neighbourhoods. A metro line would have involved far greater costs and engineering challenges.

An aerial ropeway, planners argue, offers a way to increase mobility while preserving the city's cultural fabric.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi had also highlighted this balance between tradition and technology when the project was announced.

Sharing details of the ropeway on social media in 2023, he described it as an "adbhut sangam" (remarkable confluence) of faith and technology and said it would not only make travel more convenient for devotees but also improve access to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple.

The government now sees ropeways as a solution that can complementânot replaceâexisting transport systems.

Can ropeways really work as urban public transport?

The idea may appear futuristic in India, but urban ropeways have been operating successfully in several parts of the world for years.

Perhaps the best-known example is La Paz, Bolivia, where the Mi TelefÃ©rico network has evolved into one of the world's largest urban cable car systems. With multiple interconnected lines stretching across the city and neighbouring El Alto, it carries hundreds of thousands of passengers every day while navigating mountainous terrain that makes conventional transport difficult.

Another frequently cited example is Mexico City, whose CablebÃºs system has transformed commuting for residents living in densely populated hillside settlements.

What once took well over an hour by road can now be completed in a fraction of the time using aerial cabins integrated with the city's wider public transport network.

These examples have demonstrated that ropeways need not remain tourist attractions.

They can function as reliable mass transit systems when integrated with buses, railways and pedestrian infrastructure.

Varanasi is now attempting to replicate those successes

Unlike metro systems that require passengers to travel underground or elevated through fixed corridors, ropeways can fly directly over existing development, reducing construction challenges and avoiding traffic altogether.

Continuous movement of gondolas also means passengers spend less time waiting compared to conventional bus services.

However, experts caution that ropeways are not a universal solution.

Their passenger capacity is considerably lower than metro rail systems, making them suitable only for specific corridors rather than citywide transport. Weather conditions, periodic maintenance and evacuation protocols also require careful planning. Unlike buses, expanding routes later is neither simple nor inexpensive.

Consequently, transport planners view ropeways as a niche solutionâbest suited for heritage cities, mountainous terrain or highly congested corridors where traditional transport networks are difficult to expand.

Could Varanasi become a model for other Indian cities?

That is perhaps the biggest question surrounding the project.

If the ropeway succeeds in reducing congestion, attracting regular commuters and integrating smoothly with the city's existing transport network, it could become a blueprint for similar projects elsewhere.

The Centre has already identified several ropeway proposals across the country under the Parvatmala programme, particularly in Himalayan states and pilgrimage destinations.

Cities facing severe geographical or heritage constraints are also studying whether aerial mobility could complement existing infrastructure.

But the success of the Varanasi ropeway will ultimately depend on far more than engineering.

Passengers must find it affordable enough to use regularly. The stations need seamless connections with railway stations, buses, auto-rickshaws and pedestrian routes. Safety standards, maintenance schedules and operational reliability will determine whether commuters choose the ropeway over conventional road transport.

Ridership will also be critical.

Unlike tourist ropeways that witness seasonal demand, an urban transport system must attract consistent daily commutersâoffice-goers, students, residents and pilgrimsâto remain financially viable over the long term.

There is also the question of whether ropeways can genuinely ease congestion or merely shift it from roads to stations if passenger management is inadequate.

These are precisely the issues transport planners and policymakers across India will be watching once commercial operations begin.

The bigger picture

India's urban transport story has traditionally revolved around roads, flyovers, suburban railways and metro systems. Ropeways are rarely featured in discussions about everyday commuting.

Varanasi could change that.

By carrying passengers above one of the country's oldest and most congested cities, the project represents an attempt to rethink how mobility solutions are designed for places where conventional infrastructure has reached its limits.

Its significance therefore extends beyond the four-kilometre journey between Cantt and Godowlia.

If successful, it could demonstrate that innovative transport systems can coexist with heritage conservation, allowing cities to modernise without fundamentally altering their historic character.

At the same time, the project is also a reminder that no single technology can solve every urban mobility challenge.

Ropeways are unlikely to replace metros or buses in India's largest cities. Instead, they could become another tool in the transport planner's toolkitâone best deployed where geography, density or heritage leave few alternatives.

For Varanasi, the benefits could be immediate. Faster journeys for pilgrims, easier access to one of India's holiest temples, reduced traffic on chronically congested roads and a cleaner mode of transport for residents and visitors alike.

For India, however, the stakes are much larger.

The country's first urban public transport ropeway is not merely about moving people from one station to another.

It is a test of whether the next generation of urban infrastructure can think beyond roads and rails and whether its oldest cities can embrace modern mobility without sacrificing the heritage that defines them.

World.title: IMD flags below-normal rainfall in August; heavy rain alerts for Kerala, Assam, Northeast
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Friday forecast below-normal rainfall in August across India, at 94 per cent of the long-period average. It also issued weather alerts across several parts of the country, including Kerala, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and other northeastern states, warning of heavy to very heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, flash floods and landslides over the next few days.

The latest warnings come as several states continue to grapple with flood and landslide risks during the monsoon season. The IMD said monthly average rainfall over India as a whole is most likely to be below normal in August after the country recorded near-average rainfall in July, raising concerns about crop yields and broader economic activity.

"Rainfall in August is likely to be below 94% of the long-period average," Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, director-general of the India Meteorological Department, told a press conference.

August outlook raises concerns for crops and economy

The IMDâs latest forecast of below-normal August rainfall comes after a season marked by intense regional downpours despite broadly average rainfall across the country in July. The weather officeâs assessment suggests that while parts of southern and northeastern India may continue to experience heavy rain in the immediate term, rainfall across India as a whole is expected to remain below the long-term average during August.





Kerala under orange alert, schools shut in several districts

In Kerala, the IMD issued an orange alert for 11 districts on Friday, including Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod. An orange alert indicates the likelihood of very heavy rainfall ranging between 115.6 mm and 204.4 mm within 24 hours at isolated places.

For August 1, orange alerts remain in place for Idukki, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod, while yellow alerts have been issued for several southern districts through August 2.

Following the warnings, educational institutions in several Kerala districts were declared closed on Friday. The Kerala State Disaster Management Authority advised residents in areas vulnerable to landslides, mudslides and flash floods to move to safer locations if directed by authorities. People living near riverbanks, downstream of dams and in houses with weak roofs were also urged to remain vigilant.

Flash flood warning issued for Arunachal Pradesh

In Arunachal Pradesh, the IMD forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning from July 31 and issued a flash flood alert for nine districts, including Tawang, West Kameng, East Kameng, Kurung Kumey, Upper Subansiri, Anjaw, Dibang Valley, Tirap and Changlang.

Very heavy rainfall of 12 cm to 20 cm in 24 hours is expected at isolated places in Papum Pare district through Saturday, while Lower Subansiri is likely to receive heavy rainfall of 6 cm to 11 cm. The weather office warned that heavy rain could trigger surface runoff and inundation in saturated and low-lying areas and advised district administrations to remain on high alert.

The ongoing spell of floods and landslides has already claimed seven lives and affected 1,53,553 people across Arunachal Pradesh.

The monsoon has affected 373 circles and 668 villages in 27 districts so far.

Assam and northeast brace for another spell of heavy rain

A fresh spell of heavy to very heavy rainfall has also been forecast across Assam and several northeastern states over the next three to four days. An orange alert has been issued for Tinsukia district in Assam, while similar alerts are in place for Mon, Mokokchung and Wokha districts of Nagaland.

The IMD said widespread rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms is likely between July 30 and August 1 across parts of Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

Runoff from districts in Arunachal Pradesh, including East Siang, Lohit, Namsai, Longding, Papumpare, Lower Subansiri and Lower Dibang Valley, could affect Tinsukia, Dhemaji and Lakhimpur districts in Assam.

The Assam State Disaster Management Authority warned that the fresh spell of rain could worsen flooding, trigger urban waterlogging and flash floods, and cause localised landslides, particularly in hilly and vulnerable areas. District administrations have been instructed to closely monitor the situation and residents have been urged to avoid non-essential travel during periods of intense rainfall.

World.title: PM Modi, UK PM Andy Burnham discuss AI, defence, Strait of Hormuz in first phone call
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday held his first telephone conversation with newly elected UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, congratulating him on assuming office as the two leaders agreed to deepen cooperation in technology, artificial intelligence, defence, trade and security while also discussing the situation in the Middle East, including efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

In a post on X after the call, PM Modi said he congratulated Burnham on taking office and reaffirmed India's commitment to strengthening the bilateral partnership.

"Delighted to speak with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Andy Burnham. Congratulated him on assuming office and conveyed my best wishes for a successful tenure."

The Prime Minister said both leaders agreed to expand cooperation across multiple strategic sectors.

"We agreed to work together across sectors such as technology, innovation, defence, security, clean energy, education and people-to-people ties and take the India-UK Comprehensive Strategic Partnership to new heights."

PM Modi also said both countries would seek to maximise the benefits of the recently operationalised India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement.

"We will also collaborate closely to fully harness the trade and investment opportunities presented by the recently operationalized India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, for the shared prosperity and well-being of both our people."





UK highlights AI cooperation and vision 2035

According to a statement issued by the UK Prime Minister's Office, Burnham described the India-UK relationship as a strong partnership that had made a significant contribution to communities across Britain.

The statement said Burnham outlined his ambition to further strengthen bilateral ties through the UK-India Vision 2035 framework and stronger people-to-people connections.

The UK Prime Minister also praised the contribution of the Indian community to British society, while PM Modi referred to the historical connection between Manchester and Ahmedabad, describing the Gujarat city as the "Manchester of India".

Leaders discuss AI and emerging technologies

The UK Prime Minister's Office said Burnham reaffirmed his commitment to advancing the UK-India Technology Security Initiative, with both leaders identifying artificial intelligence and other cutting-edge technologies as key areas for future collaboration.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The leaders also welcomed the opportunities created by the recently introduced India-UK Free Trade Agreement, saying it would generate economic benefits and create opportunities for people in both countries.

Middle East and Strait of Hormuz discussed

Beyond bilateral ties, the two leaders discussed the evolving situation in the Middle East and agreed to work closely towards de-escalation.

According to Downing Street, both sides also agreed to cooperate in efforts aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically vital maritime route for global energy supplies and international trade.

The UK Prime Minister's Office said both leaders agreed to remain in close contact and looked forward to speaking again soon and meeting in person at the earliest opportunity.

World.title: ‘Abuses never solve anything, let’s guide the misguided’: PM Modi on Jantar Mantar protests
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday (July 31, 2026) reached out to Gen Z and said that abuse is not a solution to anything. He posted the video message on X in which he was talking about the July 20 Jantar Mantar protest against irregularities in NEET examination paper.

“I can understand the anguish prevailing in society, but this is the time to embrace our youth and guide them on the right path,” the Prime Minister said. “These are misguided children; punishing them or making them go through court proceedings will not solve the problem,” he added.

Abuses never solve anything.



Let's guide the misguided.



Let's work together.



Let's work for Bharat. pic.twitter.com/yAePG60KYL — Narendra Modi (@narendramodi) July 31, 2026

PM Modi said he wants to forgive all those who used abusive language against him and even his mother. “I want to forgive them; people make mistakes, but this is a cultural shock that our daughters are using such abusive language,"he said.

“We must forgive our youth who were misguided; after all, they are our children. It’s our duty to show them the right path,” he said in the video message. Mr. Modi also added that “we don’t disown our teeth even if they bite our tongue; both belong to us, just as our youth are our own”.

World.title: Sept. 30 set as deadline to clear debris from Cooum
World.content:
Civic agencies have set September 30 as the deadline to clear construction debris from the Cooum as part of flood preparedness, ahead of the onset of the Northeast monsoon.

At a meeting on Friday to finalise flood defence measures for the Cooum, the Water Resources Department (WRD) insisted on completing the removal of debris by September 30, an official said.

Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) Commissioner G.S. Sameeran said the civic body was closely coordinating with the WRD, the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), the Highways Department, and other stakeholder agencies to ensure that all ongoing construction activities in and around the Cooum did not adversely affect flood conveyance during the Northeast monsoon.

The major ongoing construction activity is the NHAI’s Chennai Port-Maduravoyal Elevated Corridor, large stretches of which run along the Cooum. The GCC consistently insisted on removing all temporary obstructions, including earth bunds, boulders, and other construction materials, well before the onset of monsoon, so that the hydraulic capacity of the river was not compromised.

At the government-level, inter-departmental review meetings have been conducted under the chairmanship of the Minister for Public Works and Highways as well as the Chief Secretary to the government. All agencies concerned were instructed to work in coordination to ensure timely completion of pre-monsoon preparedness activities.

The GCC is continuously coordinating with the WRD and NHAI to monitor compliance with these directions, an official said.

Apart from the elevated corridor, bridge construction works being executed by the Highways Department and other agencies across the Cooum have also been reviewed. Wherever construction activities have the potential to obstruct water flow during heavy rainfall events, the executing agencies have been advised either to complete the critical portions of the works before the monsoon or, wherever completion is not feasible, to remove temporary obstructions and restore adequate waterway to ensure uninterrupted flow.

Detailed assessment

Recognising the importance of assessing the hydraulic impact of permanent structures, the WRD has entrusted Anna University with conducting a detailed scientific impact assessment of the piers constructed on the river for the elevated corridor. It will evaluate their impact on river hydraulics, flood conveyance, sediment transport, and water levels during extreme rainfall events. Based on the findings, Anna University will recommend appropriate mitigation measures, which will be implemented by NHAI, in consultation with the WRD and other agencies, an official said.

GCC, in coordination with WRD, is also undertaking its routine pre-monsoon preparedness measures, including desilting of storm water drains, removal of encroachments and floating debris wherever required, inspection of vulnerable locations, and continuous monitoring of river conditions. A joint coordination mechanism has been established among GCC, WRD, NHAI and the Highways Department to review progress periodically and address any emerging issues promptly, an official said.

World.title: Suresh Rajpurohit and S. Sreejith promoted as DGPs
World.content:
The State government promoted Suresh Rajpurohit and S. Sreejith to the rank of Director General of Police (DGP) on Friday.

The promotions were implemented shortly after the retirement of Director General of Kerala Fire and Rescue Services Nitin Agrawal.

Notably, Mr. Rajpurohit’s promotion has been made on a proforma basis since he is presently away on Central deputation. Mr. Sreejith, who is presently posted as Director General of Prisons and Correctional Services, will continue to hold the position.

Home Department sources indicated that more transfers are on the offing to fill the post of Managing Director of the Kerala State Beverages Corporation (BEVCO), which has remained vacant for nearly a week since the suspension of Additional Director General of Police (ADGP) M.R. Ajith Kumar, and the position of the Director General of Kerala Fire and Rescue Services.

Meanwhile, speaking at his farewell parade held at the SAP ground in Peroorkada, Mr. Agrawal called Kerala Police as a model force for the country. He said the experience and training he received in the state had greatly contributed to his professional career and enabled him to serve more effectively in different assignments.

A 1989-batch IPS officer, Mr. Agrawal is the recipient of several prestigious honours, including the Medal for Meritorious Service (2007), the President’s Police Medal for Distinguished Service (2014) and multiple gold medals and commendations from various armed forces.

State Police Chief Ravada A. Chandrasekhar, Road Safety Commissioner Yogesh Gupta, Vigilance Director Manoj Abraham and other senior police officers attended the farewell ceremony.

World.title: Villagers demand operation of overhead tank for regular water supply in Tiruvannamalai
World.content:
As parched lakes and ponds turn borewells dry, residents in Palanandal village near Tiruvannamalai town have demanded operation of an Overhead Tank in the village to provide regular water supply, especially to tail-end areas.

Residents said Palanandal village comprises nine wards that come under Thurinjapuram Panchayat Union in the district. Seven remote hamlets, including Veluganandal, Mangalam, Pudur, and Nookkambadi with around 2,300 families are located in the village.

While recent weeks have seen soaring temperatures, water supply has not reached the tail-end areas of these hamlets in the village. Among these hamlets, Pudur hamlet alone has around 150 families, who depend on water supplied by the panchayat.

Irregular supply of water has made residents travel at least 5-10 km to fetch a few pots of water from Kilpennathur and Tiruvannamalai towns. ” As groundwater in the area is salty, we depend on water provided by the panchayat for consumption. However, the local panchayat has not connected water pipelines to the newly built Overhead Tank,” said R. Ganesh, a resident.

Residents said that the tank, which has a storage capacity of 10,000 litres, was built more than five years before the COVID-19 pandemic to ensure houses in the tail-end areas get regular water supply. However, residents said that the tank has not been fully operational due to low-power generators that give less water to the tank. As a result, water in the tank does not have enough pressure to reach tail-end areas.

Panchayat officials said on an average, 3.5 lakh litres of water is required for household consumption alone every day. Most of the water is sourced from five borewells in the village. Water from these bore wells is pumped to four Over Head Tanks in the village to provide water through pipelines and street corner taps. Every day, water is supplied for two hours for household consumption.

Initial inquiry by panchayat officials found that motor pump sets that upload water to the new overhead tank were not working. The existing water pipelines were also not connected to the tank, which was built after the previous one collapsed many years ago. Panchayat officials said that efforts have been taken to provide water to households through private tanker lorries before water supply is resumed through the new tank.

World.title: A genetic blueprint for saving Asia’s iconic hornbills
World.content:
With oversized beaks, striking casque structures and distinctive calls, hornbills are among the most recognisable birds of the wet tropics. Yet behind their charismatic appearance lies a growing conservation concern. Many species face mounting pressure from habitat loss, forest fragmentation, hunting and illegal wildlife trade. Several now survive in small, isolated populations across south and southeast Asia, raising concerns about their long-term survival.

A new study by scientists from the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB), Hyderabad and Nature Conservation Foundation (NCF), Mysore, offers insight into how these birds evolved and how their populations have changed over time.

The research team involved Pooja Pawar and Rohit Naniwadekar from NCF, along with Gopi Krishnan and Jahnavi Joshi from CCMB. Using advanced genome sequencing technologies, researchers have decoded the complete genetic makeup of four Asian hornbill species and reconstructed their demographic history over millions of years.

The species examined were the Great Hornbill (Buceros bicornis), Wreathed Hornbill (Rhyticeros undulatus), Rufous-necked Hornbill (Aceros nipalensis) and Malabar Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus).

According to the researchers, this represents a significant advance in hornbill biology. Before this work, complete genome information was available for only two of the 32 recognised Asian hornbill species. Genomes are often described as biological archives. By analysing entire genomes, scientists can trace fluctuations in population sizes across thousands and even millions of years. Such information helps reveal how species responded to climatic upheavals, habitat changes and other environmental pressures long before systematic observations became possible.

Ms. Pawar said the study found evidence that all four hornbill species experienced population declines associated with climatic fluctuations during the Pleistocene epoch, which spanned from about 2.58 million years ago to roughly 11,700 years ago. The genomic analyses suggest that repeated cycles of cooling and warming dramatically influenced tropical forests across Asia, affecting habitat availability for forest-dependent hornbills.

Among the four species studied, the Wreathed Hornbill emerged as an exception. Researchers found that it maintained significantly larger population sizes than the other species throughout much of its history. Its peak effective population size was roughly three times that of the Great Hornbill and Rufous-necked Hornbill.

Scientists believe the species may have benefited from its migratory behaviour and broader habitat use. Unlike resident hornbills restricted to pockets of wet evergreen forest, Wreathed Hornbills undertake long-distance seasonal movements and occupy a wider variety of habitats. Large and connected populations generally retain greater genetic diversity, improving resilience and adaptability. The findings align with broader studies showing that migratory bird species often maintain larger long-term populations than non-migratory species.

The researchers also uncovered important clues about hornbill evolution. Comparison with African hornbill lineages revealed substantial expansion in gene families associated with structural keratin, the protein that forms feathers, beaks and claws.

Such evolutionary changes may have contributed to the unique characteristics that distinguish Asian hornbills today, including their prominent casques and other specialised physical features. The study also identified expansion in genes associated with reproductive functions, providing fresh insight into the evolutionary pathways that shaped these unusual birds.

Hornbills are often referred to as “farmers of the forest” because of their ecological role as seed dispersers. Unlike savanna hornbills, which are largely carnivorous, many Asian forest hornbills depend heavily on fruits. By carrying seeds across long distances and depositing them away from parent trees, they play a critical role in forest regeneration. This close association with forests also makes them particularly vulnerable when habitats disappear.

The researchers found that species occupying evergreen forests, such as the Great Hornbill and Rufous-necked Hornbill, were especially sensitive to historical contractions of wet tropical forests. Reductions in forest cover during glacial periods likely contributed to long-term declines and fragmentation. The Malabar Pied Hornbill, which favours moist deciduous forests, displayed a somewhat different demographic pattern but also showed evidence of historical decline.

Three of the four species studied, the Great Hornbill, Wreathed Hornbill and Rufous-necked Hornbill, are listed as ‘Vulnerable’ on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. The Malabar Pied Hornbill is classified as ‘Near Threatened’.

Researchers say the new genomic resources could significantly strengthen conservation planning. Genetic data can reveal levels of allelic diversity within populations, identify isolated groups, measure gene flow and help determine which populations require urgent intervention.

The study also has applications for captive breeding programmes. Previous genetic work found little differentiation among captive Great Hornbills held across several zoos in Thailand, demonstrating the value of genomic information in managing ex-situ conservation efforts.

Samples for the present study were obtained from several locations, including Arunachal Pradesh, the Western Ghats and the Nehru Zoological Park in Hyderabad, enabling comparisons across geographic regions. The researchers have deposited the genome assemblies and sequence data in the National Centre for Biotechnology Information repository, making them available to scientists worldwide. “We believe that this study provides robust genomic resources to support future comparative and conservation genomics efforts for hornbills,” said Mr. Joshi.

World.title: Maharaja Co-operative Urban Bank eyes small finance bank status as business volume hits over ₹612 crore
World.content:
The Maharaja Co-operative Urban Bank Ltd. has set its sights on transitioning into a Small Finance Bank, marking a significant strategic evolution for the urban cooperative institution. Members approved the proposal at the bank’s 26th Annual General Meeting, held on Friday at Kshatriya Kalyana Mandapam in Seethammadhara.

Founding chairman M. Ramakrishnam Raju announced robust financial milestones for the 2025–26 fiscal year. As of March 31, 2026, the bank registered a total business volume of ₹612.55 crore, backed by ₹374.22 crore in deposits and ₹238.33 crore in loans.

The institution posted a gross income of ₹2.32 crore for the year. After paying ₹0.60 crore in income tax, the net income stood at ₹1.72 crore. Reinforcing its financial health, the bank reported a capital base of ₹17.66 crore alongside reserves and provisions totaling ₹17.35 crore, elevating its net worth to ₹32.28 crore. Furthermore, the board declared a 10% dividend for shareholders.

Strong momentum has carried into the current fiscal year. Management noted that as of July 28, 2026, total deposits climbed to ₹384 crore and loans reached ₹238 crore, pushing the aggregate business volume to ₹622 crore. Buoyed by this growth, the bank has outlined an ambitious target to touch ₹700 crore in total business by March 31, 2027.

Expanding its operational footprint, the bank launched new branches in Narsipatnam, Vijayawada, and Ramachandrapuram over the past year, and plans to inaugurate two more branches soon. Demonstrating community commitment, the bank awarded approximately ₹8 lakhs in scholarships to the children of staff members.

The meeting drew several prominent figures, including RERA Member and Federation Director M. Venkata Ratnam, Pochampally Co-operative Urban Bank CEO Seetha Srinivas, Paida Group Chairman Paida Krishna Prasad, Jalavihar Group Chairman N.V. Rama Raju, Retired PF Commissioner S.V.S.S. Rama Chandra Raju, and Balaji Group Chairman Mandava Ravi Kumar, General Manager N.N. Satyanarayana said in a release here.

World.title: Delayed aid, prolonged ordeal
World.content:
Sandhya, in her 40s, insists she completed every dose of medication prescribed for her tuberculosis (TB) treatment. Yet, as she sits crouched outside her mud house in a remote tribal hamlet near Paderu in Alluri Sitharama Raju district, her frail frame makes her appear decades older than her age.

Her struggle extends beyond the disease itself. Like, many other TB patients in the State, Sandhya has been waiting for financial assistance meant to support her through treatment, exposing the consequences of delays in disbursing aid to some of the most vulnerable patients.

The disease is just one of the many hardships she carries. Sandhya, who was diagnosed with pulmonary TB in December 2025, is dependent on her elder daughter, the sole breadwinner for their family of four—Sandhya and her three children.

Sandhya was placed on a regimen for drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB), which lasts for six months and includes four drugs. Her claim of completing the treatment, however, is denied by her neighbours, who say she stopped her medication in the second month after severe stomach pain made it difficult for her to continue.

Even as neighbours urge Sandhya to seek treatment at the Primary Health Centre, nearly 10 km away, she denies. “I cannot make the journey,” she says softly, her voice fading into the breeze before she can finish her sentence.

For Sandhya, who belongs to a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), getting nutritious food and visiting a doctor are uphill tasks. The hamlet, home to 200 individuals, sits on a hillock, accessible only by a muddy, unpaved road. There is no school or anganwadi within 5 km of the hamlet, and the nearest shop is 2 km away, making eggs or milk a once-a-month indulgence.

Distance is only one part of the problem. Sandhya’s family survives on her elder daughter’s income of only ₹100 or ₹150 per day, which she earns when she finds work in an agricultural field. On other days, the family has no income to sustain themselves.

“All she can afford is ragi ambali for breakfast and rice with chaaru for lunch and dinner,” says Satya, her neighbour and also the caretaker for those in need of medical assistance in the absence of an Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA). The villagers say that ASHA worker from a nearby village visits only in times of need.

Healthcare workers point out that stomach irritation is considered one of the common side effects of anti-TB drugs. They recommend higher fluid intake and a proper diet to minimise gastrointestinal issues, and a consultation with a doctor is also suggested for further complications.

“Nutrition has a direct role to play in determining treatment outcomes for a patient, and undernutrition, as is the case with Sandhya, creates the most favorable condition for the disease to progress, increasing the risk of death by four to five times,” says Dr. Swathi Krishna, a public health physician and TB researcher based in Maharashtra.

Now, seven months after the discontinuation of her medications, Sandhya is burning with fever and experiencing body aches. The discontinuation of anti-TB drugs may lead to a relapse of the illness, and the condition may progress into a more serious form of TB, known as multidrug-resistant TB. However, this cannot be confirmed until Sandhya visits a hospital.

A medical expert working with an NGO who assessed Sandhya’s condition says she may not live long if she does not immediately resume her medications and eat properly.

Dr. Swathi Krishna says that a Body Mass Index of less than 18.5 should be considered a definite criterion for admitting patients to hospitals; Sandhya mostly falls into this category. “But this crucial risk factor is often missed at the time of diagnosis,” she adds.

Government scheme

According to the WHO’s Global TB Report 2025, India has the highest number of TB cases in the world and accounted for 28% of the deaths due to TB globally. As of July 3, 2026, Andhra Pradesh had reported 37,130 TB cases. Tuberculosis, caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is often referred to as the disease of the poor. As long as there is poverty, data shows, the disease will thrive.

In response to such concerns, especially poverty and undernutrition, among people from the economically backward sections of the society, the Union government launched the Nikshay Poshan Yojana in 2018, under which all notified TB patients would receive ₹500 per month during the course of their six-month treatment. In 2024, this amount was increased to ₹1,000 per month, which is funded by the Union and State governments in a ratio of 60:40. However, many patients in Andhra Pradesh have not been receiving this amount for at least six months or more.

When asked about the payment delays, A.P. State Nodal Officer T. Ramesh said that updating the payment platforms had been causing delays in depositing the amount since December 2025, but the process would be streamlined soon. He added that payment was made to nearly 29,000 patients in March.

The absence of this crucial support has left many TB patients in a lurch, with the impact felt among people living in remote and underdeveloped regions such as Sandhya’s.

Sandhya’s ordeal is not an isolated one. This reporter spoke with five TB patients from Alluri Sitharama Raju, NTR, Chittoor, and Eluru districts and identified seven others who said they had not received financial aid. One patient, who began treatment in May 2025, said they did not receive the financial support or the nutritional kit.

The experience is no different for Lakshmi, a 37-year-old farmer. A resident of another tribal hamlet in ASR district, she was diagnosed with extra pulmonary TB in June of this year. When asked about her nutritional intake, she says having milk or eggs or even vegetables is a luxury.

Her ordeal, however, began long before the diagnosis. Multiple visits to the Government General Hospital in Paderu finally led to the confirmation of TB. A bit hesitant to share her experience at first, she later opens up and shares that she has had cold abscesses on her neck and chest for more than three years. She claims that no one could figure out what was troubling her.

“They hurt a lot sometimes,” she says when asked if she is able to do her everyday work. But that does not stop her from going to the agricultural field. The family does not have a regular income but has an acre of land where they grow paddy, carrots, and turmeric. While paddy is for their own consumption, they sell turmeric and carrots in November and December every year. The amount they earn from this sustains them for the rest of the year. “Sometimes, we receive a good amount, like ₹20,000,” says Lakshmi.

Nutritional support

According to research by medical expert Anurag Bhargava and others, titled “Nutritional Supplementation to Prevent Tuberculosis Incidence in Household Contacts of Patients with Pulmonary Tuberculosis in India (RATIONS): A Field-Based, Open-Label, Cluster-Randomised, Controlled Trial,” supplementation with micro- and macronutrients for six months is effective in substantially reducing the incidence of confirmed tuberculosis in a group at high risk due to close contact with an infectious person and a high prevalence of undernutrition.

Based on these studies, the Union government emphasised the nutritional aspect in the treatment of TB. In 2022, with this aim, the government introduced the Ni-kshay Mitra initiative. Under which, the government encouraged the public and corporations to come forward and donate nutritional baskets to TB patients, in an effort to promote public participation in the national efforts to eliminate TB.

While many donors had enrolled as ‘Mitras’ in the first year of the programme’s launch, the initiative soon fizzled out as donor fatigue set in. Dr. Ramesh, the State TB Officer, says that more than four lakh food baskets have been distributed between 2022 and July 2026 in A.P.

The statistics, however, indicate that each patient requires six baskets—one per month—meaning that four lakh baskets would support more than 66,000 patients. This number is fewer than the cases reported in the State in a single year, specifically 2025.

According to a frontline health worker in Annamayya district, securing a donor has become a difficult task, and the government has now shifted the responsibility of motivating the public onto them. “Even health staff at the Primary or Community Health Centre do not come forward to donate food baskets. How can we motivate the public?” the worker asks.

Dr. Anand Zachariah, a senior professor in the Department of Medicine at Christian Medical College in Vellore, says that the main problem with ‘Ni-kshay Mitra’ is its complete dependence on donors. “The scheme is structured in such a way that only the chosen ones receive the support. Social welfare programmes cannot be based on donors or voluntary contributions,” he says.

Not just in remote areas; donors are not easily secured in cities like Vijayawada either. According to frontline health worker Divya, even if an individual or an NGO donates food baskets, it happens only once or twice a year, and only 10 out of 100 people receive them.

She says that in her area, there are five people currently under treatment for TB. None of them have received cash or nutritional baskets, she adds. “Since we are the closest representatives of the government for them, they often look to us for updates on the status of the transactions, and we have no answers,” she says.

Chandramma, a 65-year-old street vendor in Vijayawada, recounts her experience after her husband—a rickshaw puller—was put on TB treatment in May 2025. She says she had to make multiple trips to the TB unit at the nearest Community Health Centre and to her bank for updates on the payment. “I was once told that there is no budget with the government,” she says.

Chandramma adds, “While he has now recovered, he lost a considerable amount of weight during the treatment and stopped going to work after his diagnosis.” Now, I sell maize and biscuits in front of a school from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. to make a living. “My earnings per day stay below ₹200,” she adds.

“The doctors had told me to take good care of him by providing nutritious food during his treatment, but I could not do much,” she says. With her meagre wages and an old-age pension of ₹4,000, she could only afford to buy him a packet of milk and Horlicks. She also borrowed ₹20,000 to purchase nutritious food for her husband, which she has yet to pay back.

While patients and their families recount months of uncertainty and trouble, health officials maintain that digital hurdles are the main cause. When this reporter spoke with ASHAs, Community Health Officers, and TB supervisors from across the State, they stated that digital hurdles, such as the creation of an Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) ID for TB patients, are the reasons for the delays.

“One has to link a patient’s bank details with Aadhaar, then open the Ni-kshay portal and enter the details. Once a QR is generated, we open the ABHA app on another system and scan the QR. Then, the ABHA ID has to be created using the iris of the patient for the face authentication. While in an area with good network, this process takes a maximum of one hour, but in remote areas, it takes up to a week,” says a TB Supervisor from a remote area in Rayalaseema.
