World.title: The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal Billie Eder August 1, 2026 — 2:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Australia’s cycling team is unhappy but unable to appeal a decision by race officials to disqualify a rider from a bronze medal race over the taping of her shoulders, even though she had them taped when she won gold a day earlier. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who was part of the women’s team that won gold in the team pursuit, was disqualified on Friday from the women’s 4000m individual pursuit for wearing strapping tape under her race suit. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory after the women’s 4000m team pursuit finals. Getty Images The 21-year-old cyclist finished fourth fastest in individual qualifying to book herself a spot in the bronze medal race against Scotland’s Erin Boothman, before officials from world cycling’s governing body, the UCI, disqualified her for a breach of equipment and uniform rules. Those officials deemed that the tape, on Wilson-Haffenden’s shoulders, caused a “morphological change” – a change to the physical shape, outer appearance or internal structure of the body – which is against racing rules.



The official rule says, “clothing and other items or accessories worn by a rider may not modify the morphology of the rider”. It is unclear how and why officials picked up on the taping on Friday and not Thursday, and whether the check of the two Australian athletes was random. The UCI has been contacted for comment and clarification. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden during the individual pursuit. Quinn Rooney The same officials ruled that another Australian, Sophie Edwards, would also be disqualified for having “excessive” padding in her helmet. Both Wilson-Haffenden and Edwards had the same taping and helmet, respectively, when they raced the previous day. No clothing or equipment issues were raised after officials completed inspections on Thursday.



Executive general manager of performance at Aus Cycling, Jesse Korf, said the Australian team was frustrated by the decision to disqualify Wilson-Haffenden. He described the decision as subjective and said Wilson-Haffenden received taping to her shoulders after having discomfort and mobility issues. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images “On inspection after the race, the UCI [Union Cycliste Internationale] concluded that the taping of the shoulder constituted, according to them in the rule book, a morphological change, but they weren’t able to articulate what that exactly was because it’s a grey area. You cannot measure what a morphological change is,” Korf said. “They made that conclusion, we looked into it and, being that it’s non-measurable and subjective, unfortunately that conclusion is final, which we’re most certainly not happy with and Felicity is upset, of course.”



Korf said the team was also disappointed in the decision to disqualify Edwards, but she had not qualified for a medal race. The Australian team does not believe there is a risk that the team’s gold medal will be stripped or under review, given both riders passed inspections on the day. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images “We heard nothing after inspections yesterday,” Korf said. “After races, riders get inspected, there’s always checks, and there was no challenge, no nothing yesterday, so that’s in the clear. “The challenges [today] are from what was faced in the individual pursuits and the conclusions of the commissaires.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Korf said Australia would seek more clarification on the rules moving forward. “Well, we’ll definitely try to learn more around how the assessment is done so that we can learn and mitigate,” Korf said. New Zealand’s Bryony Boothman has now been promoted to the bronze medal race. Glasgow 2026 has also been contacted for comment.



Before her disqualification, Wilson-Haffenden had said she was looking forward to the bronze medal race despite appearing quite distressed and unwell after qualifying. She needed extra recovery time, was shaky, and needed assistance when leaving the track. “No doubt I’ll be riding tonight. I mean, a 4000m effort takes a lot out of you, and I needed a little longer to recover, but I’ll be all good,” she said. It was only her second individual 4000m pursuit, and said her post-race condition was a result of giving it her all. “I enjoy suffering, so I quite enjoy this race,” she said.

World.title: ‘We came here to win, not to be safe’: Beveridge’s home truths as Docker juggernaut marches on
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We came here to win, not to be safe’: Beveridge’s home truths as Docker juggernaut marches on Steve Barrett August 1, 2026 — 12:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge has denied he deliberately plotted to drag Fremantle into a congested, defensive scrap in the Dockers’ 37-point win on Friday night, 11.12 (78) to 5.11 (41). To most observers, Beveridge and his team appeared to come in with a clear blueprint to turn the game into a stifling, contested battle by setting up in numbers behind the ball to clog Fremantle’s forward half and deny the Dockers the space they thrive on. By Luke Beveridge’s own admission, the Bulldogs “fuelled Fremantle’s game” at Optus Stadium. AFL Photos Frustrated, Fremantle were made to sweat for the best part of three quarters, before turning on the afterburners late to move to an 18-2 record, all but putting a bow on the minor premiership. But Beveridge rejected suggestions he devised the unconventional plan of attack, insisting his side was forced into the scrappy style.



“I had them [extra defenders] back because Fremantle had territory, and we couldn’t get it into our front half – that’s why,” he explained. “We didn’t plan to play like that. “It wasn’t by design that we had saturation in numbers behind the ball. View post on X “We wanted to press up at different times, and we didn’t get our execution right. We came here tonight to win the game, not to be safe and not to eliminate risk.



“But we didn’t execute well enough.” Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects Whether by design or not, the Dogs transformed the first half into a stoppage grind, strangling and sandbagging Fremantle’s transition game, silencing the 53,524-strong crowd and reducing the league’s most potent attacking side to a scrap. But there were fleeting glimpses of the usual Docker brilliance. Luke Jackson soared for a majestic mark over opponent Tim English before converting the game’s opening goal with 23 minutes already elapsed.



Then, in the second quarter, Patrick Voss produced a powerful one-on-two mark over Michael Sellwood and James O’Donnell as the Dockers threatened to break clear. Related Article AFL 2026 Geelong reach settlement with Stengle as Hill departs Collingwood Scores were level at half-time, but there was a sense the Bulldogs were just clinging on, their 14 first-half inside-50s the third-lowest tally on record. It was always going to be a difficult way to win for the Dogs, made even more challenging when their scoring completely dried up after half-time. Josh Treacy and Hayden Young celebrated their 100th games in style, the former booting three goals to break open the stalemate, and the latter curbing the influence of the great Marcus Bontempelli.



Jackson shaded English in the ruck, while unsung backs Karl Worner and Oscar McDonald intercepted with aplomb to strangle the Dogs’ forward line. Josh Treacy is one of the AFL’s most imposing forces up forward. Getty Images The Bulldogs showed there is a formula to keep Fremantle in check for a quarter, two quarters or even three. But eventually the Dockers’ relentless pressure and superior class proved too much. “We had field position on our terms for the majority of the night, and we just persisted really well,” Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir said. “Usually when you get that much supply versus the opposition and that much time in forward half, the dam wall eventually breaks.



“In that last quarter, it did.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Nothing in normal life can prepare you for this surreal voyage
World.content:
InspirationAntarctica Nothing in normal life can prepare you for this surreal voyage Carolyn Beasley August 1, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s difficult to think of penguins as violent. And yet, from my position in a double sea kayak between two Antarctic islands, I’m witnessing a full-blown penguin dust-up. Above us on the rocks, two gentoo penguins are flippering, slapping and scrapping in a way that looks like it might end badly. Finally, they simmer down, and our kayak group slides forward. We’re winding through a fantasy landscape straight out of a Dr Seuss picture book; an iceberg graveyard, where powder-blue ice shapes, artfully sculpted by the elements, remain trapped until they wither. The sea is glassy, reflecting mountain tops draped in a moving shawl of cloud. We pause for a moment of silence; motionless in a place so surreal that it’s difficult to process. From your first Zodiac ride to jumping into frigid water, Antarctica provides countless pinch-me moments. It’s one of countless pinch-me moments on the 12-day Highlights of Antarctica cruise with HX Expeditions. The journey onboard MS Roald Amundsen had promised spectacular scenery and wildlife delights, but it is the collective mood, the enthusiastic high of the passengers, that fills this trip with joy. Turns out, there’s science in this phenomenon. Psychologists have long known that when people are pushed beyond their comfort zone, physically or mentally, and they succeed, the experience delivers a strong emotional pay-off. There’s the relief of having conquered something difficult, but when the experience exceeds expectations, there is a dopamine-triggered uplift.



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zones, with every aspect of this trip being unfamiliar. Take the crossing of the Drake Passage, the 1000-kilometre-stretch of tumultuous ocean between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula. Many passengers dread it, but after surviving the two-day crossing, there’s a sense of elation. 



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zone. The feeling of awe is ever present, that mind-stretching sense of appreciating something so much bigger than yourself. The shared wonder is the ultimate icebreaker, with strangers frequently turning to each other to talk it through, processing their adventures. Most passengers view their Antarctica expedition as a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and as their bravery grows, they’re bagging as many dopamine-filled additional activities as the expedition team can offer. Choose your vessel: the Roald Amundsen, or a sea kayak? Kayaking is a popular option, and HX Expeditions offers two separate formats, both available to beginners. The first is adventure kayaking, the 1½-half-hour guided format I had experienced with the penguin brawl. This option requires moderate fitness, and the need to wear a rubber-sealed survival dry suit.



New for the 2025/26 season is discovery kayaking, a gentler format using stable, inflatable kayaks. These are easy to climb into, and guests paddle unguided within a delineated zone, watched over by four guides in Zodiacs. As I tootled around with my partner, I relished the chance to slow right down, listening to the sounds of penguins and in the distance, the cracking of glaciers. Kayak guide Lise Drejstel says if guests are concerned about their fitness or confidence on the water, then discovery kayaking is a great option. Gentoo penguins get ready for their close-up. “It’s only one hour, but you can go back after 15 minutes; it’s up to you,” Drejstel says. “You can sit out in the kayak and just look around. Don’t paddle at all, if you like.” Drejstel, in her fifth season guiding in Antarctica, says her favourite part of the job is helping expeditioners unlock awe.



“Guests come in, they start paddling, and then the first penguins come jumping,” she says. “The guests are almost screaming. I can just remember my first time down here, and I was just the same, tears in my eyes.” Those wishing to sleep outside their comfort zone are catered for, too. Conditions permitting, HX offers camping onshore in two-person tents, and in the 2025/26 season introduced the more adventurous “bivvy bag” option, a glorified swag in the snow for one. My trip takes place in late March and due to insufficient snow, neither camping activity was operating. But earlier in the season, I’m told bivvy bag campers had revelled in the solitude of staring at the southern sky, serenaded by the unfamiliar sounds of penguins. A passenger takes the plunge. Another foreign concept for many is the complete lack of a published itinerary. Daily activities are subject to frequent changes, dictated by prevailing winds or iceberg locations. “Our itinerary is deliberately vague,” says expedition leader Torstein Gaustad with a laugh. He says this helps to avoid disappointment, and he hopes that for guests, learning to embrace the unpredictable is liberating. For Gaustad, the flexible nature of Antarctic cruising is part of the thrill.



“My best days are the days when we have to change everything,” he says. “I love that about this job, that we have plan B, C and D.” On our last afternoon in Antarctica, Gaustad springs a plan that no one sees coming. Over the public address system, he announces the option of a “polar plunge”, the chance to voluntarily dip in the frigid ocean, which is bobbing with ice. Questioning my wisdom, I find myself swapping perfectly warm clothing for swimwear, pretty confident there will be only a handful of plungers. But down by the Zodiac dock, there’s an astonishing sight: a queue. The guests, buoyed by their success in every other adventure thus far are egging each other on. Over half of the 360 passengers on board have shown up to blast their comfort zones out of the stratosphere. Now it’s my turn, and as I’m strapped into a life jacket, harness and retrieval rope, the ship’s doctor stands by with his defibrillator. I’m counted down and jump, albeit feebly. The cold compresses the air from my lungs and I surface, blurting out expletives. But then I’m climbing the ladder, accepting a towel, and I’ve done it. Amid whoops and cheers, I high-five the queue of strangers. Tingling from head to toe and grinning, I head straight for the rooftop hot tub.



Related Article Opinion

Savvy traveller The terrifying stretch of sea standing between you and your dream trip The plunge has unleashed a ship-full of dopamine, and even non-plungers are caught up in the buzz. This expedition has seen every one of us stretch our boundaries and live the awe. The shared adventure has made us friends, and mass champagne-toasting is the only thing for it. THE DETAILS CRUISE

The 12-day Highlights of Antarctica cruise includes charter flights from Buenos Aires to Ushuaia, meals, beverages, landings and Zodiac cruising. Additional fees apply for kayaking, camping and snowshoeing. The 2026/27 season departures are from $15,227 a person in a Polar Outside cabin. Suites start at $23,436 a person, which includes meals at the fine-dining restaurant and premium beverages. Some suites feature private hot tubs. FLY

Qantas and Latam Airlines fly to Santiago, Chile, from Sydney and Melbourne (Latam only). Then connect with Latam Airlines or KLM to Buenos Aires, Argentina. A private charter flight to Ushuaia meets the ship. See qantas.com

World.title: How many people recreating on a beach is too many? This Perth council says 30 is the limit.
World.content:
NationalWATrends How many people recreating on a beach is too many? This Perth council says 30 is the limit. Indigo Lemay-Conway August 1, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An early morning beach yoga class could be at risk of having its numbers capped under a new draft trading policy by the Town of Mosman Park. Amy Nicholls runs sunrise yoga sessions at Mosman Beach. Over the past year, her classes have grown from around 20, to as large as 200 people. The largest class Nicholls has taught was 200 people. Amy Nicholls But she could soon have a group limit of 30 people if the Town’s new policy is approved by council later this year. The Trading in Public Places policy is currently out for public comment and aims “to cut red tape and make setting up shop in our public spaces easier, fairer, and more consistent.”



“Do you want to see more coffee carts, pop-up food vendors, fitness classes, and alfresco dining in Mosman Park?” the council website states. “We’re aiming to give traders a clearer pathway, while instilling confidence in our community that public spaces will be activated in a way that’s enjoyable for everyone in Mosman Park. “Before we move forward, we want to hear your thoughts as the draft policy also needs to detail how we can safeguard or minimise impact to residential and public amenity.” As part of the policy, the Town is looking to limit how many people can recreate on public land in a group at one time. “Applications for recreation and fitness classes conducted on public land will be assessed to ensure that the use of shared spaces is managed fairly and safely,” the draft reads.



“To preserve public amenity and prevent the monopolisation of public spaces, permits for trading in public places will only be granted for groups up to a maximum of 30 participants. “This includes, but is not limited to, fitness and recreation classes, dog walking groups, river diving classes, and school sports operators utilising public park equipment.” Groups with 10 or fewer participants would be exempt from requiring a permit. Nicholls – who runs Amy Flows – said the change would drastically reduce the number of participants she could have in her classes. “They are obviously open to having 30 people on the beach, but my classes have grown a significant amount over the last 12 months,” she said.



Amy Nicholls teaching a class at Mosman Beach. @Breemeadow.photo “It’s not that every single class has hundreds of people … It can be anywhere between 50 people, and then my biggest class that I had was over 200 people. But even with that class, I’ve always capped the numbers myself to what I was comfortable teaching in front of.” Nicholls typically arrives at the beach at 5:30am and starts hosting her class at 6am. Following that, the group will typically go for a beach dip and meet up for coffee at the Beach Bus. She says that capping the numbers on her classes would also impact the Beach Bus and is the main reason she wouldn’t want to move the sessions to another beach.



“The whole reason I want to keep it at Mosman Beach is because of the Beach Bus because I work so closely with them, and it’s not just supporting my business - it’s supporting their business,” she said. “Especially those mornings … when it’s a bit cooler. Not everyone’s up and about so early, but bringing a significant amount of people to them in the morning really helps their business too.” The business posted to their social media supporting Nicholls and urged the community to voice their opinions on the draft policy. “Movement improves physical health, mental health and social connection. Putting an arbitrary cap on class sizes makes it harder for people to access affordable outdoor exercise and join a community,” the Beach Bus posted to their Instagram on Monday. “Let’s manage behaviour – not numbers. If a group is respectful, safe and shares the space well, it shouldn’t matter whether there are 12 people or 50. It’s a big beach!”



Nicholls said she was confused why the town decided on 30 people as being the appropriate number for recreational activity groups on public land. “I think it’s definitely not fair because it really limits the community connection. I think I’d understand if it was a really small section of the beach with no parking nearby, but it is obviously a huge beach,” she said. “I think 30 is such a random number too. My classes that I teach now, for example, I can fit more than 30 people in a single room. So I think they really need to look at the understanding of how the communities are managed, rather than capping it at a number.” While she currently hosts yoga sessions at Trigg Beach as well – Nicholls isn’t keen on leaving her Mosman Beach community. Instead, she’s holding out hope the Town will change their mind about putting a limit on group fitness numbers.



Town of Mosman Park Mayor Paul Shaw said the reason for the proposed cap of 30 is because there is an “obligation to ensure our shared public spaces are managed safely and fairly for all users.” “If a community member wishes to run fitness classes with greater than 30 participants, they are welcome to register and apply for an event permit to ensure that the Town can provide guidance around the management of the place and to ensure ongoing amenity is enjoyed by all users of public spaces and places,” Shaw said. “The Town actively encourages community connection, physical activity and local businesses using our public spaces - that’s something we want to see more of, not less. At the same time, we have a responsibility to make sure these shared spaces remain safe, accessible and enjoyable for everyone, not just those attending a class. “This isn’t about limiting community connection or discouraging active, outdoor lifestyles - it’s about making sure one group’s use of a space doesn’t come at the expense of everyone else’s ability to enjoy it. The draft policy is about bringing clarity and consistency to this space.” Public consultation on the draft policy closes on August 6.

World.title: TikTok, a judge and a take-down order after footage was leaked from inside a Perth court
World.content:
Analysis NationalWACourts TikTok, a judge and a take-down order after footage was leaked from inside a Perth court Rebecca Peppiatt August 1, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A British YouTuber accused of raping a fan nearly had his trial aborted after he was filmed sitting inside the dock of a Perth court. It can now be revealed that District Court judge Linda Black had to order the take-down of a TikTok video after she was made aware it was circulating online showing Andres Barrientos sitting in the dock during his trial last week. Yung Filly arrives at Perth District Court. 9News Perth Barrientos, whose stage name is Yung Filly, was found not guilty of raping the 20-year-old fan after a Hillarys gig in September 2024. However, he was also found guilty of two counts of assaulting her - but not of strangling her and not of raping her.



The jury could not come to a decision on three of the 10 charges he was facing. Whether he faces a retrial on those charges will be decided at a later date. Loading Earlier during his trial, his bid for freedom almost came to a grinding halt when Black called an urgent hearing of the start of day six of the trial to issue a stern warning to social media sleuths who were reporting on the case online. “I will not have any hesitation in jailing anyone who breaches my orders,” she barked to everyone sitting in the gallery, issuing a court order that the footage be deleted immediately. She then boarded up the court’s windows and ordered a strict policy that identification had to be shown before entering the court.



She also revealed that online videos and posts had been made revealing the identity of Barrientos’s alleged victim which was in direct violation of the court’s orders. “I am generally nice but I can certainly lose my cool if people don’t follow the rules,” said Black who has a reputation for fairness and fierceness. Yung Filly walks into court. 9News Perth The two-week trial drew attention from around the world. Barrientos boasts over 7 million followers across Instagram, YouTube and TikTok where he describes himself as “an influencer/artist” and thousands of people were commenting on the trial and posting about its progress online. Those posts were, at times, in contradiction with the rules that traditional media have to abide by but policing their content is difficult, especially when they are not present in the court at the time.



It no doubt raises many questions for lawyers and judges who are expected to conduct a fair trial for anyone accused of a crime. But while the heightened publicity almost brought his trial to a grinding halt, it no doubt didn’t do his career any harm. Who is Yung Filly? Barrientos made a name for himself online as a teenager telling stories about his dating experiences. He called them ‘Sunday Stories’. One post about how an ex cheated on him went viral and launched his career. Yung Filly. Zac Goodwin/PA Images via Getty Images



“I woke up, and I was like, ‘2000 views on Snap? I’m going in!’” he said in an interview with GRM Daily. “And then I thought, let me put this on Facebook, see what it does. And I remember getting a million views in like two days, if not a day. No joke.” The move launched his career buoyed by boyish charm, good looks, a London accent and a wicked sense of humour. He began making comedy content online in 2013 and is best-known for making videos with the Beta Squad, which also includes his best friend and popular YouTuber and presenter, Chunkz. Soon after he was asked to host the launch of hugely popular video game FIFA 20 and more mainstream requests have followed, even appearing in popular cooking show The Great British Bake Off and playing for England in the Soccer Aid for Unicef charity match in 2020 where he scored a goal. In 2017 he launched his music career which is described as “blending rap, Afroswing, and Latin influences” earning him chart success with multiple hits such as Hold and Clean Up.



Yung Filly had millions of followers across social media. Bloomberg In 2021 he won the award for Best Media Personality at the Music of Black Origin (MOBO) Awards. Life wasn’t always so easy for Barrientos, though. Born in Columbia, he moved to the UK when he was two years old as a refugee with two siblings and his mum and has spoken publicly about being proud of his roots while being open about how much he and his family struggled financially when he was a child. “I’m most proud of the fact that I was a refugee,” he said in 2020. “I’m proud that I had to struggle. It makes you appreciate all the lit stuff a lot more. I don’t think I really took in how poor we was … it makes me so much more grateful because I’ve lived in the worst of the worst situations.”



He grew up in a religious home in southeast London with a single mum, once saying that “God has my back”. He failed at school and has said that if he didn’t become a YouTube star, he doesn’t know what he would be doing with his life. He has spoken openly about suffering with anxiety and panic attacks, claiming that “being known” is what gives him anxiety. While Barrientos’ wealth is unknown, in October 2024 UK newspaper the Mirror speculated that he was worth between $1million and $2million USD. In a BBC interview posted to TikTok, Barrientos boasted that he took around 25 holidays a year to destinations such as Dubai, Spain, Qatar and Miami and that he owned a $200,000 Mercedes G-Wagon.



His love of fast cars is not surprise given that he was arrested - and later pleaded guilty to - speeding while on bail in Perth. He was caught driving at 158km/h on Roe Highway in High Wycombe, leading to his car being impounded and further charges of reckless driving. He will be sentenced for that charge at a later date.

World.title: This new Club Bay View brings great service, splendid drinks and good snacks to Claremont
World.content:
Review Eating outClaremont This new Club Bay View brings great service, splendid drinks and good snacks to Claremont Max Veenhuyzen August 1, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 3 Swordfish belly skewer (front) with mortadella and octopus skewers. Il Santo 2 / 3 Swordfish belly skewer with capsicum agrodolce. Il Santo 3 / 3 House baked cantucci with Vin Santo. Il Santo Previous Slide Next Slide 14.5 / 20 How we score Il Santo Italian$$$$ Lyndon Waples isn’t the most Italian sounding name in the phone book. Yet, that hasn’t deterred the one-time Print Hall head honcho from running busy Italian eateries in affluent Perth neighbourhoods. (Ciao Il Lido, ciao Canteen Pizza.) His newest interest is Il Santo in Claremont: a slender, wine tunnel of a room on Bay View Terrace that opened in May. Or more accurately reopened.



Nico Lunardi and Sally Lovell. Il Santo Following a makeover led by Adelaide’s Studio Gram, the old Nolita site emerged with a modern, pared-back look sporting just enough bling. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up The calibre of Il Santo’s wine and cocktail offering certainly makes agreeing to “just one more” dangerously easy. Sure, prices are higher than your local bowlo might charge, but so is the quality of what attentive waitstaff are splashing into your glass. Previously at CBD member’s club Lawson Flats, restaurant manager Silvia Gelves leads by engaged, smiley example. She’s ably supported by Sally Lovell and Melanie Watts: career hospitality pros and high-ranking officers in Waples’ organisation. Collectively, they’re a friendly bunch and strike me as hosts that are invested in showing guests a good time. Having given the menu a good shake over multiple visits, I’d say the surest way to achieving good times is by assembling a small table of friends – two or three feels right – and going hard on the small plates.



The grilled skewer contrasting cubes of fatty swordfish belly against a sharp, almost plummy capsicum agrodolce, say. Or the debonair veal carpaccio, spicy with creamed horseradish, jagged spears of mizuna and good olive oil. Bubbly ingots of focaccia are perfect for mopping up plates but play equally nice with the Vegemite-spiked butter they come with. You’ll spy all these snacky, wine bar-style dishes on the top half of Il Santo’s concise menu under the heading of “to start”. Much like an Italian Tim Tam slam, cantucci is often dunked in Vin Santo to soften these hard, rusk-like biscuits. Il Santo You’ll also spy a pork cutlet and steak (a tender, fatcap-off striploin that’s been carefully grilled and sliced thick) among the larger plates here. In lieu of chips or fries, glorious roast potatoes with the perfect ratio of crunch to fluff will be your empty carbohydrate pleasure for today. There is also, naturally, pasta. Here, the kitchen deploys pastas (made at Il Lido) in time-honoured combinations such as linguine vongole and cavatelli in a cream sauce enriched with pebbles of fennel-spiked pork.



While both these pastas were a little off the mark – the clams brought little oceanic flavour to the party; some of my chubby, worm-like cavatelli had clumped together to form a chewy mess – these shortfalls were fast forgotten after inhaling the mafaldine e fagioli - chef Nicola Lunardi’s inspired remake of a pasta soup found in his native Veneto. Starring frilly mafaldine noodles and red borlotti beans (fagioli) bound in an addictive bean broth and blanketed with shaved Parmigianna Regiano, this ugly-delicious jumble is one of the best vegetarian things I’ve eaten all year. It’s also exactly the kind of nourishing, homely food that I’d hope to encounter if I was out dining solo. Mafaldine and fagioli with grilled octopus skewer with chilli gremolata. Il Santo And so we come to the end of the meal where a pert citrus tart and, predictably, tiramisu and cheese await. Consider, too, the cantucci and Vin Santo one-two: a dessert meal deal pairing rusk-like biscuits studded with almonds plus a pour of the caramelly sweet wine that contributed to the restaurant’s name.



Traditionally, eaters softened cantucci by dunking pieces of it into their Vin Santo, a bit like an Italian Tim Tam Slam. Some keep their biscuit almost dry. Others let it soak until it attains a semi-liquid state. How you enjoy your cantucci is, much like Il Santo, entirely up to you. The low-down Atmosphere: a likeable (and loud) suburban Italian wine bar with a focus on service and good snacks Go-to dishes: mafaldine e fagioli ($33), veal carpaccio ($28), swordfish belly skewer ($18) Drinks: a classy cocktail and wine list with personality. Consider the fancy stuff by the glass, but buying by the bottle offers the biggest bang for buck Cost: about $180 for two people, excluding drinks Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal
World.content:
SportCyclingCommonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal Billie Eder August 1, 2026 — 2:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Australia’s cycling team is unhappy but unable to appeal a decision by race officials to disqualify a rider from a bronze medal race over the taping of her shoulders, even though she had them taped when she won gold a day earlier. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who was part of the women’s team that won gold in the team pursuit, was disqualified on Friday from the women’s 4000m individual pursuit for wearing strapping tape under her race suit. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory after the women’s 4000m team pursuit finals. Getty Images The 21-year-old cyclist finished fourth fastest in individual qualifying to book herself a spot in the bronze medal race against Scotland’s Erin Boothman, before officials from world cycling’s governing body, the UCI, disqualified her for a breach of equipment and uniform rules. Those officials deemed that the tape, on Wilson-Haffenden’s shoulders, caused a “morphological change” – a change to the physical shape, outer appearance or internal structure of the body – which is against racing rules.



The official rule says, “clothing and other items or accessories worn by a rider may not modify the morphology of the rider”. It is unclear how and why officials picked up on the taping on Friday and not Thursday, and whether the check of the two Australian athletes was random. The UCI has been contacted for comment and clarification. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden during the individual pursuit. Quinn Rooney The same officials ruled that another Australian, Sophie Edwards, would also be disqualified for having “excessive” padding in her helmet. Both Wilson-Haffenden and Edwards had the same taping and helmet, respectively, when they raced the previous day. No clothing or equipment issues were raised after officials completed inspections on Thursday.



Executive general manager of performance at Aus Cycling, Jesse Korf, said the Australian team was frustrated by the decision to disqualify Wilson-Haffenden. He described the decision as subjective and said Wilson-Haffenden received taping to her shoulders after having discomfort and mobility issues. Australia’s gold medal winning women’s pursuit team. Getty Images “On inspection after the race, the UCI [Union Cycliste Internationale] concluded that the taping of the shoulder constituted, according to them in the rule book, a morphological change, but they weren’t able to articulate what that exactly was because it’s a grey area. You cannot measure what a morphological change is,” Korf said. “They made that conclusion, we looked into it and, being that it’s non-measurable and subjective, unfortunately that conclusion is final, which we’re most certainly not happy with and Felicity is upset, of course.”



Korf said the team was also disappointed in the decision to disqualify Edwards, but she had not qualified for a medal race. The Australian team does not believe there is a risk that the team’s gold medal will be stripped or under review, given both riders passed inspections on the day. Felicity Wilson-Haffenden celebrates victory in the women’s team pursuit. Getty Images “We heard nothing after inspections yesterday,” Korf said. “After races, riders get inspected, there’s always checks, and there was no challenge, no nothing yesterday, so that’s in the clear. “The challenges [today] are from what was faced in the individual pursuits and the conclusions of the commissaires.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist Korf said Australia would seek more clarification on the rules moving forward. “Well, we’ll definitely try to learn more around how the assessment is done so that we can learn and mitigate,” Korf said. New Zealand’s Bryony Boothman has now been promoted to the bronze medal race. Glasgow 2026 has also been contacted for comment.



Before her disqualification, Wilson-Haffenden had said she was looking forward to the bronze medal race despite appearing quite distressed and unwell after qualifying. She needed extra recovery time, was shaky, and needed assistance when leaving the track. “No doubt I’ll be riding tonight. I mean, a 4000m effort takes a lot out of you, and I needed a little longer to recover, but I’ll be all good,” she said. It was only her second individual 4000m pursuit, and said her post-race condition was a result of giving it her all. “I enjoy suffering, so I quite enjoy this race,” she said.

World.title: ‘We came here to win, not to be safe’: Beveridge’s home truths as Docker juggernaut marches on
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We came here to win, not to be safe’: Beveridge’s home truths as Docker juggernaut marches on Steve Barrett August 1, 2026 — 12:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge has denied he deliberately plotted to drag Fremantle into a congested, defensive scrap in the Dockers’ 37-point win on Friday night, 11.12 (78) to 5.11 (41). To most observers, Beveridge and his team appeared to come in with a clear blueprint to turn the game into a stifling, contested battle by setting up in numbers behind the ball to clog Fremantle’s forward half and deny the Dockers the space they thrive on. By Luke Beveridge’s own admission, the Bulldogs “fuelled Fremantle’s game” at Optus Stadium. AFL Photos Frustrated, Fremantle were made to sweat for the best part of three quarters, before turning on the afterburners late to move to an 18-2 record, all but putting a bow on the minor premiership. But Beveridge rejected suggestions he devised the unconventional plan of attack, insisting his side was forced into the scrappy style.



“I had them [extra defenders] back because Fremantle had territory, and we couldn’t get it into our front half – that’s why,” he explained. “We didn’t plan to play like that. “It wasn’t by design that we had saturation in numbers behind the ball. View post on X “We wanted to press up at different times, and we didn’t get our execution right. We came here tonight to win the game, not to be safe and not to eliminate risk.



“But we didn’t execute well enough.” Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects Whether by design or not, the Dogs transformed the first half into a stoppage grind, strangling and sandbagging Fremantle’s transition game, silencing the 53,524-strong crowd and reducing the league’s most potent attacking side to a scrap. But there were fleeting glimpses of the usual Docker brilliance. Luke Jackson soared for a majestic mark over opponent Tim English before converting the game’s opening goal with 23 minutes already elapsed.



Then, in the second quarter, Patrick Voss produced a powerful one-on-two mark over Michael Sellwood and James O’Donnell as the Dockers threatened to break clear. Related Article AFL 2026 Geelong reach settlement with Stengle as Hill departs Collingwood Scores were level at half-time, but there was a sense the Bulldogs were just clinging on, their 14 first-half inside-50s the third-lowest tally on record. It was always going to be a difficult way to win for the Dogs, made even more challenging when their scoring completely dried up after half-time. Josh Treacy and Hayden Young celebrated their 100th games in style, the former booting three goals to break open the stalemate, and the latter curbing the influence of the great Marcus Bontempelli.



Jackson shaded English in the ruck, while unsung backs Karl Worner and Oscar McDonald intercepted with aplomb to strangle the Dogs’ forward line. Josh Treacy is one of the AFL’s most imposing forces up forward. Getty Images The Bulldogs showed there is a formula to keep Fremantle in check for a quarter, two quarters or even three. But eventually the Dockers’ relentless pressure and superior class proved too much. “We had field position on our terms for the majority of the night, and we just persisted really well,” Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir said. “Usually when you get that much supply versus the opposition and that much time in forward half, the dam wall eventually breaks.



“In that last quarter, it did.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Nothing in normal life can prepare you for this surreal voyage
World.content:
InspirationAntarctica Nothing in normal life can prepare you for this surreal voyage Carolyn Beasley August 1, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s difficult to think of penguins as violent. And yet, from my position in a double sea kayak between two Antarctic islands, I’m witnessing a full-blown penguin dust-up. Above us on the rocks, two gentoo penguins are flippering, slapping and scrapping in a way that looks like it might end badly. Finally, they simmer down, and our kayak group slides forward. We’re winding through a fantasy landscape straight out of a Dr Seuss picture book; an iceberg graveyard, where powder-blue ice shapes, artfully sculpted by the elements, remain trapped until they wither. The sea is glassy, reflecting mountain tops draped in a moving shawl of cloud. We pause for a moment of silence; motionless in a place so surreal that it’s difficult to process. From your first Zodiac ride to jumping into frigid water, Antarctica provides countless pinch-me moments. It’s one of countless pinch-me moments on the 12-day Highlights of Antarctica cruise with HX Expeditions. The journey onboard MS Roald Amundsen had promised spectacular scenery and wildlife delights, but it is the collective mood, the enthusiastic high of the passengers, that fills this trip with joy. Turns out, there’s science in this phenomenon. Psychologists have long known that when people are pushed beyond their comfort zone, physically or mentally, and they succeed, the experience delivers a strong emotional pay-off. There’s the relief of having conquered something difficult, but when the experience exceeds expectations, there is a dopamine-triggered uplift.



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zones, with every aspect of this trip being unfamiliar. Take the crossing of the Drake Passage, the 1000-kilometre-stretch of tumultuous ocean between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula. Many passengers dread it, but after surviving the two-day crossing, there’s a sense of elation. 



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zone. The feeling of awe is ever present, that mind-stretching sense of appreciating something so much bigger than yourself. The shared wonder is the ultimate icebreaker, with strangers frequently turning to each other to talk it through, processing their adventures. Most passengers view their Antarctica expedition as a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and as their bravery grows, they’re bagging as many dopamine-filled additional activities as the expedition team can offer. Choose your vessel: the Roald Amundsen, or a sea kayak? Kayaking is a popular option, and HX Expeditions offers two separate formats, both available to beginners. The first is adventure kayaking, the 1½-half-hour guided format I had experienced with the penguin brawl. This option requires moderate fitness, and the need to wear a rubber-sealed survival dry suit.



New for the 2025/26 season is discovery kayaking, a gentler format using stable, inflatable kayaks. These are easy to climb into, and guests paddle unguided within a delineated zone, watched over by four guides in Zodiacs. As I tootled around with my partner, I relished the chance to slow right down, listening to the sounds of penguins and in the distance, the cracking of glaciers. Kayak guide Lise Drejstel says if guests are concerned about their fitness or confidence on the water, then discovery kayaking is a great option. Gentoo penguins get ready for their close-up. “It’s only one hour, but you can go back after 15 minutes; it’s up to you,” Drejstel says. “You can sit out in the kayak and just look around. Don’t paddle at all, if you like.” Drejstel, in her fifth season guiding in Antarctica, says her favourite part of the job is helping expeditioners unlock awe.



“Guests come in, they start paddling, and then the first penguins come jumping,” she says. “The guests are almost screaming. I can just remember my first time down here, and I was just the same, tears in my eyes.” Those wishing to sleep outside their comfort zone are catered for, too. Conditions permitting, HX offers camping onshore in two-person tents, and in the 2025/26 season introduced the more adventurous “bivvy bag” option, a glorified swag in the snow for one. My trip takes place in late March and due to insufficient snow, neither camping activity was operating. But earlier in the season, I’m told bivvy bag campers had revelled in the solitude of staring at the southern sky, serenaded by the unfamiliar sounds of penguins. A passenger takes the plunge. Another foreign concept for many is the complete lack of a published itinerary. Daily activities are subject to frequent changes, dictated by prevailing winds or iceberg locations. “Our itinerary is deliberately vague,” says expedition leader Torstein Gaustad with a laugh. He says this helps to avoid disappointment, and he hopes that for guests, learning to embrace the unpredictable is liberating. For Gaustad, the flexible nature of Antarctic cruising is part of the thrill.



“My best days are the days when we have to change everything,” he says. “I love that about this job, that we have plan B, C and D.” On our last afternoon in Antarctica, Gaustad springs a plan that no one sees coming. Over the public address system, he announces the option of a “polar plunge”, the chance to voluntarily dip in the frigid ocean, which is bobbing with ice. Questioning my wisdom, I find myself swapping perfectly warm clothing for swimwear, pretty confident there will be only a handful of plungers. But down by the Zodiac dock, there’s an astonishing sight: a queue. The guests, buoyed by their success in every other adventure thus far are egging each other on. Over half of the 360 passengers on board have shown up to blast their comfort zones out of the stratosphere. Now it’s my turn, and as I’m strapped into a life jacket, harness and retrieval rope, the ship’s doctor stands by with his defibrillator. I’m counted down and jump, albeit feebly. The cold compresses the air from my lungs and I surface, blurting out expletives. But then I’m climbing the ladder, accepting a towel, and I’ve done it. Amid whoops and cheers, I high-five the queue of strangers. Tingling from head to toe and grinning, I head straight for the rooftop hot tub.



Related Article Opinion

Savvy traveller The terrifying stretch of sea standing between you and your dream trip The plunge has unleashed a ship-full of dopamine, and even non-plungers are caught up in the buzz. This expedition has seen every one of us stretch our boundaries and live the awe. The shared adventure has made us friends, and mass champagne-toasting is the only thing for it. THE DETAILS CRUISE

The 12-day Highlights of Antarctica cruise includes charter flights from Buenos Aires to Ushuaia, meals, beverages, landings and Zodiac cruising. Additional fees apply for kayaking, camping and snowshoeing. The 2026/27 season departures are from $15,227 a person in a Polar Outside cabin. Suites start at $23,436 a person, which includes meals at the fine-dining restaurant and premium beverages. Some suites feature private hot tubs. FLY

Qantas and Latam Airlines fly to Santiago, Chile, from Sydney and Melbourne (Latam only). Then connect with Latam Airlines or KLM to Buenos Aires, Argentina. A private charter flight to Ushuaia meets the ship. See qantas.com

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Para-cyclist Devon Briggs wins gold, sets new record
World.content:
Para-cyclist Devon Briggs has won a gold medal for New Zealand, and set a new Commonwealth Games record in the process.

Briggs has taken first place in the 1km C1-3 time trial final in Glasgow.

Earlier cyclist Ellese Andrews' was taken out of the medal race in the individual sprint.

The Olympic champion was beaten in consecutive races in a best-of-three quarter final against Welsh rider Emma Finucane.

Ellesse Andrews during the Women's Sprint Qualifying at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games. Olly Hassell / SWPix / Photosport

Andrews was also part of the New Zealand sprint team that was bundled out during qualifying on Friday.

Rebecca Petch and Olivia King both were unable to get past the round-of-16 stage in their respective sprints.

On the endurance side, Bryony Botha has been given a second life in the 4000m individual pursuit following the disqualification of two Australian riders, and will now line up for bronze later Saturday morning.

AusCycling executive general manager of performance Jesse Korf addresses media after two of his team were disqualified. RNZ / Adam Burns

Botha initially failed to qualify, placing fifth, as did team-mate Emily Shearman, who finished eighth.

However, officials said Australian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who originally finished fourth, broke protocols due to strapping on her shoulder that "altered her morphology".

Fellow Australian rider Sophie Edwards was also disqualified due to a non-compliant helmet.

Botha will face Scotland's Erin Boothman for bronze from 3.30am NZT.

World.title: Doctors considering weight-loss drugs for detained man to be kept in physical restraints
World.content:
An autistic man who has spent more than 20 years in secure care has become so "obese" his doctors are considering giving him the weight-loss drug Wegovy so physical restraints he has outgrown can again be used on him, the Family Court has heard.

The man, known only as 'J', has been taken on 10 outings in the past year but never been allowed to leave the van transporting him. He has also not seen a psychologist in the last year as she had been on leave, then left her role at Auckland's Mason Clinic where he lived.

A long-awaited Family Court review of whether J should remain detained under the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act began on Friday.

The review was ordered by the Supreme Court in August 2025 after it ruled the previous legal test used to detain J was wrong. It told the Family Court to have another look at his case.

The hearing has been delayed for almost a year due to trouble securing court time and the availability of witnesses.

A specialist assessor told the court the outings were part of efforts to gradually increase J's exposure to, and tolerance of, being in the community, despite him remaining inside the van each time.

"But that does not take away from these experiences. He sees things outside the window," the assessor, a psychiatrist, said.

Clinicians were now considering taking J to a quiet beach and allowing him outside the van for the first time to test how he coped, he said.

"It's hard to know what [his] response will be to that kind of outing, but I think it certainly deserves to be tried."

The court also heard J had begun spending more time outside his private rooms where he lived alone within the Auckland's Mason Clinic to interact with staff and other clients.

While he did not have access to his psychologist for the last year other staff interacted with him in a "psychologically informed manner", the assessor said.

He has recommended J remain in secure care for another three years to give him time to rehabilitate, and for a new home in the community to be found for him.

"I think that's a realistic timeframe."

A February 2026 assessment of J found he continued to make threats and was occasionally violent but some of his behaviours, including an obsession with feet, were not sexual in nature.

The assessor said J had more recently appeared "more cheerful" due to the gradual introduction of "socialisation" activities.

However, he admitted the pace of rehabilitation had been slower than intended due to staff availability.

The court heard J had become severely obese, which meant mechanical restraints could no longer be used on him. This limited the number of staff who felt comfortable accompanying him on outings.

The Mason Clinic was considering treating him with weight-loss drug Wegovy so he could fit restraints again. These restraints were made of soft "leather-like" fabric wrapped around his wrists, attached to a belt, designed to restrict his movement.

Under cross examination by the court-appointed lawyer for J, Andrew Finnie, the assessor said if J was released into the community, he would likely be arrested "in a short space of time" as he was likely to engage in "potentially aggressive...socially embarrassing behaviour".

The lawyer for J's mother, Tony Ellis, argued J's detention was not justified given the original offence of breaking windows would have resulted in only three months' imprisonment. He likened J's detention to being like a "gorilla kept in a cage", saying he was being treated like an animal, not a human being.

Now in his 40s, J has been detained since 2006 after breaking windows in 2004. Repeated assessments have found he was too dangerous to release. For the past five years he has spent almost all his time in seclusion within his "cluster" of two rooms and a bathroom at the Mason Clinic.

World.title: Police officers rescue seal pup wandering through South Auckland suburb
World.content:
Police say a seal pup that was spotted making its way through the South Auckland suburb of Papakura has been taken back to its natural environment.

In a social media post, Counties Manukau police said they received a call from a concerned member of the public and then consulted with the Department of Conservation on the best way to help.

Police consulted DOC about how to help the seal pup. Supplied / Counties Manukau Police

After receiving advice, officers were able to relocate the pup back to a more appropriate place.

"An ex-seal-ent job by everyone involved and a happy ending for this little traveller!" the post said.

World.title: Police officer shot by Tom Phillips returns to work
World.content:
The officer who was shot in the head by Tom Phillips is returning to work.

The officer, who has not been named, was critically injured when Phillips shot him several times last September.

Phillips died shortly after a shootout with another officer, when police were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025, after 1358 days in the bush with his children.

It is understood the officer who was shot underwent numerous surgeries at Waikato Hospital, after being hit in his skull and his right shoulder.

Waikato District Commander Scott Gemmell said he had made positive progress in his recovery and was continuing rehabilitation.

World.title: Weekend weather: Snow warnings and strong wind watches as chilly days ahead
World.content:
The country is set to face a chilly weekend as subantarctic winds move up the country, MetService says.

In the South Island, temperatures will start to drop in the south on Friday morning as the southerly pushes through Otago, and then into Canterbury this afternoon, with colder temperatures expected overnight Friday and Saturday.

MetService has road snowfall warnings in place for South Island mountain passes on Friday and the Desert Road on Saturday, with motorists told to avoid travel.

The mountain passes include Crown Range Road, Lindis Pass, Milford Road, Arthur's, Porters and Lewis Pass.

The Civil Defence said just a few centimetres of snow would make driving dangerous on Desert Road, and said to only do so if necessary.

MetService forecasted snow showers lowering to 800 metres and 1 to 2cm of snow could accumulate about the summit.

Meanwhile, the northern Cook Strait and the North Taranaki Bight have experienced thunderstorms.

Strong wind watches are also in place for parts of the South Island.

Coastal Otago's watch is in place from noon to 10pm on Friday, where southwest winds may approach severe gale in exposed places.

A watch for Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains kicks off from 5pm Friday until 1am Saturday.

The watch for coastal Southland and southern Fiordland kicked in late Thursday and continues until 5pm Friday.

All watches have a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

MetService said subantarctic air was being dragged north by southerly winds - resulting in "bitterly cold conditions".

It would make temperatures feel close to -2C in Invercargill on Friday afternoon "and even colder for higher elevations".

The cold weather would move up to the North Island during Saturday, it said, "with the wind chill cooling things to a feels-like temperature of just 1C in Wellington".

For those running or on the sidelines at the Taupō marathon, meteorologist Braydon While suggested dressing warm.

"Those preparing for the marathon, whether competing or cheering on the sidelines, will want to wrap up warm and bring a cosy jacket in case a few showers manage to sneak over the hills."

Sunday would bring clear skies for most of the country, MetService said, and "widespread frosts".

World.title: Silver Ferns to meet England in Commonwealth Games semi-finals
World.content:
The Silver Ferns will have to beat England in the semi-finals in Glasgow if they are to make their first Commonwealth Games gold medal match since 2014.

England will have their tails up after putting up their best performance in Glasgow by far with a 58-54 win over the fifth-ranked South Africa on Friday morning.

Anticipation was high that South Africa would pull off an upset over the third ranked England Roses in the last pool match of the tournament.

Earlier in the week, the Diamonds posted a 19-goal win over England, before beating South Africa by a 10-goal margin.

With South Africa beating England 2-1 in a series earlier in the year, Pool A was always considered the 'Pool of Death'.

The Silver Ferns topped Pool B earlier in the day after demolishing Trinidad and Tobago 83-23 to make it five straight wins.

Australia went through Pool A unbeaten, and will meet Jamaica in the second semi-final at midnight Saturday evening. The Silver Ferns and England will meet at 8pm Saturday New Zealand time.

The New Zealanders were reduced to 10 players for their final pool match with young defender Catherine Hall awaiting a MRI scan to determine the extent of a knee injury suffered in the previous match against Wales.

Shooter Georgia Heffernan was also left off the team sheet after suffering an ankle knock in the same match but coach Dame Noeline Taurua said Heffernan would be available for selection for the semi-final.

At the 2023 Netball World Cup, the Silver Ferns suffered a massive blow when strike shooter Grace Nweke suffered a tournament ending injury in pool play. The Ferns finished outside of the medals in fourth.

Taurua said selectors picked a versatile squad.

"We're always looking at the depth and making sure that if an injury happens or people can't take the court, we've already got the depth and we knew that in each position we've got three deep," Taurua said.

"The positive is that we're in towards the business end. We're not at the beginning, so we've got fresh legs and that's why those combinations and the changes that we've made earlier in the tournament, we've got something in our back pocket."

The 10 players were rotated throughout the match as New Zealand went on to post their highest score and biggest winning margin in 24 outings against a poor Trinidad & Tobago.

The Silver Ferns went through pool play unbeaten, with earlier wins over Scotland, Jamaica, Uganda, and Wales.

The Proteas boast one of the best shooters in the world in Elmeré van der Berg, who scored the most goals in her debut season in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition this year.

South Africa came out strong to win the first quarter 17-11 but a defensive change for England saw them mount a fight-back in the second spell.

Coming on at goal keep Halimat Adio applied all kinds of pressure on van der Berg and put doubt into the feeders minds.

At half-time, South Africa held a slim 29-28 goal lead.

South Africa lost their starting wing attack to a head knock in the third quarter, which disrupted the Proteas attacking end.

England ramped up their efforts in the third quarter, to lead by four going into the final turn.

Liv Tchine and Lois Pearson combined brilliantly in the England shooting end.

Pearson has stepped up brilliantly into the goal attack position, with the England Roses missing the experienced Helen Housby through injury.

The Roses also lost impressive defender Jaz Brown in the lead-up to the event to injury but Adio's efforts against South Africa show what she is capable of.

The Silver Ferns and England have played out some tight matches in recent years.

England beat New Zealand on their way to finishing runners up at the 2023 World Cup to Australia.

World.title: El Niño could bring a 'highly unusual warm' spring
World.content:
A scientist says El Niño could bring an 'highly unusual warm' spring to New Zealand.

El Niño was officially declared at the start of July and could strongly influence the upcoming seasons.

Earth Sciences New Zealand's chief scientist Chris Brandolino said they expect more profound and more noticeable weather conditions beyond 1 September.

"We're expecting to see more westerly pipe winds, so that could be maybe northwest or southwest or somewhere in between," he told RNZ.

"We're expecting it to become more persistent, more regular, and more intense with time."

Rainfall for lower South Islands, dry spells for North

He said that did favour increased rainfall for the western and lower part of the South Island.

Meanwhile, Brandolino said the upper North Island and many other parts of the country were at risk of dryness.

He said areas such as Northland, the Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Waikato, Auckland would most likely receive below normal rainfall.

"In terms of temperatures over the next three months, we think in spite of a pretty cold start to the August month, there will be some pretty chilly mornings over the next, probably four to nine days, the first week of August roughly," Brandolino said.

"But that won't be a theme, we think, when we look at the three-month period as a collective, as in its totality. We think temperatures are probably going to end up being somewhere between the average or even above average category for the next three months."

Brandolino said the hottest temperature recorded in New Zealand was 42.4 degrees in 1973.

He said that was during a "super El Niño", which is what we are experiencing now.

"El Niño is expected to become very strong, or so-called super El Niño in intensity. So, I'm not predicting a new national record, don't get me wrong, that's not my prediction," Brandolino said.

"But I'm just sort of making the linkage that when we have these westerly winds and we have El Niño, because of these westerly winds, that does cause Australia to go through these hum spells, or at least increased risk of these hot spells of weather or heat waves.

"When our air or our wind does come from Australia, that will bring it into New Zealand, that will happen."

Weather events harder to predict

Brandolino said there would be an increase in spiky temperatures.

He said that could see periods of one to three days of "highly unusually warm" temperatures for September, October and beyond.

"That's followed up by perhaps a big sharp downturn in temperature. So, big variability, roller coaster type weather.

"But when our winds align, so that it's kind of plugging air from Australia, and if their air is warm, we're going to get that warm air."

Brandolino said the odds particularly favoured spells of unusually warm temperatures for eastern areas of both islands.

Whether or not that translates into a record or not, we'll have to wait and see, but it certainly loads the dice for those outcomes, he said.

He said climate change was making it harder to use historical weather events to predict the future.

"Ordinarily we'd like to say we know the average outcome of El Niño, but no El Niño is average," Brandolino said.

"So, we know the average outcome and when you throw in climate change, that does tend to underscore that statement.

World.title: 'We're not going to the finals': Storm set for 16-year first after loss
World.content:
Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy has conceded his side will not be playing finals in 2026, with the club set to miss out for just the fourth time in its history.

The Storm entered the round 22 clash needing to win all five of their remaining games to finish the season on 32 points, which has been needed to make two of the past three finals series.

Missing captain Harry Grant, five-eighth Cameron Munster, and halfback Jahrome Hughes ruled out 90 minutes before kick-off, the Storm threatened a famous upset win when they led 22-16 early in the second half.

But the Bulldogs rallied with the final four tries of the match to record a sixth win in their last seven matches, and leapfrog North Queensland into the NRL top-eight.

The loss ends Melbourne's realistic chance of making the top eight, but Bellamy said he will not be accepting a drop in standards during the final month of the home and away season.

Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy (left) says his side will not be playing finals in 2026. (NRL)

"If anyone wants to go through the motions, if I see that at training and feel that at training, they won't be playing first grade," he said on Friday.

"At the end of the day, every game is important. It's not quite as important as it has been the last few years because we're not going to the finals now.

"But we're out there to play for each other and play for our fans."

The Storm have only missed finals three times since their inaugural season in 1998. The Victorian club missed finals in 2001 and 2002, the two seasons prior to Craig Bellamy becoming head coach.

Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years The Roosters have scored the third-most points ever seen in Australian rugby league first grade match and beaten the clock against a hapless North Queensland side.

The only time the Storm have not made finals under Bellamy was in 2010, when the club was not allowed to earn premiership points as punishment for salary cap breaches which led to the stripping of the 2007 and 2009 premierships.

The Storm, who have lost the previous two grand finals, have been one of the league's most injury-affected teams in 2026.

Several players have made their NRL debuts this year for the Storm, including playmakers Hayden Watson and Jai Bowden on Friday night.

Bellamy, who is contracted until the end of the 2028 season, said the tough results the club is going through now will hopefully be worth it in coming seasons.

"We haven't got a lot of that experience playing at the moment, with these guys making their debuts or it's their third or fourth game," Bellamy said.

"But next year and the year after, that experience will be really handy for us.

"It's just hard to see past the results at the moment of our games."

Earlier, the Dolphins consolidated fifth place on the NRL ladder with a nervous 28-22 win over the last-placed St George Illawarra Dragons.
